19-
20---  ## Behavioral Equivaleence
21-
22---  In an earlier chapter, we investigated the correctness of a very simple
23---  program transformation: the `optimize0plus` function. The programming
24---  language we were considering was the first version of the language of
25---  arithmetic expressions -- with no variables -- so in that setting it
26---  was very easy to define what it means for a program transformation to
27---  be correct: it should always yield a program that evaluates to the same
28---  number as the original.
29-
30---  To talk about the correctness of program transformations for the full
31---  Imp language -- in particular, assignment -- we need to consider the
32---  role of mutable state and develop a more sophisticated notion of
33---  correctness, which we'll call *behavioral equivalence*.
34-
35---  For example:
36-
37---  - `X + 2` is behaviorally equivalent to `1 + X + 1`
38---  - `X - X` is behaviorally equivalent to `0`
39---  - `(X - 1) + 1` is *not* behaviorally equivalent to `X`
40-
41---  ### Definitions
42-
43---  For `aexp`s and `bexp`s with variables, the definition we want is
44---  clear: Two `aexp`s or `bexp`s are "behaviorally equivalent" if they
45---  evaluate to the same result in every state.
46-
47-def Aexp.Equiv (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : Prop :=
48-  ∀ (st : State),
49-    a₁.eval st = a₂.eval st
50-
51-theorem Aexp.equiv_def {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} :
52-    a₁.Equiv a₂ ↔ ∀ (st : State), a₁.eval st = a₂.eval st := by rfl
53-
54-def Bexp.Equiv (b₁ b₂ : Bexp) : Prop :=
55-  ∀ (st : State),
56-    b₁.eval st = b₂.eval st
57-
58-theorem Bexp.equiv_def {b₁ b₂ : Bexp} :
59-    b₁.Equiv b₂ ↔ ∀ (st : State), b₁.eval st = b₂.eval st := by rfl
60-
61---  Here are some simple examples of equivalences of arithmetic and boolean
62---  expressions.
63-
64-example : Aexp.Equiv
65-    (aexp { X - X })
66-    (aexp { 0 }) := by
67-  rw [Aexp.equiv_def]
68-  intro st
69-  simp
70-
71-example : Bexp.Equiv
72-    (bexp { X - X = 0 })
73-    (bexp { true }) := by
74-  rw [Bexp.equiv_def]
75-  intro st
76-  simp
77-
78---  For commands, the situation is a little more subtle. We can't simply
79---  say "two commands are behaviorally equivalent if they evaluate to the
80---  same ending state whenever they are started in the same initial state,"
81---  because some commands, when run in some starting states, don't
82---  terminate in any final state at all!
83-
84---  What we need instead is this: two commands are behaviorally equivalent
85---  if, for any given starting state, they either (1) both diverge or else
86---  (2) both terminate in the same final state. A compact way to express
87---  this is "if the first one terminates in a particular state then so does
88---  the second, and vice versa."
89-
90-def Com.Equiv (c₁ c₂ : Com) : Prop :=
91-    ∀ {st st' : State},
92-      (st =[ c₁ ]=> st') ↔ (st =[ c₂ ]=> st')
93-
94-theorem Com.equiv_def {c₁ c₂ : Com} : c₁.Equiv c₂ ↔
95-    ∀ {st st' : State}, (st =[ c₁ ]=> st') ↔ (st =[ c₂ ]=> st') := by rfl
96-
97---  ### Simple Examples
98-

101---  For examples of command equivalence, let's start by looking at a
102---  trivial equivalence involving `skip`.
103-
104-theorem skip_left {c : Com} : (imp { skip; ~c }).Equiv c := by
105-  rw [equiv_def]
106-  intro st st''
107-  constructor
108-  · intro h
109-    inversion h with
110-    | seq st' h1 h2 =>
111-      inversion h1
112-      exact h2
113-  · intro h
114-    exact EvalR.seq EvalR.skip h

119---  equivalent program.
120-
121-theorem skip_right {c : Com} : (imp { ~c; skip }).Equiv c := by
122-  rw [equiv_def]
123-  intro st st''
124-  constructor
125-  · intro h
126-    inversion h with
127-    | seq st' h1 h2 =>
128-      inversion h2
129-      exact h1
130-  · intro h
131-    exact EvalR.seq h EvalR.skip

133---  Similarly, here is a simple equivalence that optimises `if` commands.
134-
135-theorem if_true_simple {c₁ c₂ : Com} : (imp {if (true) {~c₁} else {~c₂}}).Equiv c₁ := by
136-  rw [equiv_def]
137-  intro st st'
138-  constructor
139-  · intro h
140-    inversion h with
141-    | ifTrue hb hc => exact hc
142-    | ifFalse hb hc => simp at hb
143-  · intro h
144-    apply EvalR.ifTrue _ h
145-    simp
146-
147---  Of course, no programmer would write a conditional whose condition is
148---  literally `true`. (At least, no human programmer -- compilers and macro
149---  preprocessors do this sort of thing internally all the time!) But they
150---  might write one whose condition is *equivalent* to true:
151-
152---  Note to developers (Sati @satiscugcat):
153---      The to_verso script seems to use `\[\]` blocks, but these seem to
154---      cause problems with the tilde. Currently skipping them and just
155---      using backticks.
156-
157---  *Theorem*: If `b` is equivalent to `true`, then
158---  `if (~b) {~c₁}
159---  else {~c₂}` is equivalent to `c₁`. *Proof*:
160-
161---  - (`->`) We must show, for all `st` and `st'`, that if
162---    `st =[ imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}} ]=> st'` then
163---    `st =[ c₁ ]=> st'`.
164-
165---    Proceed by cases on the rules that could possibly have been used to
166---    show `st =[ imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}} ]=> st'`, namely
167---    `Com.EvalR.ifTrue` and `Com.EvalR.ifFalse`.
168-
169---    - Suppose the final rule in the derivation of
170---      `st =[ imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}} ]=> st'` was
171---      `Com.EvalR.ifTrue`. We then have, by the premises of
172---      `Com.EvalR.ifTrue`, that `st =[ c₁ ]=> st'`. This is exactly what
173---      we set out to prove.
174-
175---    - On the other hand, suppose the final rule in the derivation of
176---      `st =[ imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}} ]=> st'` was
177---      `Com.EvalR.ifFalse`. We then know that `b.eval st = false` and
178---      `st =[ c₂ ]=> st'`.
179-
180---      Recall that `b` is equivalent to `true`, i.e., forall `st`,
181---      `b.eval st = (bexp {true}).eval st`. In particular, this means that
182---      `b.eval st = true`, since `(bexp {true}).eval st = true`. But this
183---      is a contradiction, since `Com.EvalR.ifFalse` requires that
184---      `b.eval st = false`. Thus, the final rule could not have been
185---      `Com.EvalR.ifFalse`.
186-
187---  - (`<-`) We must show, for all `st` and `st'`, that if
188---    `st =[ c₁ ]=> st'` then
189---    `st =[ imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}} ]=> st'`.
190-
191---    Since `b` is equivalent to `true`, we know that `b.eval st` =
192---    `(bexp {true}).eval st = true` = `true`. Together with the assumption
193---    that `st =[ c₁ ]=> st'`, we can apply `Com.EvalR.ifTrue` to derive
194---    `st =[ imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}} ]=> st'`.
195-
196---  Here is the formal version of this proof:
197-
198-theorem if_true {b : Bexp} {c₁ c₂ : Com} (hb : b.Equiv (bexp {true})) :
199-    (imp {if (~b) {~c₁} else {~c₂}}).Equiv c₁ := by
200-  rw [equiv_def]
201-  rw [Bexp.equiv_def] at hb
202-  intro st st'
203-  constructor
204-  · intro h
205-    inversion h with
206-    | ifTrue hb' hc =>
207-      exact hc
208-    | ifFalse hb' hc =>
209-      rw [hb] at hb'
210-      simp at hb'
211-  · intro h
212-    apply EvalR.ifTrue _ h
213-    rw [hb]
214-    simp

264---  For `while` loops, we can give a similar pair of theorems. A loop whose
265---  guard is equivalent to `false` is equivalent to `skip`, while a loop
266---  whose guard is equivalent to `true` is equivalent to
267---  `while (true) {skip;} end` (or any other non-terminating program).
268-
269---  The first of these facts is easy.
270-
271-theorem while_false_equiv {b : Bexp} {c : Com} (hb : b.Equiv (bexp {false})) :
272-    (imp {while (~b) {~c}}).Equiv
273-    (imp {skip}) := by
274-  rw [equiv_def]
275-  rw [Bexp.equiv_def] at hb
276-  intro st st''
277-  constructor
278-  · intro h
279-    inversion h with
280-    | whileFalse => exact EvalR.skip
281-    | whileTrue st' hb' hc hloop =>
282-      simp [hb] at hb'
283-  · intro h
284-    inversion h
285-    apply EvalR.whileFalse
286-    simp [hb]

288---  ### Exercise (2 stars): while_false_informal (Advanced, manually graded) ⭐⭐
289-
290---  Write an informal proof of `while_false_equiv`.
291-
292---  To prove the second fact, we need an auxiliary lemma stating that
293---  `while` loops whose guards are equivalent to `true` never terminate.
294-
295---  *Lemma*: If `b` is equivalent to `true`, then it cannot be the case
296---  that `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'`.
297-
298---  *Proof*: Suppose that `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'`. We show, by
299---  induction on a derivation of `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'`, that this
300---  assumption leads to a contradiction. The only two cases to consider are
301---  `Com.EvalR.whileFalse` and `Com.EvalR.whileTrue`; the others are
302---  contradictory.
303-
304---  - Suppose `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'` is proved using rule
305---    `Com.EvalR.whileFalse`. Then by assumption `b.eval st = false`. But
306---    this contradicts the assumption that `b` is equivalent to `true`.
307-
308---  - Suppose `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'` is proved using rule
309---    `Com.EvalR.whileTrue`. We must have:
310-
311---    1. `b.eval st = true`, and
312-
313---    2. there is some `st₀` such that `st =[ c ] => st₀` and
314---       `st₀ =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'`.
315-
316---    3. Also, we are given an induction hypothesis saying that
317---       `st₀ =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'` leads to a contradiction,
318-
319---    We obtain a contradiction by 2 and 3.
320-
321-theorem while_true_nonterm {b : Bexp} {c : Com} {st st' : State} (hb : b.Equiv (bexp {true})) :
322-    ¬ st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st' := by
323-  intro contra
324-  generalize heq : (imp {while (~b) {~c}}) = com at contra
325-  induction contra with
326-  | @whileFalse b' s0 c0 hb' =>
327-    injection heq with hbeq hceq
328-    subst hbeq
329-    rw [Bexp.equiv_def] at hb
330-    simp [hb] at hb'
331-  | @whileTrue s0 s0' s0'' b' c0 hb' hc' hwhile ih1 ih2 =>
332-    exact ih2 heq
333-  | skip | asgn | seq | ifTrue | ifFalse =>
334-    contradiction -- heq says that different commands are equal
335-

342---  Prove the following theorem. *Hint*: You'll want to use

345-theorem while_true {b : Bexp} {c : Com} (hb : b.Equiv (bexp {true})) :
346-    (imp {while (~b) {~c}}).Equiv
347-    (imp {while (true) {skip}}) := by
348-  rw [equiv_def]
349-  intro st st'
350-  constructor
351-  · intro h
352-    exfalso
353-    exact while_true_nonterm hb h

355-    exfalso
356-    apply while_true_nonterm _ h
357-    rw [Bexp.equiv_def]
358-    intro
359-    rfl

361---  A more interesting fact about `while` commands is that any number of
362---  copies of the body can be "unrolled" without changing meaning.
363-
364---  Loop unrolling is an important transformation in any real compiler, so
365---  its correctness is of more than just academic interest!
366-
367-theorem loop_unrolling {b : Bexp} {c : Com} :
368-    (imp {while (~b) {~c}}).Equiv
369-    (imp {
370-      if (~b) {~c} else {skip};
371-      while (~b) {~c}
372-    }) := by
373-  rw [equiv_def]
374-  intro st st'
375-  constructor
376-  · intro h
377-    inversion h with
378-    | whileFalse hb =>
379-      apply EvalR.seq (st' := st)
380-      · exact EvalR.ifFalse hb EvalR.skip
381-      · exact EvalR.whileFalse hb
382-    | whileTrue stmid hb hc hloop =>
383-      apply EvalR.seq _ hloop
384-      exact EvalR.ifTrue hb hc
385-  · intro h
386-    inversion h with
387-    | seq stmid h1 h2 =>
388-      inversion h1 with
389-      | ifTrue hb hc =>
390-        exact EvalR.whileTrue hb hc h2
391-      | ifFalse hb hc =>
392-        inversion hc
393-        exact h2

448---  ## Properties of Behavior Equivalence
449-
450---  We next consider some fundamental properties of program equivalence.
451-
452---  ### Behavioral Equivalence is an Equivalence
453-
454---  First, let's verify that the equivalences on `Aexp`s, `Bexp`s, and
455---  `Com`s really are *equivalences* -- ie, that they are reflexive,
456---  symmetric, and transitive. These proofs are all easy.
457-
458-end Com
459-
460-theorem Aexp.equiv_refl (a : Aexp) : a.Equiv a := by
461-  rw [equiv_def]
462-  intro st
463-  rfl
464-
465-theorem Aexp.equiv_symm {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} (h : a₁.Equiv a₂) : a₂.Equiv a₁ := by
466-  rw [equiv_def] at h ⊢
467-  intro st
468-  rw [h]
469-

471-    a₁.Equiv a₃ := by
472-  rw [equiv_def] at h₁ h₂ ⊢
473-  intro st
474-  rw [h₁, h₂]
475-

479-  rfl

508---  ### Behavioral Equivalence is a Congruence
509-
510---  Less obviously, behavioral equivalence is also a *congruence*. That is,
511---  the equivalence of two subprograms implies the equivalence of the
512---  larger programs in which they are embedded:
513-
514---  aequiv a a' ------------------------- cequiv (x := a) (x := a')
515-
516---  cequiv c1 c1' cequiv c2 c2' -------------------------- cequiv (c1;c2)
517---  (c1';c2')
518-
519---  ... and so on for the other forms of commands.
520-
521---  (Note that we are using the inference rule notation here not as part of
522---  an inductive definition, but simply to write down some valid
523---  implications in a readable format. We prove these implications below.)
524-
525---  We will see a concrete example of why these congruence properties are
526---  important in the following section (in the proof of
527---  `fold_constants_com_sound`), but the main idea is that they allow us to
528---  replace a small part of a large program with an equivalent small part
529---  and know that the whole large programs are equivalent *without* doing
530---  an explicit proof about the parts that didn't change -- i.e., the
531---  "proof burden" of a small change to a large program is proportional to
532---  the size of the change, not the program!
533-
534-theorem Com.congruence.asgn {x : Ident} {a a' : Aexp} (ha : a.Equiv a') :
535-    (imp {x := ~a}).Equiv
536-    (imp {x := ~a'}) := by
537-  rw [equiv_def]
538-  intro st st'
539-  constructor <;>
540-  · intro h
541-    inversion h with
542-    | asgn n h =>
543-      subst h
544-      apply Com.EvalR.asgn
545-      rw [Aexp.equiv_def] at ha
546-      rw [ha]
547-
548---  The congruence property for loops is a little more interesting, since
549---  it requires induction.
550-
551---  *Theorem*: Equivalence is a congruence for `while` -- that is, if `b`
552---  is equivalent to `b'` and `c` is equivalent to `c'`, then
553---  `while (~b) {~c}` is equivalent to `while (~b') {~c'}`.
554-
555---  *Proof*: Suppose `b` is equivalent to `b'` and `c` is equivalent to
556---  `c'`. We must show, for every `st` and `st'`, that
557---  `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'` iff `st = while (~b') {~c'}
558---  ]=> st'`.
559---  We consider the two directions separately.
560-
561---  - (`->`) We show that `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'` implies
562---    `st =[ while (~b') {~c'} ]=> st'`, by induction on a derivation of
563---    `st =[ while (~b) {~c} ]=> st'`. The only nontrivial cases are when
564---    the final rule in the derivation is `Com.EvalR.whileFalse` or
565---    `Com.EvalR.whileTrue`.
566-
567---    - `Com.EvalR.whileFalse`: In this case, the form of the rule gives us
568---      `beval st b = false` and `st = st'`. But then, since `b` and `b'`
569---      are equivalent, we have `beval st b' =false`, and
570---      `Com.EvalR.whileFalse` applies, giving us
571---      `st =[ while (~b') {~c'} ]=> st'`, as required.
572-
573---    - `Com.EvalR.whileTrue`: The form of the rule now gives us
574---      `beval st b = true`, with `st =[ c ]=> st'0` and
575---      `st'0 =[ while {~b} {~c} ]=> st'` for some state `st'0`, with the
576---      induction hypothesis `st'0 =[ while (~b') {~c'} ]=> st'`.
577-
578---      Since `c` and `c'` are equivalent, we know that `st =[ c']=> st'0`.
579---      And since `b` and `b'` are equivalent, we have
580---      `beval st b' = true`. Now `Com.EvalR.whileTrue` applies, giving us
581---      `st =[ while (~b') {~c'} ]=> st'`, as required.
582-
583---  - (`<-`) Similar.

55-
56---  In an earlier chapter, we began applying the mathematical tools
57---  developed in the first part of the course to studying the theory of a
58---  small programming language, Imp.
59-
60---  - We defined a type of *abstract syntax trees* for Imp, together with
61---    an *evaluation relation* (a partial function on states) that
62---    specifies the *operational semantics* of programs.
63-
64---    The language we defined, though small, captures some of the key
65---    features of full-blown languages like C, C++, and Java, including the
66---    fundamental notion of mutable state and some common control
67---    structures.
68-
69---  - We proved a number of *metatheoretic properties* -- "meta" in the
70---    sense that they are properties of the language as a whole, rather
71---    than of particular programs in the language. These included:
72-
73---    - determinism of evaluation
74-
75---    - equivalence of some different ways of writing down the definitions
76---      (e.g., functional and relational definitions of arithmetic
77---      expression evaluation)
78-
79---    - guaranteed termination of certain classes of programs
80-
81---    - correctness (in the sense of preserving meaning) of a number of
82---      useful program transformations
83-
84---    - behavioral equivalence of programs (in the Equiv chapter).
85-
86---  If we stopped here, we would already have something useful: a set of
87---  tools for defining and discussing programming languages and language
88---  features that are mathematically precise, flexible, and easy to work
89---  with, applied to a set of key properties. All of these properties are
90---  things that language designers, compiler writers, and users might care
91---  about knowing. Indeed, many of them are so fundamental to our
92---  understanding of the programming languages we deal with that we might
93---  not consciously recognize them as "theorems." But properties that seem
94---  intuitively obvious can sometimes be quite subtle (sometimes also
95---  subtly wrong!).
96-
97---  In another volume of this series (*Type Systems*), we expand upon the
98---  theme of metatheoretic properties of whole languages when we discuss
99---  *types* and *type soundness*. In this chapter, though, we turn to a
100---  different set of issues.
101-
102---  Our goal in this chapter is to develop the tools to work through some
103---  simple examples of *program verification* -- i.e., to use the precise
104---  definition of Imp to prove formally that particular programs satisfy
105---  particular specifications of their behavior.
106-
107---  We'll develop a reasoning system called *Floyd-Hoare Logic* -- often
108---  shortened to just *Hoare Logic* -- in which each of the syntactic
109---  constructs of Imp is equipped with a generic "proof rule" that can be
110---  used to reason compositionally about the correctness of programs
111---  involving this construct.
112-
113---  Hoare Logic originated in the 1960s, and it continues to be the subject
114---  of intensive research right up to the present day. It lies at the core
115---  of a multitude of tools that are being used in academia and industry to
116---  specify and verify real software systems.
117-
118---  Hoare Logic combines two beautiful ideas: a natural way of writing down
119---  *specifications* of programs, and a *structured proof technique* for
120---  proving that programs are correct with respect to such specifications
121---  -- where by "structured" we mean that the structure of proofs directly
122---  mirrors the structure of the programs that they are about.
123-
124---  Note to developers:
125---      `HIDE: MRC'20: The terse version used to start with just an outline of
126---      what we've done and of this chapter, but it never mentioned Hoare logic!
127---      The text above seems like a better intro.
128---
129---      MRC'20: this is the former terse intro.
130---
131---       What we've done so far:
132---
133---       - Formalized Imp
134---            - identifiers and states
135---            - abstract syntax trees
136---            - evaluation functions (for [aexp]s and [bexp]s)
137---            - evaluation relation (for commands)
138---
139---       - Proved some _metatheoretic_ properties
140---           - determinism of evaluation
141---           - equivalence of some different ways of writing down the
142---             definitions (e.g., functional and relational definitions of
143---             arithmetic expression evaluation)
144---           - guaranteed termination of certain classes of programs
145---           - meaning-preservation of some program transformations
146---           - behavioral equivalence of programs ([Equiv])
147---
148---       We've dealt with a few sorts of properties of Imp programs:
149---         - Termination
150---         - Nontermination
151---         - Equivalence
152---
153---       Topic:
154---         - A systematic method for reasoning about the _functional
155---           correctness_ of programs in Imp
156---
157---       Goals:
158---         - a natural notation for _program specifications_ and
159---         - a _compositional_ proof technique for program correctness
160---
161---       Plan:
162---         - specifications (assertions / Hoare triples)
163---         - proof rules
164---         - loop invariants
165---         - decorated programs
166---         - examples`

168---  ## Assertions
169-
170---  An *assertion* is a logical claim about the state of a program's memory
171---  -- formally, a predicate of `State`s.
172-
173-open scoped Com MyGetElem
174-
175-abbrev Assertion := State → Prop
176-
177---  Note to developers:
178---      HIDE: MRC'20: pulled up these examples from the quiz/optional
179---      exercise so that there would be some modeling of the kinds of
180---      answers we expect.
181-
182---  For example,
183-
184---  - `fun st => st[X] = 3` holds for states `st` in which value of `X` is
185---    `3`,
186-
187---  - `fun st => True` hold for all states, and
188-
189---  - `fun st => False` holds for no states.
190-
191---  _Quiz:_
192-
193---  Paraphrase the following assertions in English (i.e., say which states
194---  satisfy them)
195-
196---  (A) `fun st => st[X] ≤ st[Y]`
197-
198---  (B) `fun st => st[X] = 3 ∨ st[X] ≤ st[Y]`
199-
200---  (C)
201---  `fun st => st[Z] * st[Z] ≤ st[X] ∧ ¬ ((st[Z] + 1) * (st[Z] + 1) ≤ st[X])`
202-
203---  ### Exercise (1 star): assertions (Optional) ⭐
204-
205---  Paraphrase the following assertions in English (or your favorite
206---  natural language).

208-namespace ExAssertions
209-def assertion1 : Assertion := fun st => st[X] ≤ st[Y]
210-def assertion2 : Assertion :=
211-  fun st => st[X] = 3 ∨ st[X] ≤ st[Y]
212-def assertion3 : Assertion :=
213-  fun st => st[Z] * st[Z] ≤ st[X] ∧
214-            ¬ ((st[Z] + 1) * (st[Z] + 1) ≤ st[X])
215-def assertion4 : Assertion :=
216-  fun st => st[Z] = max st[X] st[Y]
217-
218---  1. The value of X is less or equal than the value of Y.
219---  2. The value of X is 3 or is less or equal than the value of Y.
220---  3. The value of Z is the integer square root of X.
221---  4. The value of Z is the greater of the values of X and Y
222-
223-end ExAssertions

225---  ### Notations for Assertions
226-
227---  This way of writing assertions can be a little bit heavy, for two
228---  reasons: (1) every single assertion that we ever write is going to
229---  begin with `fun st => `; and (2) this state `st` is the only one that
230---  we ever use to look up variables in assertions (we will almost never
231---  need to talk about two different memory states at the same time). For
232---  discussing examples informally, we'll adopt some simplifying
233---  conventions: we'll drop the initial `fun st =>`, and we'll write just
234---  `X` to mean `st[X]`. Thus, instead of writing
235-
236---    fun st => st[X] = m
237-
238---  we'll write just
239-
240---    {{ X = m }}.
241-
242---  Here the "doubly curly" braces `{{` and `}}` delimit the scope of an
243---  assertion. We'll see more examples below.
244-
245---  This example also illustrates a convention that we'll use throughout
246---  the Hoare Logic chapters: in informal assertions, capital letters like
247---  `X`, `Y`, and `Z` are Imp variables, while lowercase letters like `x`,
248---  `y`, `m`, and `n` are ordinary Lean variables (of type `Nat`). This is
249---  why, when translating from informal to formal, we replace `X` with
250---  `st[X]` but leave `m` alone.
251-

281---  magic, using coercions and a custom grammar, much as we did with the

283---  `Aexp`s, numbers, and `Prop`s into `Assertion`s when they appear
284---  between the `{{ _ }}` brackets, or when Lean knows that the type of an
285---  expression is `Assertion`.

319---      There is now a custom entry [assn] for defining the syntax of
320---      assertions.  Like the delimiters <{ }> used for Imp programs,
321---      we now also have {{ }} delimiters for use with Assertions.
322---

338-@[term_elab assn]
339-def assnElab : TermElab := fun stx _type? => do
340-  match stx with
341-  | `(assn($st; $t:term)) =>
342-    let t ← elabTerm t none
343-    let ty ← Meta.inferType t
344-    -- if (← Meta.isDefEq ty (mkConst ``_root_.Ident)) then -- this incorrectly assigns metavariables
345-    if (ty.constName == ``_root_.Ident) then
346-      return mkApp6 (mkConst ``_root_.MyGetElem.getElem)
347-        (mkApp2 (mkConst ``TotalMap) (mkConst ``String) (mkConst ``Nat))
348-        (mkConst ``String)
349-        (mkConst ``Nat)
350-        (← Meta.synthInstance <| mkApp3 (mkConst ``_root_.MyGetElem)
351-          (mkApp2 (mkConst ``TotalMap) (mkConst ``String) (mkConst ``Nat))
352-          (mkConst ``String)
353-          (mkConst ``Nat))
354-        (← elabTerm st none) t
355-    if (ty.constName == ``_root_.Aexp) then -- Detect an embedded `Aexp` and turn it into `Aexp.eval st t`
356-      return (mkApp2 (mkConst ``Aexp.eval) (← elabTerm st none) t)
357-    else if (ty.constName == ``_root_.Bexp) then  -- Detect an embedded `Bexp` and turn it into `Bexp.eval st t`
358-      return (mkApp2 (mkConst ``Bexp.eval) (← elabTerm st none) t)
359-    else if ty.isMVar then -- This is a hack to guard against `Meta.isDefEq` assigning the type to be an `Assertion`
360-      return t
361-    else if (← Meta.isDefEq ty (mkConst ``_root_.Assertion)) then
362-      return mkApp t (← elabTerm st none)
363-    else
364-      return t
365-  | _ => throwUnsupportedSyntax

368-macro_rules
369-  | `({{ $t }}) => `((fun st : _root_.State => assn(st; $t) : Assertion))

371-macro_rules
372-  | `(assn($st; ($P))) => ``((assn($st; $P)))
373-  | `(assn($st; $l = $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) = assn($st; $r))
374-  | `(assn($st; $l + $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) + assn($st; $r))
375-  | `(assn($st; $l - $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) - assn($st; $r))
376-  | `(assn($st; $l * $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) * assn($st; $r))
377-  | `(assn($st; $l ≤ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ≤ assn($st; $r))
378-  | `(assn($st; $l < $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) < assn($st; $r))
379-  | `(assn($st; $l ≥ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ≥ assn($st; $r))
380-  | `(assn($st; $l > $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) > assn($st; $r))
381-  | `(assn($st; $l ∧ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ∧ assn($st; $r))
382-  | `(assn($st; $l ∨ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ∨ assn($st; $r))
383-  | `(assn($st; $l → $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) → assn($st; $r))
384-  | `(assn($st; $l ↔ $r)) => ``(assn($st; $l) ↔ assn($st; $r))
385-  | `(assn($st; ¬ $t)) => ``(¬ assn($st; $t))
386-  | `(assn($st; $f $args*)) => do
387-    let mut result := f
388-    for arg in args do
389-      result ← `($result assn($st; $arg))
390-    return result
391-end

437---  Function applications inside assertions automatically interpret their
438---  arguments in the current state. Thus, `{{ f e1 ... en }}` stands for
439---  `fun st => f (e1 st) ... (en st)`.
440-
441---  Occasionally it is simpler to write an assertion directly as a Lean
442---  function. Such a function can be placed inside the assertion notation
443---  without an escape marker.
444-
445---  For example, `{{ fun st => ∀ x, st[x] = 0 }}` indicates an assertion
446---  that every variable maps to `0` in the given state.

449-
450---  Here are some example assertions that take advantage of this new
451---  notation.
452-
453-namespace ExamplePrettyAssertions
454-
455-def assertion1 : Assertion := {{ X = 3 }}
456-def assertion2 : Assertion := {{ True }}
457-def assertion3 : Assertion := {{ False }}
458-def assertion4 : Assertion := {{ True ∨ False }}
459-def assertion5 : Assertion := {{ X ≤ Y }}
460-def assertion6 : Assertion := {{ X = 3 ∨ X ≤ Y }}
461-def assertion7 : Assertion := {{ Z = max X Y }}
462-def assertion8 : Assertion := {{ Z * Z ≤ X
463-                                 ∧ ¬ (((Nat.succ Z) * (Nat.succ Z)) ≤ X) }}
464-def assertion9 : Assertion := {{ Nat.add X Y > max Y X }}
465-variable {xs : List Nat}
466--- #check {{ xs = X }}
467-/--
468-info: def ExamplePrettyAssertions.assertion8 : Assertion :=
469-fun st => st[Z] * st[Z] ≤ st[X] ∧ ¬st[Z].succ * st[Z].succ ≤ st[X]
470--/

472-#print assertion8

476---  ### Printing Assertions
477-
478---  As in the Imp chapter, the assertion notation above is *input* only:
479---  Lean reads `{{ X ≤ 5 }}` but still prints the underlying function, as
480---  `#print assertion8` just showed. The delaborators below close the loop
481---  for plain assertions: a state lambda whose body Lean can rebuild is
482---  printed back in `{{ … }}` notation, and an assertion Lean cannot
483---  rebuild falls back to the raw `fun st => …` form, which is exactly this
484---  notation's escape syntax, so what you see is always valid input. Each
485---  time a new notation involving assertions appears below (implication,
486---  Hoare triples, substitution), a small delaborator defined next to it
487---  will extend this printing to cover it. As before, there is no need to
488---  understand the details.
489-
490---  THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: printing assertions back
491-
492-namespace Assertion.Delab
493-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Imp.Delab
494-
495-/-- Rebuild the surface form of an assertion body, undoing the state
496-threading the `assn` elaborator performs: `st[X]` prints as `X`,
497-`Aexp.eval st a` as `a`, `Bexp.eval st b = true` as `b`, an applied
498-assertion `P st` as `P`, and a subterm that does not mention the state
499-prints as itself. -/
500-partial def delabBody (stId : FVarId) : DelabM Term := do
501-  let e ← getExpr
502-  if !e.containsFVar stId then
503-    delab
504-  else
505-    match_expr e with
506-    | MyGetElem.getElem _ _ _ _ st _ =>
507-      guard (st == .fvar stId)
508-      withNaryArg 5 delab
509-    | Aexp.eval st _ =>
510-      guard (st == .fvar stId)
511-      withAppArg delab
512-    | HAdd.hAdd _ _ _ _ _ _ =>
513-      `($(← withNaryArg 4 (delabBody stId)) + $(← withNaryArg 5 (delabBody stId)))
514-    | HSub.hSub _ _ _ _ _ _ =>
515-      `($(← withNaryArg 4 (delabBody stId)) - $(← withNaryArg 5 (delabBody stId)))
516-    | HMul.hMul _ _ _ _ _ _ =>
517-      `($(← withNaryArg 4 (delabBody stId)) * $(← withNaryArg 5 (delabBody stId)))
518-    | Eq _ l r =>
519-      -- `Bexp.eval st b = true` is the threaded form of a bare boolean `b`
520-      if r.isConstOf ``Bool.true && l.isAppOfArity ``Bexp.eval 2
521-          && l.appFn!.appArg! == .fvar stId then

590---  ### Assertion Implication
591-
592---  Given two assertions `P` and `Q`, we say that `P` *implies* `Q`,
593---  written `P ->> Q`, if, whenever `P` holds in some state `st`, `Q` also
594---  holds.
595-
596-def AssertImplies (P Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
597-  ∀ st, P st → Q st
598-
599---  Note that the notation for *assertion implication* is analogous to the
600---  "usual" Lean implication `→`.
601-
602-notation:26 P:27 " ->> " Q:27 => AssertImplies P Q
603-
604-theorem assertImplies_def {P Q : Assertion} : P ->> Q ↔ ∀ st, P st → Q st := by rfl
605-
606---  We'll also want the "iff" variant of implication between assertions:
607-
608-notation:26 P:27 " <<->> " Q:27 => AssertImplies P Q ∧ AssertImplies Q P
609-
610-theorem assertIff_def {P Q : Assertion} : P <<->> Q ↔ AssertImplies P Q ∧ AssertImplies Q P
611-    := by rfl
612-
613---  The matching delaborators print implications and equivalences between
614---  assertions back in `->>` and `<<->>` notation.
615-
616---  THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: printing implications back
617-
618-namespace Assertion.Delab
619-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr
620-
621-@[delab app.AssertImplies]
622-def delabAssertImplies : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
623-  guard <| (← getExpr).isAppOfArity ``AssertImplies 2
624-  `($(← delabAssnArg 0) ->> $(← delabAssnArg 1))
625-
626-/-- `<<->>` abbreviates a conjunction of two `AssertImplies`, so its
627-delaborator is keyed on `∧` and bails out unless the two conjuncts mirror
628-each other. -/
629-@[delab app.And]
630-def delabAssertIff : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
631-  let e ← getExpr
632-  guard <| e.isAppOfArity ``And 2
633-  let l := e.appFn!.appArg!
634-  let r := e.appArg!
635-  guard <| l.isAppOfArity ``AssertImplies 2 && r.isAppOfArity ``AssertImplies 2
636-  guard <| l.appFn!.appArg! == r.appArg! && l.appArg! == r.appFn!.appArg!
637-  `($(← withNaryArg 0 <| delabAssnArg 0) <<->> $(← withNaryArg 0 <| delabAssnArg 1))
638-
639-end Assertion.Delab

642-
643---  ## Hoare Triples, Informally
644-
645---  A *Hoare triple* is a claim about the state before and after executing
646---  a command. A commond notation for Hoare triples, and the one we use in
647---  this book, is
648-
649---    {{P}} c {{Q}}
650-
651---  meaning:
652-
653---  - If command `c` begins execution in a state satisfying assertion `P`,
654---  - and if `c` eventually terminates in some final state,
655---  - then that final state will satisfy the assertion `Q`.
656-
657---  Assertion `P` is called the *precondition* of the triple, and `Q` is
658---  the *postcondition*.
659-
660---  For example,
661-
662---  - The Hoare triple
663-
664---    {{X = 0}} X := X + 1 {{X = 1}}
665-
666---  states that command `X := X + 1` will transform a state in which
667---  `X = 0` to a state in which `X = 1`.
668-
669---  - On the other hand,
670-
671---    ∀ m, {{X = m}} X := X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}
672-
673---  is a *proposition* stating that the Hoare triple
674---  `{{X = m}} X :=
675---  X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}` is valid for any choice of `m`.
676---  Note that `m` in the two assertions is a reference to the *Lean*
677---  variable `m`, which is bound outside the Hoare triple.
678-
679---  _Quiz:_
680-
681---  Paraphrase the following in English.
682-
683---    1) {{True}} c {{X = 5}}
684-
685---    2) ∀ m, {{X = m}} c {{X = m + 5}}
686-
687---    3) {{X ≤ Y}} c {{Y ≤ X}}
688-
689---    4) {{True}} c {{False}}
690-
691---    5) ∀ m,
692---         {{X = m}}
693---         c
694---         {{Y = real_fact m}}
695-
696---    6) ∀ m,
697---         {{X = m}}
698---         c
699---         {{(Z * Z) ≤ m ∧ ¬ ((Z + 1) * (Z + 1) ≤ m)}}
700-

704---  between `P`, `c`, and `Q` true?

707-
708---  (A) Yes

825---  ## Hoare Triples, Formally
826-
827---  We formalize valid Hoare triples in Lean as follows:
828-
829-open scoped HasEval
830-
831-def ValidHoareTriple
832-    (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
833-  ∀ {st st' : State},
834-    (st =[ c ]=> st') →
835-    P st →
836-    Q st'
837-
838---  Note to developers (Niklas Halonen @xhalo32):
839---      Somethings strange is going on in `theorem if_example`, using
840---      `apply hoare_consequence_pre` followed by `· exact hoare_asgn`
841---      works, but `refine hoare_consequence_pre hoare_asgn ?_` or
842---      `apply hoare_consequence_pre hoare_asgn` don't. The only solution I
843---      found was to mark `ValidHoareTriple` irreducible.
844---
845---      It has to do something with `apply` and `refine` looking inside the
846---      implication in `∀ {st st'}, ...`
847-
848---  Notation for Hoare triples. The command between the two assertions is
849---  parsed with the same grammar as the `imp { … }` notation, so a command
850---  that is a Lean variable (rather than concrete syntax) is spliced in
851---  with `~c`, just as in the `st =[ c ]=> st'` notation.
852-
853-class HasTriple (Com : Type) where
854-  Triple : Assertion → Com → Assertion → Prop
855-
856-namespace HasTriple
857-
858-/-- Hoare triple: `{{ P }} c {{ Q }}` -/
859-scoped notation:lead "{{" P "}} " c:lead " {{" Q "}}" => Triple ({{ P }}) c ({{ Q }})
860-
861-/-- Hoare triple with `imp_com` command syntax -/
862-scoped syntax:lead (priority := high) "{{" term "}} " imp_com:lead " {{" term "}}" : term
863-scoped macro_rules
864-  | `({{ $P }} $c:imp_com {{ $Q }}) =>
865-      ``(HasTriple.Triple ({{ $P }}) (imp { $c }) ({{ $Q }}))
866-end HasTriple
867-
868-instance : HasTriple Com where
869-  Triple := ValidHoareTriple
870-
871-open scoped HasTriple
872-
873-theorem validHoareTriple_def {P : Assertion} {c : Com} {Q : Assertion} :
874-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} ↔ ∀ {st st' : State},
875-      (st =[ c ]=> st') →
876-      P st →
877-      Q st' := by rfl
878-
879-attribute [irreducible] ValidHoareTriple
880-

882-
883---  The delaborator is agnostic to the command type: it prints the command
884---  with whatever printer is registered for its constructors and splices
885---  the result into the triple, so a language-extension chapter only has to
886---  register a printer for its own `Com`.
887-
888-namespace Assertion.Delab
889-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Imp.Delab
890-@[delab app.HasTriple.Triple]
891-def delabTriple : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
892-  guard <| (← getExpr).isAppOfArity ``HasTriple.Triple 5
893-  let P ← withNaryArg 2 delabAssn
894-  let c ← withNaryArg 3 delab
895-  let Q ← withNaryArg 4 delabAssn
896-  match c with
897-  | `(imp { $c:imp_com }) => ``({{ $P }} $c:imp_com {{ $Q }})
898-  | c => ``({{ $P }} ~$c {{ $Q }})
899-
900-end Assertion.Delab

908-

910---  postcondition is valid.
911-
912-theorem hoare_post_true {P Q : Assertion} {c : Com} (h : ∀ st, Q st) :
913-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
914-  rw [validHoareTriple_def]
915-  intro st st' hc hpre

918---  ### Exercise (1 star): hoare_pre_false (Optional) ⭐
919-
920---  Prove that if `P` holds in no state, then any triple with `P` as its
921---  precondition is valid.
922-
923-theorem hoare_pre_false {P Q : Assertion} {c : Com} (h : ∀ st, ¬ (P st)) :
924-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
925-  rw [validHoareTriple_def]
926-  intro st st' hc hpre
927-  specialize h st

930---  ## Proof Rules
931-
932---  The goal of Hoare logic is to provide a *compositional* method for
933---  proving the validity of specific Hoare triples. That is, we want the
934---  structure of a program's correctness proof to mirror the structure of
935---  the program itself. To this end, in the sections below, we'll introduce
936---  a rule for reasoning about each of the different syntactic forms of
937---  commands in Imp -- one for assignment, one for sequencing, one for
938---  conditionals, etc. -- plus a couple of "structural" rules for gluing
939---  things together. We will then be able to prove programs correct using
940---  these proof rules, without ever unfolding the definition of
941---  `ValidHoareTriple`.
942-
943---  ### Skip
944-
945---  Since `skip` doesn't change the state, it preserves any assertion `P`:
946-
947---    --------------------  (hoare_skip)
948---    {{ P }} skip {{ P }}
949-
950-theorem hoare_skip {P : Assertion} :
951-    {{ P }} skip {{ P }} := by
952-  rw [validHoareTriple_def]
953-  intro st st' h hpre
954-  inversion h
955-  exact hpre
956-
957---  ### Sequencing
958-
959---  If command `c1` takes any state where `P` holds to a state where `Q`
960---  holds, and if `c2` takes any state where `Q` holds to one where `R`
961---  holds, then doing `c1` followed by `c2` will take any state where `P`
962---  holds to one where `R` holds:
963-
964---     {{ P }} c1 {{ Q }}
965---     {{ Q }} c2 {{ R }}
966---    ----------------------  (hoare_seq)
967---    {{ P }} c1; c2 {{ R }}
968-
969-theorem hoare_seq {P Q R : Assertion} {c1 c2 : Com}
970-    (h1 : {{ Q }} ~c2 {{ R }}) (h2 : {{ P }} ~c1 {{ Q }}) :
971-    {{ P }} ~c1; ~c2 {{ R }} := by
972-  rw [validHoareTriple_def]
973-  intro st st' h hpre
974-  inversion h with
975-  | seq st'' hc1 hc2 =>
976-    rw [validHoareTriple_def] at h1 h2
977-    exact h1 hc2 (h2 hc1 hpre)
978-
979---  Note that, in the formal rule `hoare_seq`, the premises are given in
980---  backwards order (`c2` before `c1`). This matches the natural flow of
981---  information in many of the situations where we'll use the rule, since
982---  the natural way to construct a Hoare-logic proof is to begin at the end
983---  of the program (with the final postcondition) and push postconditions
984---  backwards through commands until we reach the beginning.
985-
986---  ### Assignment
987-
988---  The rule for assignment is the most fundamental of the Hoare logic
989---  proof rules. Here's how it works.
990-
991---  Consider this incomplete Hoare triple:
992-
993---    {{ ??? }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
994-
995---  We want to assign `Y` to `X` and finish in a state where `X` is `1`.
996---  What could the precondition be?
997-
998---  One possibility is `Y = 1`, because if `Y` is already `1` then
999---  assigning it to `X` causes `X` to be `1`. That leads to a valid Hoare
1000---  triple:
1001-
1002---    {{ Y = 1 }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
1003-
1004---  It may seem as though coming up with that precondition must have taken
1005---  some clever thought. But there is a mechanical way we could have done
1006---  it: if we take the postcondition `X = 1` and in it replace `X` with
1007---  `Y`---that is, replace the left-hand side of the assignment statement
1008---  with the right-hand side---we get the precondition, `Y = 1`.
1009-
1010---  That same idea works in more complicated cases. For example:
1011-
1012---    {{ ??? }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
1013-
1014---  If we replace the `X` in `X = 1` with `X + Y`, we get `X + Y = 1`. That
1015---  again leads to a valid Hoare triple:
1016-
1017---    {{ X + Y = 1 }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
1018-
1019---  Why does this technique work? The postcondition identifies some
1020---  property `P` that we want to hold of the variable `X` being assigned.
1021---  In this case, `P` is "equals `1`". To complete the triple and make it
1022---  valid, we need to identify a precondition that guarantees that property
1023---  will hold of `X`. Such a precondition must ensure that the same
1024---  property holds of *whatever is being assigned to* `X`. So, in the
1025---  example, we need "equals `1`" to hold of `X + Y`. That's exactly what
1026---  the technique guarantees.
1027-
1028---  In general, the postcondition could be some arbitrary assertion `Q`,
1029---  and the right-hand side of the assignment could be some arbitrary
1030---  arithmetic expression `a`:
1031-
1032---    {{ ??? }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
1033-
1034---  The precondition would then be `Q`, but with any occurrences of `X` in
1035---  it replaced by `a`.
1036-
1037---  Let's introduce a notation for this idea of replacing occurrences:
1038---  Define `Q \[X ↦ a`] to mean "`Q` where `a` is substituted in place of
1039---  `X`".
1040-
1041---  This yields the Hoare logic rule for assignment:
1042-
1043---    {{ Q [X ↦ a] }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
1044-
1045---  One way of reading this rule is: If you want statement `X := a` to
1046---  terminate in a state that satisfies assertion `Q`, then it suffices to
1047---  start in a state that also satisfies `Q`, except where `a` is
1048---  substituted for every occurrence of `X`.
1049-
1050---  To many people, this rule seems "backwards" at first, because it
1051---  proceeds from the postcondition to the precondition. Actually it makes
1052---  good sense to go in this direction: the postcondition is often what is
1053---  more important, because it characterizes what will be true after
1054---  running the code.
1055-
1056---  Nonetheless, it's also possible to formulate a "forward" assignment
1057---  rule. We'll do that later in some exercises.
1058-
1059---  Here are some valid instances of the assignment rule:
1060-
1061---    {{ (X ≤ 5) [X ↦ X + 1] }}         (that is, X + 1 ≤ 5)
1062---      X := X + 1
1063---    {{ X ≤ 5 }}
1064-
1065---    {{ (X = 3) [X ↦ 3] }}              (that is, 3 = 3)
1066---      X := 3
1067---    {{ X = 3 }}
1068-
1069---    {{ (0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5) [X ↦ 3] }}.  (that is, 0 ≤ 3 ∧ 3 ≤ 5)
1070---      X := 3
1071---    {{ 0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5 }}
1072-
1073---  To formalize the rule, we must first formalize the idea of
1074---  "substituting an expression for an Imp variable in an assertion", which
1075---  we refer to as assertion substitution, or `Assertion.subst`.
1076-
1077---  Intuitively, given a proposition `P`, a variable `X`, and an arithmetic
1078---  expression `a`, we want to derive another proposition `P'` that is just
1079---  the same as `P` except that `P'` should mention `a` wherever `P`
1080---  mentions `X`.
1081-
1082---  This operation is related to the idea of substituting Imp expressions
1083---  for Imp variables that we saw in *Equiv* (`subst_aexp` and friends).
1084---  The difference is that, here, `P` is an arbitrary Lean assertion, so we
1085---  can't directly "edit" its text.
1086-
1087---  However, we can achieve the same effect by evaluating `P` in an updated
1088---  state, defined as follows:
1089-
1090-def Assertion.subst (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) (P : Assertion) : Assertion :=
1091-  fun (st : State) => P (x →ₜ a.eval st ; st)
1092-
1093---  Note to developers (One An @meluge, before next release):
1094---      Introduce a notation typeclass for this (e.g. HasSubst)
1095-
1096-namespace Assertion
1097-
1098-/-- Assertion substitution, written inside the braces: `{{ (P) [X ↦ a] }}`.
1099-The substituted assertion is re-read with the same notation, so Imp
1100-variables in it mean state lookups as usual; a named assertion is passed
1101-through directly. -/
1102-scoped syntax:max term:arg " [" ident " ↦ " imp_aexp "]" : term
1103-
1104-macro_rules
1105-  | `(assn($st; $P [$x ↦ $a:imp_aexp])) =>
1106-    match P with
1107-    | `($_:ident) => ``(Assertion.subst $x (aexp { $a }) $P $st)
1108-    | _ => ``(Assertion.subst $x (aexp { $a }) ({{ $P }}) $st)
1109-

1152---  That is, `P [X ↦ a]` stands for an assertion -- let's call it `P'` --
1153---  that behaves just like `P` except that, wherever `P` looks up the
1154---  variable `X` in the current state, `P'` instead uses the value of the
1155---  expression `a`.
1156-
1157---  To see how this works in more detail, let's calculate what happens with
1158---  a couple of examples. First, suppose `P'` is `(X ≤ 5) [X ↦ 3]` -- that
1159---  is, more formally, `P'` is the Lean expression
1160-
1161---    fun st =>
1162---      (fun st' => st'[X] ≤ 5)
1163---      (X →ₜ Aexp.eval st 3 ; st),
1164-
1165---  which simplifies to
1166-
1167---    fun st =>
1168---      (fun st' => st'[X] ≤ 5)
1169---      (X →ₜ 3 ; st)
1170-
1171---  and further simplifies to
1172-
1173---    fun st =>
1174---      ((X →ₜ 3 ; st)[X]) ≤ 5
1175-
1176---  and finally to
1177-
1178---    fun st =>
1179---      3 ≤ 5.
1180-
1181---  That is, `P'` is the assertion that `3` is less than or equal to `5`
1182---  (as expected).
1183-

1185---  X + 1]`.
1186---  Formally, `P'` is the Lean expression
1187-
1188---    fun st =>
1189---      (fun st' => st'[X] ≤ 5)
1190---      (X →ₜ Aexp.eval st (aexp { X + 1 }) ; st),
1191-
1192---  which simplifies to
1193-
1194---    fun st =>
1195---      (X →ₜ Aexp.eval st (aexp { X + 1 }) ; st)[X] ≤ 5
1196-
1197---  and further simplifies to
1198-
1199---    fun st =>
1200---      (Aexp.eval st (aexp { X + 1 })) ≤ 5.
1201-
1202---  That is, `P'` is the assertion that `X + 1` is at most `5`.

1299---  ### Exercise (2 stars): hoare_asgn_wrong ⭐⭐

1301---  The assignment rule looks backward to almost everyone the first time
1302---  they see it. If it still seems puzzling to you, it may help to think a
1303---  little about alternative "forward" rules. Here is a seemingly natural
1304---  one:
1305-
1306---    ------------------------------ (hoare_asgn_wrong)
1307---    {{ True }} X := a {{ X = a }}
1308-
1309---  Give a counterexample showing that this rule is incorrect and use it to
1310---  complete the proof below, showing that it is really a counterexample.
1311---  (Hint: The rule universally quantifies over the arithmetic expression
1312---  `a`, so your counterexample needs to exhibit an `a` for which the rule
1313---  doesn't work.)

1323-theorem hoare_asgn_wrong : ∃ a : Aexp,
1324-    ¬ {{ True }} X := ~a {{ X = a }} := by
1325-  exists aexp { X + 1 }
1326-  intro hc
1327-  rw [validHoareTriple_def] at hc
1328-  have h2 : (X →ₜ 1)[X] = (aexp { X + 1 }).eval (X →ₜ 1) := by
1329-    apply hc (st := ∅) (st' := X →ₜ 1)
1330-    · apply Com.EvalR.asgn; rfl
1331-    · exact True.intro
1332-  simp at h2

1334---  If `a` itself mentions `X`, then the value of `a` may be different in
1335---  the final state because of this update. For example, if `a` is `X + 1`,
1336---  then setting `X` to `a` certainly does not achieve the postcondition
1337---  `X = X + 1`! The underlying problem is that the state in which the
1338---  postcondition will be checked is different than the state in which `a`
1339---  was evaluated when it was assigned to `X`.

1407---  ### Consequence
1408-
1409---  Sometimes the preconditions and postconditions we get from the Hoare
1410---  rules won't quite be the ones we want in the particular situation at
1411---  hand -- they may be logically equivalent but have a different syntactic
1412---  form that fails to unify with the goal we are trying to prove, or they
1413---  actually may be logically weaker (for preconditions) or stronger (for
1414---  postconditions) than what we need.
1415-
1416---  For instance,
1417-
1418---    {{(X = 3) [X ↦ 3]}} X := 3 {{X = 3}},
1419-
1420---  follows directly from the assignment rule, but
1421-
1422---    {{True}} X := 3 {{X = 3}}
1423-
1424---  does not. This triple is valid, but it is not an instance of
1425---  `hoare_asgn` because `True` and `(X = 3) \[X ↦ 3`] are not
1426---  syntactically equal assertions.
1427-
1428---  However, they are logically *equivalent*, so if one triple is valid,
1429---  then the other must certainly be as well. We can capture this
1430---  observation with the following rule:
1431-
1432---       {{P'}} c {{Q}}
1433---         P <<->> P'
1434---    ---------------------
1435---       {{P}} c {{Q}}
1436-
1437---  Taking this line of thought a bit further, we can see that
1438---  strengthening the precondition or weakening the postcondition of a
1439---  valid triple always produces another valid triple. This observation is
1440---  captured by two *Rules of Consequence*.
1441-
1442---           {{P'}} c {{Q}}
1443---              P ->> P'
1444---    -----------------------------   (hoare_consequence_pre)
1445---           {{P}} c {{Q}}
1446-
1447---           {{P}} c {{Q'}}
1448---             Q' ->> Q
1449---    -----------------------------    (hoare_consequence_post)
1450---           {{P}} c {{Q}}
1451-
1452---  Here are the formal versions:
1453-
1454-theorem hoare_consequence_pre {P P' Q : Assertion} {c : Com}
1455-    (hhoare : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }}) (himp : P ->> P') :
1456-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1457-  rw [validHoareTriple_def] at hhoare ⊢
1458-  intro st st' heval hpre
1459-  apply hhoare heval
1460-  rw [assertImplies_def] at himp
1461-  exact himp _ hpre
1462-
1463-theorem hoare_consequence_post {P Q Q' : Assertion} {c : Com}
1464-    (hhoare : {{ P }} ~c {{ Q' }}) (himp : Q' ->> Q) :
1465-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
1466-  rw [validHoareTriple_def] at hhoare ⊢
1467-  intro st st' heval hpre
1468-  rw [assertImplies_def] at himp
1469-  apply himp
1470-  exact hhoare heval hpre
1471-

1533-  · exact hoare_consequence_post htriple hpost

1536---  ### Automation
1537-
1538---  Many of the proofs we have done so far with Hoare triples can be
1539---  streamlined using the automation techniques that we introduced in the
1540---  *Automation* chapter of *Logical Foundations*.
1541-
1542---  Recall that `simp` rewrites with any lemmas we pass it. The definitions
1543---  whose meaning we keep needing to expose in this chapter --
1544---  `ValidHoareTriple`, `AssertImplies`, and `Assertion.subst` -- each come
1545---  with a characterizing lemma (`validHoareTriple_def`,
1546---  `assertImplies_def`, `Assertion.subst_def`) restating the definition as
1547---  an equation. Passing these lemmas to `simp` replaces the defined
1548---  notions by their meanings wherever they appear. We'll do that
1549---  explicitly below (and shortly package the recipe up as a tactic of our
1550---  own).

1553---      The Rocq source here registers
1554---      `Hint Unfold assert_implies assertion_sub
1555---      t_update : core` for
1556---      `auto`. That only widens `auto`'s search (unlike the `Arguments /.`
1557---      commands, it does not affect `simpl`), so its Lean counterpart is
1558---      the `assertion_auto` tactic's simp list below -- not global
1559---      `@[simp]` lemmas as for the notation wrappers, whose folded names
1560---      carry no meaning in goals the way `->>` and `Assertion.subst` do.

1726-
1727---  Here's an example of a program involving both sequencing and
1728---  assignment. Note the use of `hoare_seq` in conjunction with
1729---  `hoare_consequence_pre` and `apply`'s metavariables.

1732-    {{a = n}}
1733-      X := ~a;
1734-      skip

1737-  · -- right part of seq

1739-  · -- left part of seq
1740-    apply hoare_consequence_pre
1741-    · exact hoare_asgn
1742-    · assertion_auto

1745---  is as a "decorated program" where the intermediate assertion `Q` is
1746---  written between `c1` and `c2`:
1747-
1748---             {{ a = n }}
1749---    X := a
1750---             {{ X = n }};    <--- decoration for Q
1751---    skip
1752---             {{ X = n }}

1842---  ### Exercise (4 stars): invalid_triple (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐⭐
1843-
1844---  Show that
1845-
1846---    {{ a = n }} X := 3; Y := a {{ Y = n }}
1847-
1848---  is not a valid Hoare triple for some choices of `a` and `n`.
1849-
1850---  Conceptual hint: Invent a particular `a` and `n` for which the triple
1851---  in invalid, then use those to complete the proof.
1852-
1853---  Technical hint: Hypothesis `h` below begins `∀ a n, ...`. You'll want
1854---  to instantiate that with the particular `a` and `n` you've invented.
1855---  You can do that with `have` and `apply`, but you may remember (from the
1856---  *Automation* chapter of Logical Foundations) that Lean offers an even
1857---  easier tactic: `specialize`. If you write
1858-
1859---    specialize h your_a your_n
1860-
1861---  the hypothesis will be instantiated on `your_a` and `your_n`.

1864-
1865---  - Use the (assumed) validity of the given hoare triple to derive a
1866---    state `st'` in which `Y` has some value `y1`
1867-

1869---    show that `Y` has a *different* value `y2` in the same final state
1870---    `st'`
1871-

1881-  simp only [validHoareTriple_def] at h
1882-  specialize h (aexp { X }) 2 (st := X →ₜ 2) (st' := Y →ₜ 3 ; X →ₜ 3 ; X →ₜ 2) ?_
1883-  · apply Com.EvalR.seq
1884-    · apply Com.EvalR.asgn; rfl
1885-    · apply Com.EvalR.asgn; rfl

1888---  ### Conditionals
1889-
1890---  What sort of rule do we want for reasoning about conditional commands?
1891-
1892---  Certainly, if the same assertion `Q` holds after executing either of
1893---  the branches, then it holds after the whole conditional. So we might be
1894---  tempted to write:
1895-
1896---            {{P}} c1 {{Q}}
1897---            {{P}} c2 {{Q}}
1898---    ---------------------------------
1899---    {{P}} if b then c1 else c2 {{Q}}
1900-
1901---  However, this is rather weak. For example, using this rule, we cannot
1902---  show
1903-
1904---    {{ True }}
1905---      if X = 0
1906---        then Y := 2
1907---        else Y := X + 1
1908---      end
1909---    {{ X ≤ Y }}
1910-
1911---  since the rule doesn't tell us enough about the state in which the
1912---  assignments take place in the "then" and "else" branches.
1913-
1914---  Fortunately, we can say something more precise. In the "then" branch,
1915---  we know that the boolean expression `b` evaluates to `true`, and in the
1916---  "else" branch, we know it evaluates to `false`. Making this information
1917---  available in the premises of the rule gives us more information to work
1918---  with when reasoning about the behavior of `c1` and `c2` (i.e., the
1919---  reasons why they establish the postcondition `Q`).
1920-
1921---    {{P ∧   b}} c1 {{Q}}
1922---    {{P ∧ ¬ b}} c2 {{Q}}
1923---    ------------------------------------  (hoare_if)
1924---    {{P}} if b then c1 else c2 end {{Q}}
1925-

1927---      I have removed `bassertion` as it's an unnecessary abstraction and
1928---      only adds overhead for the reader.

1932-theorem bexp_eval_false (b : Bexp) (st : State) (h : b.eval st = false) :
1933-    ¬ ({{ b }}) st := by
1934-  dsimp
1935-  simp [h]
1936-
1937---  Here, we first reduce the expression to `¬Bexp.eval st b = true` with
1938---  `dsimp`, which is trivial after we instruct `simp` to rewrite
1939---  `b.eval st` to `false`.
1940-

1942---      The Rocq proof is the single tactic `congruence`. Using simp seems
1943---      to work but should we build our own `congruence` tactic?
1944-
1945---  Now we can formalize the Hoare proof rule for conditionals and prove it
1946---  correct.
1947-
1948---  The statement of the rule reads: given `htrue : {{ P ∧ b }} ~c1 {{Q}}`
1949---  and `hfalse : {{ P ∧ ¬b }} ~c2 {{Q}}`, we can conclude
1950---  `{{P}} if (~b) { ~c1 } else { ~c2 } {{Q}}`.
1951-
1952-theorem hoare_if {P Q : Assertion} {b : Bexp} {c1 c2 : Com}
1953-    (htrue : {{ P ∧ b }} ~c1 {{ Q }}) (hfalse : {{ P ∧ ¬ b }} ~c2 {{ Q }}) :
1954-    {{ P }} if (~b) { ~c1 } else { ~c2 } {{ Q }} := by
1955-  rw [validHoareTriple_def] at htrue hfalse ⊢
1956-  intro st st' hE hpre
1957-  inversion hE with
1958-  | ifTrue hb hc1 =>
1959-    exact htrue hc1 ⟨hpre, hb⟩
1960-  | ifFalse hb hc =>
1961-    rw [← Bool.not_eq_true] at hb
1962-    exact hfalse hc ⟨hpre, hb⟩

2015---  #### Exercise: One-sided conditionals
2016-
2017---  Note to developers:
2018---      HIDE: Question from 2012, Midterm 2. One-sided conditionals.
2019-
2020---  In this exercise we consider extending Imp with "one-sided
2021---  conditionals" of the form `if1 (b) { c }`. Here `b` is a boolean
2022---  expression, and `c` is a command. If `b` evaluates to `true`, then
2023---  command `c` is evaluated. If `b` evaluates to `false`, then
2024---  `if1 (b) { c }` does nothing.
2025-
2026---  We recommend that you complete this exercise before attempting the ones
2027---  that follow, as it should help solidify your understanding of the
2028---  material.
2029-
2030---  The first step is to extend the syntax of commands and introduce the
2031---  usual notations. (We've done this for you, in a separate namespace to
2032---  prevent polluting the global name space. The `scoped` notations below
2033---  are active only inside `namespace If1`.)
2034-
2035-namespace If1
2036-
2037-inductive Com : Type where
2038-  | skip : Com
2039-  | asgn : Ident → Aexp → Com
2040-  | seq : Com → Com → Com
2041-  | cond : Bexp → Com → Com → Com
2042-  | whileDo : Bexp → Com → Com
2043-  | if1 : Bexp → Com → Com
2044-
2045-/-- One-sided conditional -/
2046-scoped syntax "if1 " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine imp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : imp_com
2047-
2048-open Lean in
2049-scoped macro_rules
2050-  | `(imp { $x:ident }) =>
2051-    if x.getId == `skip then `(Com.skip)
2052-    else Macro.throwErrorAt x s!"expected 'skip', got '{x.getId}'"
2053-  | `(imp { $c1; $c2 }) =>
2054-    `(Com.seq (imp {$c1}) (imp {$c2}))
2055-  | `(imp { $x:ident := $a }) =>
2056-    `(Com.asgn $x (aexp {$a}))
2057-  | `(imp { if ($b) {$c1} else {$c2} }) =>
2058-    `(Com.cond (bexp {$b}) (imp {$c1}) (imp {$c2}))
2059-  | `(imp { while ($b) {$c} }) =>
2060-    `(Com.whileDo (bexp {$b}) (imp {$c}))
2061-  | `(imp { if1 ($b) {$c} }) =>
2062-    `(Com.if1 (bexp {$b}) (imp {$c}))
2063-  | `(imp { ~$c }) =>
2064-    pure c
2065-
2066---  The delaborators are re-instantiated the same way: the Imp printer is
2067---  parameterized over the namespace of the command constructors, so the
2068---  extended printer is that printer at `If1.Com` plus one case for `if1`.
2069-
2070---  THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: printing the extended commands back
2071-
2072-namespace Delab
2073-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Imp.Delab
2074-
2075-/-- Rebuild `imp_com` syntax from an `If1.Com` term. -/
2076-partial def delabComInner : DelabM (TSyntax `imp_com) :=
2077-  delabComInnerFor ``Com do
2078-    let e ← getExpr
2079-    guard <| e.isAppOfArity ``Com.if1 2
2080-    let b ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabBexpInner
2081-    let c ← withAppArg If1.Delab.delabComInner
2082-    `(imp_com| if1 ($b) {$c})
2083-
2084-@[delab app.If1.Com.skip, delab app.If1.Com.asgn, delab app.If1.Com.seq,
2085-  delab app.If1.Com.cond, delab app.If1.Com.whileDo, delab app.If1.Com.if1]
2086-partial def delabCom : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
2087-  guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
2088-    | Com.skip => true
2089-    | Com.asgn _ _ => true
2090-    | Com.seq _ _ => true
2091-    | Com.cond _ _ _ => true
2092-    | Com.whileDo _ _ => true
2093-    | Com.if1 _ _ => true
2094-    | _ => false
2095-  match ← delabComInner with
2096-  | `(imp_com| ~$e) => pure e
2097-  | e => `(term| imp { $e })

2099-end Delab

2163-def ValidHoareTriple
2164-    (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
2165-  ∀ {st st' : State},
2166-    (st =[ c ]=> st') →
2167-    P st →
2168-    Q st'

2176-      P st →
2177-      Q st' := by rfl

2181---  ### Exercise (2 stars): hoare_if1 (manually graded) ⭐⭐
2182-
2183---  Invent a Hoare logic proof rule for `if1`. State and prove a theorem
2184---  named `hoare_if1` that shows the validity of your rule. Use `hoare_if`
2185---  as a guide. Try to invent a rule that is *complete*, meaning it can be

2270---  ### While Loops
2271-
2272---  The Hoare rule for `while` loops is based on the idea of a *command
2273---  invariant* (or just *invariant*): an assertion whose truth is
2274---  guaranteed after executing a command, assuming it is true before.
2275-
2276---  That is, an assertion `P` is a command invariant of `c` if
2277-
2278---    {{P}} c {{P}}
2279-
2280---  holds. Note that the command invariant might temporarily become false
2281---  in the middle of executing `c`, but by the end of `c` it must be
2282---  restored.
2283-
2284---  As a first attempt at a `while` rule, we could try:
2285-
2286---           {{P}} c {{P}}
2287---    ---------------------------
2288---    {{P}} while b do c end {{P}}
2289-
2290---  This rule is valid: if `P` is a command invariant of `c`, as the
2291---  premise requires, then, no matter how many times the loop body
2292---  executes, `P` is going to be true when the loop finally finishes.
2293-
2294---  But the rule also omits two crucial pieces of information. First, the
2295---  loop terminates when `b` becomes false. So we can strengthen the
2296---  postcondition in the conclusion:
2297-
2298---            {{P}} c {{P}}
2299---    ---------------------------------
2300---    {{P}} while b do c end {{P ∧ ¬b}}
2301-
2302---  Second, the loop body will be executed only if `b` is true. So we can
2303---  also strengthen the precondition in the premise:
2304-
2305---          {{P ∧ b}} c {{P}}
2306---    --------------------------------- (hoare_while)
2307---    {{P}} while b do c end {{P ∧ ¬b}}
2308-
2309---  That is the Hoare `while` rule. Note how it combines aspects of `skip`
2310---  and conditionals:
2311-
2312---  - If the loop body executes zero times, the rule is like `skip` in that
2313---    the precondition survives to become (part of) the postcondition.
2314-
2315---  - Like a conditional, we can assume guard `b` holds on entry to the
2316---    subcommand.
2317-

2319---      HIDE: The big comment will not display nicely. But I guess it's
2320---      folded...

2326-    (hhoare : {{P ∧ b}} ~c {{ P }}) :
2327-    {{ P }} while (~b) { ~c } {{P ∧ ¬ b}} := by
2328-  rw [validHoareTriple_def] at hhoare ⊢
2329-  intro st st' heval hpre

2331-  looping" case, its hypotheses talk about the whole loop instead
2332-  of just `c`. We begin by generalizing over an
2333-  arbitrary command, together with an equation remembering that the
2334-  command is the original loop. The cases for commands other than
2335-  `while` are dismissed because their equations are contradictory. -/
2336-  generalize heq : (imp { while (~b) { ~c } }) = cmd at heval

2338-  | @whileFalse b0 s0 c0 hb =>

2352---      `Maja says: The wording of "we will never enter the
2353---      loop" could definitely be improved. As is, it suggests a situation

2355---      a previous draft included a discussion that explicitly placed {{ P }}

2365---  We call `P` a *loop invariant* of `while b do c end` if
2366-
2367---    {{P ∧ b}} c {{P}}
2368-
2369---  is a valid Hoare triple.
2370-
2371---  This means that `P` will be true at the end of the loop body whenever
2372---  the loop body executes. If `P` contradicts `b`, this holds trivially
2373---  since the precondition is false.
2374-
2375---  For instance, `X = 0` is a loop invariant of
2376-
2377---    while X = 2 do X := 1 end
2378-
2379---  since the program will never enter the loop.

2530-theorem always_loop_hoare (Q : Assertion) :
2531-    {{True}} while (true) { skip } {{ Q }} := by
2532-  apply hoare_consequence_post
2533-  · apply hoare_while
2534-    apply hoare_post_true
2535-    intro st
2536-    exact True.intro
2537-  · intro st ⟨_, hguard⟩
2538-    simp at hguard
2539-
2540---  Of course, this result is not surprising if we remember that the
2541---  definition of `ValidHoareTriple` asserts that the postcondition must
2542---  hold *only* when the command terminates. If the command doesn't
2543---  terminate, we can prove anything we like about the post-condition.
2544-
2545---  Hoare rules that specify what happens *if* commands terminate, without
2546---  proving that they do, are said to describe a logic of *partial*
2547---  correctness. It is also possible to give Hoare rules for *total*
2548---  correctness, which additionally specifies that commands must terminate.
2549---  Total correctness is out of the scope of this textbook.

2565---  In this exercise, we'll add a new command to our language of commands:
2566---  `repeat { c } until (b)`. You will write the evaluation rule for
2567---  `repeat` and add a new Hoare rule to the language for programs
2568---  involving it.

2571-
2572-inductive Com : Type where
2573-  | skip : Com
2574-  | asgn : Ident → Aexp → Com
2575-  | seq : Com → Com → Com
2576-  | cond : Bexp → Com → Com → Com
2577-  | whileDo : Bexp → Com → Com
2578-  | repeatUntil : Com → Bexp → Com
2579-
2580---  `repeat` behaves like `while`, except that the loop guard is checked
2581---  *after* each execution of the body, with the loop repeating as long as
2582---  the guard stays *false*. Because of this, the body will always execute
2583---  at least once.

2601-  | `(imp { repeat {$c} until ($b) }) =>
2602-    `(Com.repeatUntil (imp {$c}) (bexp {$b}))
2603-  | `(imp { ~$c }) =>
2604-    pure c

2912---  ## Summary
2913-
2914---  So far, we've introduced Hoare Logic as a tool for reasoning about Imp
2915---  programs.
2916-
2917---  The rules of Hoare Logic are:
2918-
2919---           --------------------------- (hoare_asgn)
2920---           {{Q [X ↦ a]}} X:=a {{Q}}
2921-
2922---           --------------------  (hoare_skip)
2923---           {{ P }} skip {{ P }}
2924-
2925---             {{ P }} c1 {{ Q }}
2926---             {{ Q }} c2 {{ R }}
2927---            ----------------------  (hoare_seq)
2928---            {{ P }} c1;c2 {{ R }}
2929-
2930---            {{P ∧   b}} c1 {{Q}}
2931---            {{P ∧ ¬ b}} c2 {{Q}}
2932---    ------------------------------------  (hoare_if)
2933---    {{P}} if b then c1 else c2 end {{Q}}
2934-
2935---             {{P ∧ b}} c {{P}}
2936---      -----------------------------------  (hoare_while)
2937---      {{P}} while b do c end {{P ∧ ¬ b}}
2938-
2939---              {{P'}} c {{Q'}}
2940---                 P ->> P'
2941---                 Q' ->> Q
2942---       -----------------------------   (hoare_consequence)
2943---              {{P}} c {{Q}}
2944-
2945---  Our main task in this chapter has been to *define* the rules of Hoare
2946---  logic, and prove that the definitions are sound. Having done so, we can
2947---  go on and work *within* Hoare logic to prove that particular programs
2948---  satisfy particular Hoare triples. In the next chapter, we'll see how
2949---  Hoare logic is can be used to prove that more interesting programs
2950---  satisfy interesting specifications of their behavior.
2951-
2952---  Crucially, we will do so without ever again `unfold`ing the definition
2953---  of Hoare triples -- i.e., we will take the rules of Hoare logic as a
2954---  closed world for reasoning about programs.
2955-
2956---  ## Additional Exercises
2957-
2958---  ### Havoc
2959-
2960---  In this exercise, we will derive proof rules for a `havoc` command,
2961---  which is similar to the nondeterministic `any` expression from the the
2962---  Imp chapter.
2963-
2964---  First, we enclose this work in a separate namespace, and recall the
2965---  syntax and big-step semantics of Himp commands.
2966-
2967-namespace Himp
2968-
2969-inductive Com : Type where
2970-  | skip : Com
2971-  | asgn : Ident → Aexp → Com
2972-  | seq : Com → Com → Com
2973-  | cond : Bexp → Com → Com → Com
2974-  | whileDo : Bexp → Com → Com
2975-  | havoc : Ident → Com
2976-
2977-/-- Havoc: set a variable to a nondeterministically chosen number
2978-(`havoc x;`).  As with `skip`, the word `havoc` is not reserved: the
2979-production accepts any identifier and the macro below rejects
2980-everything except `havoc`. -/
2981-scoped syntax ident ident : imp_com
2982-
2983-open Lean in
2984-scoped macro_rules
2985-  | `(imp { $x:ident }) =>
2986-    if x.getId == `skip then `(Com.skip)
2987-    else Macro.throwErrorAt x s!"expected 'skip', got '{x.getId}'"
2988-  | `(imp { $c1; $c2 }) =>
2989-    `(Com.seq (imp {$c1}) (imp {$c2}))
2990-  | `(imp { $x:ident := $a }) =>
2991-    `(Com.asgn $x (aexp {$a}))
2992-  | `(imp { if ($b) {$c1} else {$c2} }) =>
2993-    `(Com.cond (bexp {$b}) (imp {$c1}) (imp {$c2}))
2994-  | `(imp { while ($b) {$c} }) =>
2995-    `(Com.whileDo (bexp {$b}) (imp {$c}))
2996-  | `(imp { $h:ident $x:ident }) =>
2997-    if h.getId == `havoc then `(Com.havoc $x)
2998-    else Macro.throwErrorAt h s!"expected 'havoc', got '{h.getId}'"
2999-  | `(imp { ~$c }) =>
3000-    pure c
3001-
3002-inductive Com.EvalR : Com → State → State → Prop where
3003-  | skip {st : State} :
3004-      EvalR (imp {skip}) st st
3005-  | asgn {st : State} {a : Aexp} {n : Nat} {x : Ident} (h : a.eval st = n) :
3006-      EvalR (imp {x := ~a}) st (x →ₜ n ; st)
3007-  | seq {c1 c2 : Com} {st st' st'' : State}
3008-      (h1 : EvalR c1 st st') (h2 : EvalR c2 st' st'') :
3009-      EvalR (imp {~c1; ~c2}) st st''
3010-  | ifTrue {st st' : State} {b : Bexp} {c1 c2 : Com} (hb : b.eval st = true)
3011-      (hc : EvalR c1 st st') :
3012-      EvalR (imp {if (~b) {~c1} else {~c2} }) st st'
3013-  | ifFalse {st st' : State} {b : Bexp} {c1 c2 : Com} (hb : b.eval st = false)
3014-      (hc : EvalR c2 st st') :
3015-      EvalR (imp {if (~b) {~c1} else {~c2} }) st st'
3016-  | whileFalse {b : Bexp} {st : State} {c : Com} (hb : b.eval st = false) :
3017-      EvalR (imp {while (~b) {~c} }) st st
3018-  | whileTrue {st st' st'' : State} {b : Bexp} {c : Com}
3019-      (hb : b.eval st = true) (hc : EvalR c st st')
3020-      (hloop : EvalR (imp {while (~b) {~c} }) st' st'') :
3021-      EvalR (imp {while (~b) {~c} }) st st''
3022-  | havoc {st : State} {x : Ident} {n : Nat} :
3023-      EvalR (imp {havoc x}) st (x →ₜ n ; st)

3025-instance : HasEval Com State State where
3026-  Eval := Com.EvalR

3029-def Com.unexpandEvalR : Lean.PrettyPrinter.Unexpander
3030-  | `($_ $c $st0 $st1) => ``($st0 =[ ~$c ]=> $st1)
3031-  | _ => throw ()

3033---  The definition of Hoare triples is exactly as before.
3034-
3035-def ValidHoareTriple
3036-    (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
3037-  ∀ {st st' : State},
3038-    (st =[ c ]=> st') →
3039-    P st →
3040-    Q st'
3041-
3042-instance : HasTriple Com where
3043-  Triple := ValidHoareTriple
3044-
3045-theorem validHoareTriple_def {P : Assertion} {c : Com} {Q : Assertion} :
3046-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} ↔ ∀ {st st' : State},
3047-      (st =[ c ]=> st') →
3048-      P st →
3049-      Q st' := by rfl
3050-
3051-attribute [irreducible] ValidHoareTriple
3052-
3053---  And the precondition consequence rule is exactly as before.

3056-    (hhoare : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }}) (himp : P ->> P') :
3057-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
3058-  rw [validHoareTriple_def] at hhoare ⊢
3059-  intro st st' heval hpre
3060-  apply_rules

3063-
3064---  Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00, before next release, 2021):
3065---      This exercise turns out to be quite hard -- a lot of people get

3069---  Complete the Hoare rule for `havoc` commands below by defining
3070---  `havoc_pre`, and prove that the resulting rule is correct.
3071-
3072-def havoc_pre (x : Ident) (Q : Assertion) (st : State) : Prop :=
3073-  (∀ (n : Nat), ({{ Q [x ↦ ~(.num n)] }}) st)
3074-
3075-theorem hoare_havoc {Q : Assertion} {x : Ident} :
3076-    {{ fun st => havoc_pre x Q st }} havoc x {{ Q }} := by
3077-  rw [validHoareTriple_def]
3078-  intro st st' heval hpre
3079-  rw [havoc_pre] at hpre
3080-  inversion heval with
3081-  | havoc n =>
3082-    specialize hpre n
3083-    simp only [Assertion.subst_apply, Aexp.eval_num] at hpre
3084-    exact hpre

3086---  ### Exercise (3 stars): havoc_post (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐
3087-
3088---  Complete the following proof without changing any of the provided
3089---  commands. If you find that it can't be completed, your definition of
3090---  `havoc_pre` is probably too strong. Find a way to relax it so that
3091---  `havoc_post` can be proved.
3092-
3093---  Hint: the `assertion_auto` tactics we've built won't help you here. You
3094---  need to proceed manually.
3095-
3096---  Note to developers (before next release):
3097---      This exercise is kind of weird. Should probably be optional.
3098-
3099-theorem havoc_post {P : Assertion} {x : Ident} :
3100-    {{ P }}
3101-    havoc x
3102-    {{ fun st => ∃ (n : Nat), ({{ P [x ↦ ~(.num n)] }}) st }} := by
3103-  apply hoare_consequence_pre
3104-  · apply hoare_havoc
3105-  · intro st hpre n
3106-    simp only [Assertion.subst_apply, Aexp.eval_num, TotalMap.update_shadow]
3107-    exists st[x]
3108-    rw [TotalMap.update_same]
3109-    exact hpre
3110-
3111-end Himp
