3113---  ### Assert and Assume
3114-
3115---  Note to developers (Claude):
3116---      The Rocq exercise region extends to End HoareAssertAssume. The
3117---      directive here covers only the initial student tasks because Verso
3118---      cannot compile the whole module as one block.
3119-
3120---  In this exercise, we will extend IMP with two commands, `assert` and
3121---  `assume`. Both commands are ways to indicate that a certain assertion
3122---  should hold any time this part of the program is reached. However they
3123---  differ as follows:
3124-
3125---  - If an `assert` statement fails, it causes the program to go into an
3126---    error state and exit.
3127-
3128---  - If an `assume` statement fails, the program fails to evaluate at all.
3129---    In other words, the program gets stuck and has no final state.
3130-
3131---  The new set of commands is:
3132-
3133-namespace HoareAssertAssume
3134-
3135-inductive Com : Type where
3136-  | skip : Com
3137-  | asgn : Ident → Aexp → Com
3138-  | seq : Com → Com → Com
3139-  | cond : Bexp → Com → Com → Com
3140-  | whileDo : Bexp → Com → Com
3141-  | assert : Bexp → Com
3142-  | assume : Bexp → Com
3143-
3144---  Note to developers:
3145---      NOTATION: LATER: Reconsider these precedences
3146-
3147-/-- Assert / assume (`assert (b);`, `assume (b);`).  As with `skip`, the
3148-words `assert` and `assume` are not reserved: the production accepts any
3149-identifier and the macro below rejects everything else. -/
3150-scoped syntax ident " (" imp_bexp ")" : imp_com
3151-
3152-open Lean in
3153-scoped macro_rules
3154-  | `(imp { $x:ident }) =>
3155-    if x.getId == `skip then `(Com.skip)
3156-    else Macro.throwErrorAt x s!"expected 'skip', got '{x.getId}'"
3157-  | `(imp { $h:ident ($b) }) =>
3158-    if h.getId == `assert then `(Com.assert (bexp {$b}))
3159-    else if h.getId == `assume then `(Com.assume (bexp {$b}))
3160-    else Macro.throwErrorAt h s!"expected 'assert' or 'assume', got '{h.getId}'"
3161-  | `(imp { $c1; $c2 }) =>
3162-    `(Com.seq (imp {$c1}) (imp {$c2}))
3163-  | `(imp { $x:ident := $a }) =>
3164-    `(Com.asgn $x (aexp {$a}))
3165-  | `(imp { if ($b) {$c1} else {$c2} }) =>
3166-    `(Com.cond (bexp {$b}) (imp {$c1}) (imp {$c2}))
3167-  | `(imp { while ($b) {$c} }) =>
3168-    `(Com.whileDo (bexp {$b}) (imp {$c}))
3169-  | `(imp { ~$c }) =>
3170-    pure c
3171-
3172---  To define the behavior of `assert` and `assume`, we need to add
3173---  notation for an error, which indicates that an assertion has failed. We
3174---  modify the `Com.EvalR` relation, therefore, so that it relates a start
3175---  state to either an end state or to `error`. The `Result` type indicates
3176---  the end value of a program, either a state or an error:
3177-
3178-inductive Result : Type where
3179-  | normal (st : State) : Result
3180-  | error : Result
3181-
3182---  Now we are ready to give you the evaluation relation for the new
3183---  language.
3184-
3185-inductive Com.EvalR : Com → State → Result → Prop where
3186-  /- Old rules, several modified -/
3187-  | skip {st : State} :
3188-      EvalR (imp {skip}) st (.normal st)
3189-  | asgn {st : State} {a : Aexp} {n : Nat} {x : Ident} (h : a.eval st = n) :
3190-      EvalR (imp {x := ~a}) st (.normal (x →ₜ n ; st))
3191-  | seqNormal {c1 c2 : Com} {st st' : State} {r : Result}
3192-      (h1 : EvalR c1 st (.normal st')) (h2 : EvalR c2 st' r) :
3193-      EvalR (imp {~c1; ~c2}) st r
3194-  | seqError {c1 c2 : Com} {st : State} (h : EvalR c1 st .error) :
3195-      EvalR (imp {~c1; ~c2}) st .error
3196-  | ifTrue {st : State} {r : Result} {b : Bexp} {c1 c2 : Com}
3197-      (hb : b.eval st = true) (hc : EvalR c1 st r) :
3198-      EvalR (imp {if (~b) {~c1} else {~c2} }) st r
3199-  | ifFalse {st : State} {r : Result} {b : Bexp} {c1 c2 : Com}
3200-      (hb : b.eval st = false) (hc : EvalR c2 st r) :
3201-      EvalR (imp {if (~b) {~c1} else {~c2} }) st r
3202-  | whileFalse {b : Bexp} {st : State} {c : Com} (hb : b.eval st = false) :
3203-      EvalR (imp {while (~b) {~c} }) st (.normal st)
3204-  | whileTrueNormal {st st' : State} {r : Result} {b : Bexp} {c : Com}
3205-      (hb : b.eval st = true) (hc : EvalR c st (.normal st'))
3206-      (hloop : EvalR (imp {while (~b) {~c} }) st' r) :
3207-      EvalR (imp {while (~b) {~c} }) st r
3208-  | whileTrueError {st : State} {b : Bexp} {c : Com}
3209-      (hb : b.eval st = true) (hc : EvalR c st .error) :
3210-      EvalR (imp {while (~b) {~c} }) st .error
3211-  /- Rules for Assert and Assume -/
3212-  | assertTrue {st : State} {b : Bexp} (hb : b.eval st = true) :
3213-      EvalR (imp {assert (~b)}) st (.normal st)
3214-  | assertFalse {st : State} {b : Bexp} (hb : b.eval st = false) :
3215-      EvalR (imp {assert (~b)}) st .error
3216-  | assume {st : State} {b : Bexp} (hb : b.eval st = true) :
3217-      EvalR (imp {assume (~b)}) st (.normal st)
3218-
3219-instance : HasEval Com State Result where
3220-  Eval := Com.EvalR
3221-
3222-@[app_unexpander Com.EvalR]
3223-def Com.unexpandEvalR : Lean.PrettyPrinter.Unexpander
3224-  | `($_ $c $st0 $st1) => ``($st0 =[ ~$c ]=> $st1)
3225-  | _ => throw ()
3226-
3227---  We redefine hoare triples: Now, `{{ P }} c {{ Q }}` means that,
3228---  whenever `c` is started in a state satisfying `P`, and terminates with
3229---  result `r`, then `r` is not an error and the state of `r` satisfies
3230---  `Q`.
3231-
3232-def ValidHoareTriple
3233-    (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
3234-  ∀ {st : State} {r : Result},
3235-    (st =[ c ]=> r) → P st →
3236-    ∃ st', r = Result.normal st' ∧ Q st'
3237-
3238-instance : HasTriple Com where
3239-  Triple := ValidHoareTriple
3240-
3241-theorem validHoareTriple_def {P : Assertion} {c : Com} {Q : Assertion} :
3242-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} ↔ ∀ {st : State} {r : Result},
3243-      (st =[ c ]=> r) → P st →
3244-      ∃ st', r = Result.normal st' ∧ Q st' := by rfl
3245-
3246-attribute [irreducible] ValidHoareTriple

3248---  ### Exercise (4 stars): assert_vs_assume ⭐⭐⭐⭐

3250---  To test your understanding of this modification, give an example
3251---  precondition and postcondition that are satisfied by the `assume`
3252---  statement but not by the `assert` statement.
3253-
3254-theorem assert_assume_differ : ∃ (P : Assertion) (b : Bexp) (Q : Assertion),
3255-    ({{ P }} assume (~b) {{ Q }})
3256-    ∧ ¬ ({{ P }} assert (~b) {{ Q }}) := by
3257-  exists {{ True }}, bexp { false }, ({{ False }})
3258-  constructor
3259-  · rw [validHoareTriple_def]
3260-    intro st r heval _
3261-    inversion heval with
3262-    | assume hb => simp at hb
3263-  · intro hC
3264-    rw [validHoareTriple_def] at hC
3265-    have h : ∅ =[ assert (false) ]=> Result.error := by
3266-      apply Com.EvalR.assertFalse
3267-      simp
3268-    obtain ⟨st', h1, h2⟩ := hC h True.intro
3269-    contradiction
3270-
3271---  Note to developers (Niklas Halonen @xhalo32):
3272---      For some reason, after `rw [validHoareTriple_def] at hC`, the
3273---      existence turns into `Exists ({{r = Result.normal ∧ False}})`.

3279-theorem assert_implies_assume (P : Assertion) (b : Bexp) (Q : Assertion)
3280-    (hhoare : {{ P }} assert (~b) {{ Q }}) :
3281-    {{ P }} assume (~b) {{ Q }} := by
3282-  rw [validHoareTriple_def] at hhoare ⊢
3283-  intro st r heval hpre
3284-  inversion heval with
3285-  | assume hb =>
3286-    exists st
3287-    have h : st =[ assert (~b) ]=> Result.normal st := by
3288-      apply Com.EvalR.assertTrue
3289-      assumption
3290-    obtain ⟨st', h1, h2⟩ := hhoare h hpre
3291-    injection h1 with hsteq
3292-    subst hsteq
3293-    exact ⟨rfl, h2⟩

3295---  Next, here are proofs for the old hoare rules adapted to the new
3296---  semantics. You don't need to do anything with these.
3297-
3298-theorem hoare_asgn {Q : Assertion} {x : Ident} {a : Aexp} :
3299-    {{Q [x ↦ ~a]}} x := ~a {{ Q }} := by
3300-  rw [validHoareTriple_def]
3301-  intro st r heval hQ
3302-  rw [Assertion.subst_apply] at hQ
3303-  inversion heval with
3304-  | asgn n h =>
3305-    exists (x →ₜ n ; st)
3306-    subst h
3307-    exact ⟨rfl, hQ⟩
3308-
3309-theorem hoare_consequence_pre {P P' Q : Assertion} {c : Com}
3310-    (hhoare : {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }}) (himp : P ->> P') :
3311-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} := by
3312-  rw [validHoareTriple_def] at hhoare ⊢
3313-  intro st r hc hpre
3314-  apply_rules
3315-
3316-theorem hoare_consequence_post {P Q Q' : Assertion} {c : Com}
3317-    (hhoare : {{ P }} ~c {{ Q' }}) (himp : Q' ->> Q) :
3318-    {{ P }} ~c {{   Q }} := by
3319-  rw [validHoareTriple_def] at hhoare ⊢
3320-  intro st r hc hpre
3321-  obtain ⟨st', hr, hQ'⟩ := hhoare hc hpre
3322-  exists st'
3323-  exact ⟨hr, himp _ hQ'⟩
3324-
3325-theorem hoare_seq {P Q R : Assertion} {c1 c2 : Com}
3326-    (h1 : {{ Q }} ~c2 {{R}}) (h2 : {{ P }} ~c1 {{ Q }}) :
3327-    {{ P }} ~c1; ~c2 {{R}} := by
3328-  rw [validHoareTriple_def] at h1 h2 ⊢
3329-  intro st r h12 hpre
3330-  inversion h12 with
3331-  | seqNormal st' hc1 hc2 =>
3332-    apply h1 hc2
3333-    specialize h2 hc1 hpre
3334-    obtain ⟨st'', heq, hQ⟩ := h2
3335-    injection heq with e
3336-    subst e
3337-    exact hQ
3338-  | seqError hc1 =>
3339-    -- Find contradictory assumption
3340-    specialize h2 hc1 hpre
3341-    obtain ⟨st', hC, _⟩ := h2
3342-    contradiction
3343-
3344---  Here are the other proof rules (sanity check)
3345-
3346-theorem hoare_skip {P : Assertion} :
3347-    {{ P }} skip {{ P }} := by
3348-  rw [validHoareTriple_def]
3349-  intro st r h hpre
3350-  inversion h
3351-  exact ⟨st, rfl, hpre⟩
3352-
3353-theorem hoare_if {P Q : Assertion} {b : Bexp} {c1 c2 : Com}
3354-    (hTrue : {{ P ∧ b}} ~c1 {{ Q }}) (hFalse : {{ P ∧ ¬ b}} ~c2 {{ Q }}) :
3355-    {{ P }} if (~b) { ~c1 } else { ~c2 } {{ Q }} := by
3356-  rw [validHoareTriple_def] at hTrue hFalse ⊢
3357-  intro st r hE hpre
3358-  inversion hE with
3359-  | ifTrue hb hc =>
3360-    -- b is true
3361-    apply_rules [And.intro]
3362-  | ifFalse hb hc =>
3363-    -- b is false
3364-    apply hFalse hc
3365-    exact ⟨hpre, by simp [hb]⟩
3366-
3367-theorem hoare_while {P : Assertion} {b : Bexp} {c : Com}
3368-    (hhoare : {{P ∧ b}} ~c {{ P }}) :
3369-    {{ P }} while (~b) { ~c } {{ P ∧ ¬ b}} := by
3370-  rw [validHoareTriple_def] at hhoare ⊢
3371-  intro st r heval hpre
3372-  generalize heq : (imp { while (~b) { ~c } }) = cmd at heval
3373-  induction heval generalizing P with
3374-  | @whileFalse b0 s0 c0 hb =>
3375-    injection heq with hbeq hceq
3376-    subst hbeq hceq
3377-    exact ⟨s0, rfl, hpre, by simp [hb]⟩
3378-  | @whileTrueNormal s0 s0' r0 b0 c0 hb hc hloop ih1 ih2 =>
3379-    injection heq with hbeq hceq
3380-    subst hbeq hceq
3381-    apply ih2 hhoare _ rfl
3382-    obtain ⟨s1, heq1, hs1⟩ := hhoare hc ⟨hpre, hb⟩
3383-    injection heq1 with he
3384-    subst he
3385-    exact hs1
3386-  | @whileTrueError s0 b0 c0 hb hc =>
3387-    injection heq with hbeq hceq
3388-    subst hbeq hceq
3389-    obtain ⟨s1, heq1, hs1⟩ := hhoare hc ⟨hpre, hb⟩
3390-    simp at heq1
3391-  | skip | asgn | seqNormal | seqError | ifTrue | ifFalse | assertTrue | assertFalse | assume =>
3392-    contradiction
3393-
3394---  Finally, state Hoare rules for `assert` and `assume` and use them to
3395---  prove a simple program correct. Name your rules `hoare_assert` and
3396---  `hoare_assume`.
3397-
3398-/- HIDE: Equivalently, we could make the postcondition Q ∧ b or the
3399-precondition Q → b ... -/
3400-theorem hoare_assert {Q : Assertion} {b : Bexp} :
3401-    {{Q ∧ b}} assert (~b) {{ Q }} := by
3402-  rw [validHoareTriple_def]
3403-  intro st r heval hpre
3404-  obtain ⟨hst, hb⟩ := hpre
3405-  exists st
3406-  inversion heval with
3407-  | assertTrue hb' => exact ⟨rfl, hst⟩
3408-  | assertFalse hb' => simp [hb'] at hb
3409-
3410-/- Stating this in a backwards-direction friendly way. -/
3411-/- HIDE: Equivalently, we could make the postcondition Q ∧ b... -/
3412-theorem hoare_assume {Q : Assertion} {b : Bexp} :
3413-    {{ b → Q }} assume (~b) {{ Q }} := by
3414-  rw [validHoareTriple_def]
3415-  intro st r heval hpre
3416-  exists st
3417-  inversion heval with
3418-  | assume hb => exact ⟨rfl, hpre hb⟩
3419-
3420---  Use your rules to prove the following triple.
3421-
3422-theorem assert_assume_example :
3423-    {{True}}
3424-      assume (X = 1);
3425-      X := X + 1;
3426-      assert (X = 2)
3427-    {{True}} := by
3428-  apply hoare_consequence_pre
3429-  · apply hoare_seq
3430-    · apply hoare_seq
3431-      · apply hoare_assert
3432-      · exact hoare_asgn
3433-    · apply hoare_assume
3434-  · assertion_auto
3435-
3436-end HoareAssertAssume

114---  ## Decorated Programs
115-
116---  The beauty of Hoare Logic is that it is *syntax directed*: the
117---  structure of proofs exactly follows the structure of programs.
118-
119---  We can record the essential ideas of a Hoare-logic proof — omitting
120---  low-level calculational details — by "decorating" a program with
121---  appropriate assertions on each of its commands.
122-
123---  Such a *decorated program* carries within itself an argument for its
124---  own correctness.
125-
126---  For example, consider the program:
127-
128---    X := m;
129---    Z := p;
130---    while X <> 0 do
131---      Z := Z - 1;
132---      X := X - 1
133---    end
134-
135---  Here is one possible specification for this program, in the form of a
136---  Hoare triple:
137-
138---    {{ True }}
139---    X := m;
140---    Z := p;
141---    while X <> 0 do
142---      Z := Z - 1;
143---      X := X - 1
144---    end
145---    {{ Z = p - m }}
146-
147---  (Note the *parameters* `m` and `p`, which stand for fixed-but-arbitrary
148---  numbers. Formally, they are simply Lean variables of type `Nat`.)
149-
150---  Here is a decorated version of this program, embodying a proof of this
151---  specification:
152-
153---    {{ True }} ->>
154---    {{ m = m }}
155---      X := m
156---                         {{ X = m }} ->>
157---                         {{ X = m /\ p = p }};
158---      Z := p;
159---                         {{ X = m /\ Z = p }} ->>
160---                         {{ Z - X = p - m }}
161---      while X <> 0 do
162---                         {{ Z - X = p - m /\ X <> 0 }} ->>
163---                         {{ (Z - 1) - (X - 1) = p - m }}
164---        Z := Z - 1
165---                         {{ Z - (X - 1) = p - m }};
166---        X := X - 1
167---                         {{ Z - X = p - m }}
168---      end
169---    {{ Z - X = p - m /\ ~ (X <> 0) }} ->>
170---    {{ Z = p - m }}
171-
172---  Note to developers:
173---      `HIDE: MRC'20: It bothers me a little in the proof above (and
174---      similarly throughout the whole file really when it comes to guards)
175---      that when we get to this part:
176---      [[
177---       while X <> 0 do {{ Z - X = p - m /\ X <> 0 }} ->>
178---      ]]
179---      we are inconsistent about [X <> 0] vs. [~(X=0)].  I admit they
180---      evaluate the same (er, sort of---the former is a [bexp] whereas the
181---      latter is an assertion), but they aren't syntactically the same.
182---      Since what we're teaching here (mechanized Hoare logic) is fussy
183---      about syntax, it strikes me as something we ought to be precise
184---      about. But it's an annoying change to propagate through the file,
185---      so I haven't done it. Is it worth a comment, or do others not get
186---      bothered by this?  Another way to fix this would be to add the [<>]
187---      operator to Imp, so that we can write the guard in the nicer way.
188---
189---      BCP 20: I think adding in a few more boolean operators at the
190---      outside is the way to go...
191---
192---      BCP 21: ... and I've now done this: <> is available in formal
193---      bexps (also >).`
194-
195---  Concretely, a decorated program consists of the program's text
196---  interleaved with assertions (sometimes multiple assertions separated by
197---  ->>).
198-
199---  A decorated program can be viewed as a compact representation of a
200---  proof in Hoare Logic: the assertions surrounding each command specify
201---  the Hoare triple to be proved for that part of the program using one of
202---  the Hoare Logic rules, and the structure of the program itself shows
203---  how to assemble all these individual steps into a proof for the whole
204---  program.
205-
206---  Our goal is to verify such decorated programs "mostly automatically."
207---  But, before we can verify anything, we need to be able to *find* a
208---  proof for a given specification, and for this we need to discover the
209---  right assertions. This can be done in an almost mechanical way, with
210---  the exception of finding loop invariants. In the remainder of this
211---  section, we explain in detail how to construct decorations for several
212---  short programs, all of which are loop free or have simple loop
213---  invariants. We'll return to finding more interesting loop invariants
214---  later in the chapter.
215-
216---  ### Example: Swapping
217-
218---  Consider the following program, which swaps the values of two variables
219---  using addition and subtraction, instead of by assigning to a temporary
220---  variable.
221-
222---    X := X + Y;
223---    Y := X - Y;
224---    X := X - Y
225-
226---  We can give a proof, in the form of decorations, that this program is
227---  correct — i.e., it really swaps `X` and `Y` — as follows.
228-
229---    (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }} ->>
230---    (2)    {{ (X + Y) - ((X + Y) - Y) = n /\ (X + Y) - Y = m }}
231---             X := X + Y
232---    (3)                     {{ X - (X - Y) = n /\ X - Y = m }};
233---             Y := X - Y
234---    (4)                     {{ X - Y = n /\ Y = m }};
235---             X := X - Y
236---    (5)    {{ X = n /\ Y = m }}
237-
238---  The decorations can be constructed as follows:
239-
240---  - We begin with the undecorated program (the unnumbered lines).
241-
242---  - We add the specification — i.e., the outer precondition (1) and
243---    postcondition (5). In the precondition, we use parameters `m` and `n`
244---    to remember the initial values of variables `X` and `Y` so that we
245---    can refer to them in the postcondition (5).
246-
247---  - We work backwards, mechanically, starting from (5) and proceeding
248---    until we get to (2). At each step, we obtain the precondition of the
249---    assignment from its postcondition by substituting the assigned
250---    variable with the right-hand-side of the assignment. For instance, we
251---    obtain (4) by substituting `X` with `X - Y` in (5), and we obtain (3)
252---    by substituting `Y` with `X - Y` in (4).
253-
254---  - Finally, we verify that (1) logically implies (2) — i.e., that the
255---    step from (1) to (2) is a valid use of the law of consequence — by
256---    doing a bit of high-school algebra.
257-
258---  Note to developers:
259---      HIDE: BCP 21: This side comment seems too technical:
260---
261---      - (Note that we are working with natural numbers rather than
262---        fixed-width machine integers, so we don't need to worry about the
263---        possibility of arithmetic overflow anywhere in this argument.
264---        This makes life quite a bit simpler!)
265---
266---      HIDE: A quick / optional exercise using just assignment here would
267---      be good.
268-
269---  ### Example: Simple Conditionals
270-
271---  Here is a simple decorated program using conditionals:
272-
273---    (1)   {{ True }}
274---            if X <= Y then
275---    (2)                    {{ True /\ X <= Y }} ->>
276---    (3)                    {{ (Y - X) + X = Y \/ (Y - X) + Y = X }}
277---              Z := Y - X
278---    (4)                    {{ Z + X = Y \/ Z + Y = X }}
279---            else
280---    (5)                    {{ True /\ ~(X <= Y) }} ->>
281---    (6)                    {{ (X - Y) + X = Y \/ (X - Y) + Y = X }}
282---              Z := X - Y
283---    (7)                    {{ Z + X = Y \/ Z + Y = X }}
284---            end
285---    (8)   {{ Z + X = Y \/ Z + Y = X }}
286-
287---  These decorations can be constructed as follows:
288-
289---  - We start with the outer precondition (1) and postcondition (8).
290-
291---  - Following the format dictated by the `hoare_if` rule, we copy the
292---    postcondition (8) to (4) and (7). We conjoin the precondition (1)
293---    with the guard of the conditional to obtain (2). We conjoin (1) with
294---    the negated guard of the conditional to obtain (5).
295-
296---  - In order to use the assignment rule and obtain (3), we substitute `Z`
297---    by `Y - X` in (4). To obtain (6) we substitute `Z` by `X - Y` in (7).
298-
299---  - Finally, we verify that (2) implies (3) and (5) implies (6). Both of
300---    these implications crucially depend on the ordering of `X` and `Y`
301---    obtained from the guard. For instance, knowing that `X <= Y` ensures
302---    that subtracting `X` from `Y` and then adding back `X` produces `Y`,
303---    as required by the first disjunct of (3). Similarly, knowing that
304---    `~ (X <= Y)` ensures that subtracting `Y` from `X` and then adding
305---    back `Y` produces `X`, as needed by the second disjunct of (6). Note
306---    that `n - m + m = n` does *not* hold for arbitrary natural numbers
307---    `n` and `m` (for example, [3 - 5 + 5 = 5]).
308-
309---  Note to developers:
310---      NOTATION: LATER: The `~` in that paragraph will typeset wrong if
311---      the space after it is removed. Maybe it's better to give up on all
312---      the unicode hacks in the generated HTML...?

314---  ### Exercise (2 stars): if_minus_plus_reloaded (Optional, manually graded) ⭐⭐
315-
316---  N.b.: Although this exercise is marked optional, it is an excellent
317---  warm-up for the (non-optional) `if_minus_plus_correct` exercise below!
318-
319---  Fill in valid decorations for the following program:
320-
321---    {{ True }}
322---      if X <= Y then
323---                {{                         }} ->>
324---                {{                         }}
325---        Z := Y - X
326---                {{                         }}
327---      else
328---                {{                         }} ->>
329---                {{                         }}
330---        Y := X + Z
331---                {{                         }}
332---      end
333---    {{ Y = X + Z }}
334-
335---  Briefly justify each use of `->>`.
336-
337---    {{ True }}
338---      if X <= Y then
339---           {{ True /\ X <= Y }} ->>
340---           {{ Y = X + (Y - X) }}
341---        Z := Y - X
342---           {{ Y = X + Z }}
343---      else
344---           {{ True /\ ~(X <= Y) }} ->>
345---           {{ X + Z = X + Z }}
346---        Y := X + Z
347---           {{ Y = X + Z }}
348---      end
349---    {{ Y = X + Z }}
350-
351---  The second use of consequence is trivial, while the first crucially
352---  depends on the `X <= Y` condition, which ensures that subtracting `X`
353---  from `Y` and then adding back `X` produces `Y`.
354-
355---  ### Example: Reduce to Zero
356-
357---  Here is a `while` loop that is so simple that `True` suffices as a loop
358---  invariant.
359-
360---    (1)    {{ True }}
361---             while X <> 0 do
362---    (2)                  {{ True /\ X <> 0 }} ->>
363---    (3)                  {{ True }}
364---               X := X - 1
365---    (4)                  {{ True }}
366---             end
367---    (5)    {{ True /\ ~(X <> 0) }} ->>
368---    (6)    {{ X = 0 }}
369-
370---  The decorations can be constructed as follows:
371-
372---  - Start with the outer precondition (1) and postcondition (6).
373-
374---  - Following the format dictated by the `hoare_while` rule, we copy (1)
375---    to (4). We conjoin (1) with the guard to obtain (2). We also conjoin
376---    (1) with the negation of the guard to obtain (5).
377-
378---  - Because the final postcondition (6) does not syntactically match (5),
379---    we add an implication between them.
380-
381---  - Using the assignment rule with assertion (4), we trivially substitute
382---    and obtain assertion (3).
383-
384---  - We add the implication between (2) and (3).
385-
386---  Finally we check that the implications do hold; both are trivial.
387-
388---  ### Example: Division
389-
390---  Let's do one more example of simple reasoning about a loop.
391-
392---  The following Imp program calculates the integer quotient and remainder
393---  of parameters `m` and `n`.
394-
395---    X := m;
396---    Y := 0;
397---    while n <= X do
398---      X := X - n;
399---      Y := Y + 1
400---    end;
401-
402---  If we replace `m` and `n` by concrete numbers and execute the program,
403---  it will terminate with the variable `X` set to the remainder when `m`
404---  is divided by `n` and `Y` set to the quotient.
405-
406---  In order to give a specification to this program we need to remember
407---  that dividing `m` by `n` produces a remainder `X` and a quotient `Y`
408---  such that `n * Y + X = m /\ X < n`.
409-
410---  It turns out that we get lucky with this program and don't have to
411---  think very hard about the loop invariant: the loop invariant is just
412---  the first conjunct, `n * Y + X = m`, and we can use this to decorate
413---  the program.
414-
415---     (1)  {{ True }} ->>
416---     (2)  {{ n * 0 + m = m }}
417---            X := m;
418---     (3)                     {{ n * 0 + X = m }}
419---            Y := 0;
420---     (4)                     {{ n * Y + X = m }}
421---            while n <= X do
422---     (5)                     {{ n * Y + X = m /\ n <= X }} ->>
423---     (6)                     {{ n * (Y + 1) + (X - n) = m }}
424---              X := X - n;
425---     (7)                     {{ n * (Y + 1) + X = m }}
426---              Y := Y + 1
427---     (8)                     {{ n * Y + X = m }}
428---            end
429---     (9)  {{ n * Y + X = m /\ ~ (n <= X) }} ->>
430---    (10)  {{ n * Y + X = m /\ X < n }}
431-
432---  Assertions (4), (5), (8), and (9) are derived mechanically from the
433---  loop invariant and the loop's guard. Assertions (8), (7), and (6) are
434---  derived using the assignment rule going backwards from (8) to (6).
435---  Assertions (4), (3), and (2) are again backwards applications of the
436---  assignment rule.
437-
438---  Now that we've decorated the program it only remains to check that the
439---  uses of the consequence rule are correct — i.e., that (1) implies (2),
440---  that (5) implies (6), and that (9) implies (10). This is indeed the
441---  case:
442-
443---  - (1) ->> (2): trivial, by algebra.
444-
445---  - (5) ->> (6): because `n <= X`, we are guaranteed that the subtraction
446---    in (6) does not get zero-truncated. We can therefore rewrite (6) as
447---    `n * Y + n + X - n` and cancel the `n`s, which results in the left
448---    conjunct of (5).
449-
450---  - (9) ->> (10): if `~ (n <= X)` then `X < n`. That's straightforward
451---    from high-school algebra. So, we have a valid decorated program.
452-
453---  ### From Decorated Programs to Formal Proofs
454-
455---  From an informal proof in the form of a decorated program, it is "easy
456---  in principle" to read off a formal proof using the Lean theorems
457---  corresponding to the Hoare Logic rules, but these proofs can be a bit
458---  long and fiddly.
459-
460---  Note that we do *not* unfold the definition of `ValidHoareTriple`
461---  anywhere in this proof: the point of the game we're playing now is to
462---  use the Hoare rules as a self-contained logic for reasoning about
463---  programs.
464-
465---  For example...
466-
467-def reduceToZero : Com :=
468-  imp {
469-    while (X ≠ 0) {
470-      X := X - 1
471-    }
472-  }
473-
474-theorem reduce_to_zero_correct' :
475-    {{ True }} ~reduceToZero {{ X = 0 }} := by
476-  -- First put the postcondition into the form expected by
477-  -- the while rule.
478-  sorry
479-
480---  In Hoare we introduced a series of tactics named `assertion_auto` to
481---  automate proofs involving assertions.
482-
483---  The following declaration introduces a more sophisticated tactic that
484---  will help with proving assertions throughout the rest of this chapter.
485---  You don't need to understand the details, but briefly: it introduces
486---  the available hypotheses, simplifies assertions, maps, and arithmetic
487---  expressions, and then asks `lia` to solve linear arithmetic goals.
488---  What's left after `verify_assertion` does its work should be just the
489---  "interesting parts" of the proof (which, if we're lucky, might be
490---  nothing at all!).
491-
492-macro "verify_assertion" : tactic =>
493-  `(tactic| assertion_auto)
494-
495---  This makes it pretty easy to verify `reduce_to_zero`:
496-
497-theorem reduce_to_zero_correct''' :
498-    {{ True }} ~reduceToZero {{ X = 0 }} := by
499-  sorry
500-
501---  This example shows that it is conceptually straightforward to read off
502---  the main elements of a formal proof from a decorated program. Indeed,
503---  the process is so straightforward that it can be automated, as we will
504---  see next.
505-
506---  ## Formal Decorated Programs
507-
508---  Our informal conventions for decorated programs amount to a way of
509---  "displaying" Hoare triples, in which commands are annotated with enough
510---  embedded assertions that checking the validity of a triple is reduced
511---  to simple logical and algebraic calculations showing that some
512---  assertions imply others.
513-
514---  In this section, we show that this presentation style can be made
515---  completely formal — and indeed that checking the validity of decorated
516---  programs can be largely automated.
517-
518---  ### Syntax
519-
520---  The first thing we need to do is to formalize a variant of the syntax
521---  of Imp commands that includes embedded assertions, which we'll call
522---  "decorations." We call the new commands *decorated commands*, or
523---  `dcom`s.
524-
525---  The choice of exactly where to put assertions in the definition of
526---  `dcom` is a bit subtle. The simplest thing to do would be to annotate
527---  every `dcom` with a precondition and postcondition — something like
528---  this...
529-
530-namespace DComFirstTry
531-
532-inductive DCom where
533-  | skip (pre : Assertion)
534-  | seq (pre : Assertion) (first : DCom)
535-      (middle : Assertion)
536-      (second : DCom) (post : Assertion)
537-  | asgn (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) (post : Assertion)
538-  | cond (pre : Assertion) (b : Bexp)
539-      (thenPre : Assertion) (thenBranch : DCom)
540-      (elsePre : Assertion) (elseBranch : DCom)
541-      (post : Assertion)
542-  | whileDo (pre : Assertion) (b : Bexp)
543-      (bodyPre : Assertion) (body : DCom)
544-      (bodyPost : Assertion) (post : Assertion)
545-  | strengthenPre (pre : Assertion) (body : DCom)
546-  | weakenPost (body : DCom) (post : Assertion)
547-
548-end DComFirstTry
549-
550---  But this would result in *very* verbose decorated programs with a lot
551---  of repeated annotations: a simple program like `skip;skip` would be
552---  decorated like this,
553-
554---    {{P}} ({{P}} skip {{P}}) ; ({{P}} skip {{P}}) {{P}}
555-
556---  with pre- and post-conditions around each `skip`, plus identical pre-
557---  and post-conditions on the semicolon!
558-
559---  In other words, we don't want both preconditions and postconditions on
560---  each command, because a sequence of two commands would contain
561---  redundant decorations — the postcondition of the first likely being the
562---  same as the precondition of the second.
563-
564---  Instead, our formal syntax of decorated commands will omit
565---  preconditions whenever possible and embed just postconditions.
566-
567---  - The `skip` command, for example, is decorated only with its
568---    postcondition
569-
570---    skip {{ Q }}
571-
572---  on the assumption that the precondition will be provided by somebody
573---  else.
574-
575---  We carry the same assumption through the other syntactic forms: each
576---  decorated command is assumed to carry its own postcondition within
577---  itself but take its precondition from its context in which it is used.
578-
579---  - Sequences `d1 ; d2` need no additional decorations.
580-
581---  Why?
582-
583---  Because inside `d2` there will be a postcondition, which also serves as
584---  the postcondition of `d1;d2`.
585-
586---  Similarly, inside `d1` there will also be a postcondition, which
587---  additionally serves as the *precondition* for `d2`.
588-
589---  - An assignment `X := a` is decorated only with its postcondition:
590-
591---    X := a {{ Q }}
592-
593---  - A conditional `if b then d1 else d2` is decorated with a
594---    postcondition for the entire statement, as well as preconditions for
595---    each branch:
596-
597---    if b then {{ P1 }} d1 else {{ P2 }} d2 end {{ Q }}
598-
599---  Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00, before next release, 2025):
600---      Maybe we need a note here about why we don't just calculate P1 and
601---      P2 later, once we know the precondition of the whole loop. Indeed,
602---      we could (and perhaps should, as discussed elsewhere), but we are
603---      doing something simpler for the moment.
604-
605---  - A loop `while b do d end` is decorated with its final postcondition
606---    plus a precondition for the body:
607-
608---    while b do {{ P }} d end {{ Q }}
609-
610---  The postcondition embedded in `d` serves as the loop invariant.
611-
612---  - Implications `->>` can be added as decorations either for a
613---    precondition...
614-
615---    ->> {{ P }} d
616-
617---  ...or for a postcondition:
618-
619---    d ->> {{ Q }}
620-
621---  The former is waiting for another precondition to be supplied by the
622---  context; the latter relies on the postcondition already embedded in
623---  `d`.
624-
625---  Putting this all together gives us the formal syntax of decorated
626---  commands:
627-
628-inductive DCom where
629-  | skip (post : Assertion)
630-  | seq (first second : DCom)
631-  | asgn (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) (post : Assertion)
632-  | cond (b : Bexp)
633-      (thenPre : Assertion) (thenBranch : DCom)
634-      (elsePre : Assertion) (elseBranch : DCom)
635-      (post : Assertion)
636-  | whileDo (b : Bexp) (bodyPre : Assertion) (body : DCom)
637-      (post : Assertion)
638-  | pre (pre : Assertion) (body : DCom)
639-  | post (body : DCom) (post : Assertion)
640-
641---  Lean keeps decorated-command notation in its own syntax category,
642---  `dcom`, so it can coexist with the ordinary Imp command syntax.
643-
644---  THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: decorated commands
645-
646-declare_syntax_cat dcom
647-
648-syntax:max "(" dcom ")" : dcom
649-syntax:max "skip" " {{" term "}}" : dcom
650-syntax:max ident " := " imp_aexp " {{" term "}}" : dcom
651-syntax:20 dcom:21 ";" ppLine dcom:20 : dcom
652-syntax:max "if " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "then" ppLine
653-  "{{" term "}}" ppLine dcom ppLine
654-  "else" ppLine "{{" term "}}" ppLine dcom ppLine
655-  "end" ppLine "{{" term "}}" : dcom
656-syntax:max "while " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "do" ppLine
657-  "{{" term "}}" ppLine dcom ppLine
658-  "end" ppLine "{{" term "}}" : dcom
659-syntax:5 "->>" " {{" term "}}" ppLine dcom:0 : dcom
660-syntax:5 dcom:6 ppLine "->>" " {{" term "}}" : dcom
661-
662-syntax:min "dcom" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine dcom
663-  ppDedent(ppLine "}") : term
664-
665-macro_rules
666-  | `(dcom { ($body:dcom) }) =>
667-      `(dcom { $body })
668-  | `(dcom { skip {{ $q }} }) =>
669-      `(DCom.skip ({{ $q }}))
670-  | `(dcom { $x:ident := $a:imp_aexp {{ $q }} }) =>
671-      `(DCom.asgn $x (aexp { $a }) ({{ $q }}))
672-  | `(dcom { $d1:dcom; $d2:dcom }) =>
673-      `(DCom.seq (dcom { $d1 }) (dcom { $d2 }))
674-  | `(dcom {
675-        if ($b:imp_bexp) then
676-          {{ $p1 }}
677-          $d1:dcom
678-        else
679-          {{ $p2 }}
680-          $d2:dcom
681-        end
682-          {{ $q }}
683-      }) =>
684-      `(DCom.cond (bexp { $b })
685-        ({{ $p1 }}) (dcom { $d1 })
686-        ({{ $p2 }}) (dcom { $d2 })
687-        ({{ $q }}))
688-  | `(dcom {
689-        while ($b:imp_bexp) do
690-          {{ $p }}
691-          $body:dcom
692-        end
693-          {{ $q }}
694-      }) =>
695-      `(DCom.whileDo (bexp { $b }) ({{ $p }})
696-        (dcom { $body }) ({{ $q }}))
697-  | `(dcom { ->> {{ $p }} $body:dcom }) =>
698-      `(DCom.pre ({{ $p }}) (dcom { $body }))
699-  | `(dcom { $body:dcom ->> {{ $q }} }) =>
700-      `(DCom.post (dcom { $body }) ({{ $q }}))
701-
702---  END DETAILS
703-
704---  To provide the initial precondition that goes at the very top of a
705---  decorated program, we introduce a new type `decorated`:
706-
707-structure Decorated where
708-  pre : Assertion
709-  body : DCom
710-
711---  Note to developers:
712---      HIDE: Add FOLD here
713-
714-example : DCom :=
715-  .skip ({{ True }})
716-
717-example : DCom :=
718-  .whileDo (bexp {true}) ({{ True }})
719-    (.skip ({{ True }})) ({{ True }})
720-
721---  To inspect the fully elaborated term behind this notation, put
722---  `set_option pp.all true in` before a `#check` or `#print` command.
723-
724---  The formal definitions can use either constructors directly or the
725---  decorated-command notation introduced above.
726-
727---  Note to developers:
728---      HIDE: Add /FOLD here
729-
730---  An example `decorated` program that decrements `X` to `0`:
731-
732-def decWhile : Decorated where
733-  pre := ({{ True }})
734-  body := dcom {
735-    while (X ≠ 0) do
736-      {{ True ∧ ¬ X = 0 }}
737-      X := X - 1 {{ True }}
738-    end
739-      {{ True ∧ X = 0 }}
740-    ->> {{ X = 0 }}
741-  }
742-
743---  It is easy to go from a `dcom` to a `com` by erasing all annotations.
744-
745-def DCom.erase (d : DCom) : Com :=
746-  match d with
747-  | .skip _ => .skip
748-  | .seq d1 d2 => .seq d1.erase d2.erase
749-  | .asgn x a _ => .asgn x a
750-  | .cond b _ d1 _ d2 _ => .cond b d1.erase d2.erase
751-  | .whileDo b _ body _ => .whileDo b body.erase
752-  | .pre _ body => body.erase
753-  | .post body _ => body.erase
754-
755-def Decorated.erase (dec : Decorated) : Com :=
756-  dec.body.erase
757-
758-example :
759-    decWhile.erase =
760-      (imp {
761-        while (X ≠ 0) {
762-          X := X - 1
763-        }
764-      }) := by
765-  rfl
766-
767---  It is also straightforward to extract the precondition and
768---  postcondition from a decorated program.
769-
770-def Decorated.precondition (dec : Decorated) : Assertion :=
771-  dec.pre
772-
773---  Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00, before next release, 2025):
774---      `It would be nice to use <{ ... }> notations
775---      in this definition and the ones below...
776---           | <{ skip {{P}} }>        => P
777---           | <{ _; d2 }>             => post d2
778---           | <{ _ := _ {{Q}} }>      => Q`
779-
780-def DCom.postcondition (d : DCom) : Assertion :=
781-  match d with
782-  | .skip q => q
783-  | .seq _ d2 => d2.postcondition
784-  | .asgn _ _ q => q
785-  | .cond _ _ _ _ _ q => q
786-  | .whileDo _ _ _ q => q
787-  | .pre _ body => body.postcondition
788-  | .post _ q => q
789-
790-def Decorated.postcondition (dec : Decorated) : Assertion :=
791-  dec.body.postcondition
792-
793-example : decWhile.precondition = {{ True }} := by
794-  funext st
795-  rfl
796-
797-example : decWhile.postcondition = {{ X = 0 }} := by
798-  funext st
799-  rfl

801---  We can then express what it means for a decorated program to be correct
802---  as follows:
803-
804-def Decorated.OuterTripleValid (dec : Decorated) : Prop :=
805-  ValidHoareTriple dec.precondition dec.erase
806-    dec.postcondition
807-
808---  For example:
809-
810-example :
811-    decWhile.OuterTripleValid =
812-      {{ True }}
813-        while (X ≠ 0) {
814-          X := X - 1
815-        }
816-      {{ X = 0 }} := by
817-  rfl
818-
819---  The outer Hoare triple of a decorated program is just a `Prop`; thus,
820---  to show that it is *valid*, we need to produce a proof of this
821---  proposition.
822-
823---  We will do this by extracting "proof obligations" from the decorations
824---  sprinkled throughout the program.
825-
826---  These obligations are often called *verification conditions*, because
827---  they are the facts that must be verified to see that the decorations
828---  are locally consistent and thus constitute a proof of validity of the
829---  outer triple.
830-
831---  ### Extracting Verification Conditions
832-
833---  The function `DCom.VerificationConditions` takes a decorated command
834---  `d` together with a precondition `P` and returns a *proposition* that,
835---  if it can be proved, implies that the triple
836-
837---    {{P}} d.erase {{d.postcondition}}
838-
839---  is valid.
840-
841---  It does this by walking over `d` and generating a big conjunction that
842---  includes
843-
844---  - local consistency checks for each form of command, plus
845-
846---  - uses of `->>` to bridge the gap between the assertions found inside a
847---    decorated command and the assertions imposed by the external
848---    precondition; these uses correspond to applications of the
849---    consequence rule.
850-
851---  *Local consistency* is defined as follows...
852-
853---  - The decorated command
854-
855---    skip {{Q}}
856-
857---  is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P` if `P ->> Q`.
858-
859---  - The sequential composition of `d1` and `d2` is locally consistent
860---    with respect to `P` if `d1` is locally consistent with respect to `P`
861---    and `d2` is locally consistent with respect to the postcondition of
862---    `d1`.
863-
864---  - An assignment
865-
866---    X := a {{Q}}
867-
868---  is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P` if:
869-
870---    P ->> Q [X |-> a]
871-
872---  - A conditional
873-
874---    if b then {{P1}} d1 else {{P2}} d2 end {{Q}}
875-
876---  is locally consistent with respect to precondition `P` if
877-
878---  (1) `P /\ b ->> P1`
879-
880---  (2) `P /\ ~b ->> P2`
881-
882---  (3) `d1` is locally consistent with respect to `P1`
883-
884---  (4) `d2` is locally consistent with respect to `P2`
885-
886---  (5) `d1.postcondition ->> Q`
887-
888---  (6) `d2.postcondition ->> Q`
889-
890---  - A loop
891-
892---    while b do {{Q}} d end {{R}}
893-
894---  is locally consistent with respect to precondition `P` if:
895-
896---  (1) `P ->> d.postcondition`
897-
898---  (2) `d.postcondition /\ b ->> Q`
899-
900---  (3) `d.postcondition /\ ~b ->> R`
901-
902---  (4) `d` is locally consistent with respect to `Q`
903-
904---  - A command with an extra assertion at the beginning
905-
906---    ->> {{Q}} d
907-
908---  is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P` if:
909-
910---  (1) `P ->> Q`
911-
912---  (2) `d` is locally consistent with respect to `Q`
913-
914---  - A command with an extra assertion at the end
915-
916---    d ->> {{Q}}
917-
918---  is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P` if:
919-
920---  (1) `d` is locally consistent with respect to `P`
921-
922---  (2) `d.postcondition ->> Q`
923-
924---  With all this in mind, we can write a *verification condition
925---  generator* that takes a decorated command and reads off a proposition
926---  saying that all its decorations are locally consistent.
927-
928---  Formally, since a decorated command is "waiting for its precondition"
929---  the main VC generator takes a `dcom` plus a given precondition as
930---  arguments.
931-
932---  Note to developers:
933---      HIDE: There was some discussion in 2016 about whether the VC
934---      generator should should use equivalence or implication in a few
935---      places. I (BCP) believe Phil (Wadler) changed some instances of the
936---      former to the latter.
937---
938---      HIDE: MRC'20: a written explanation of each part of this would be
939---      quite nice. BCP 21: Agreed!! (BCP 23: But it's kind of what's just
940---      above...)
941-
942-def DCom.VerificationConditions
943-    (P : Assertion) (d : DCom) : Prop :=
944-  match d with
945-  | .skip Q =>
946-      P ->> Q
947-  | .seq d1 d2 =>
948-      d1.VerificationConditions P ∧
949-      d2.VerificationConditions d1.postcondition
950-  | .asgn x a Q =>
951-      P ->> {{ Q [x ↦ ~a] }}
952-  | .cond b P1 d1 P2 d2 Q =>
953-      ({{ P ∧ b }} ->> P1) ∧
954-      ({{ P ∧ ¬ b }} ->> P2) ∧
955-      (d1.postcondition ->> Q) ∧
956-      (d2.postcondition ->> Q) ∧
957-      d1.VerificationConditions P1 ∧
958-      d2.VerificationConditions P2
959-  | .whileDo b bodyPre body q =>
960-      -- The body's postcondition is both the loop invariant
961-      -- and the precondition for the first iteration.
962-      (P ->> body.postcondition) ∧
963-      ({{ body.postcondition ∧ b }} ->> bodyPre) ∧
964-      ({{ body.postcondition ∧ ¬ b }} ->> q) ∧
965-      body.VerificationConditions bodyPre
966-  | .pre P' body =>
967-      (P ->> P') ∧ body.VerificationConditions P'
968-  | .post body Q =>
969-      body.VerificationConditions P ∧
970-      (body.postcondition ->> Q)
971-
972---  The following key theorem states that `DCom.VerificationConditions`
973---  does its job correctly. Not surprisingly, each of the Hoare Logic rules
974---  plays a critical role at some point in the proof.
975-
976-theorem verification_correct (d : DCom) (P : Assertion)
977-    (hvc : d.VerificationConditions P) :
978-    ValidHoareTriple P d.erase d.postcondition := by
979-  sorry
980-
981---  Now that all the pieces are in place, we can define what it means to
982---  verify an entire program.
983-
984-def Decorated.VerificationConditions
985-    (dec : Decorated) : Prop :=
986-  dec.body.VerificationConditions dec.pre
987-
988---  And this brings us to the main theorem of this section:
989-
990-theorem verification_conditions_correct (dec : Decorated)
991-    (hvc : dec.VerificationConditions) :
992-    dec.OuterTripleValid := by

1124---  ## Finding Loop Invariants
1125-
1126---  Once the outermost precondition and postcondition are chosen, the only
1127---  creative part of a verifying program using Hoare Logic is finding the
1128---  right loop invariants. The reason this is difficult is the same as the
1129---  reason that inductive mathematical proofs are:
1130-
1131---  - Strengthening a *loop invariant* means that you have a stronger
1132---    assumption to work with when trying to establish the postcondition of
1133---    the loop body, but it also means that the loop body's postcondition
1134---    is harder to prove.
1135-
1136---  - Similarly, strengthening an *induction hypothesis* means that you
1137---    have a stronger assumption to work with when trying to complete the
1138---    induction step of the proof, but it also means that the statement
1139---    being proved inductively is harder to prove.
1140-
1141---  This section explains how to approach the challenge of finding loop
1142---  invariants through a series of examples and exercises.
1143-
1144---  ### Example: Slow Subtraction
1145-
1146---  The following program subtracts the value of `X` from the value of `Y`
1147---  by repeatedly decrementing both `X` and `Y`. We want to verify its
1148---  correctness with respect to the pre- and postconditions shown:
1149-
1150---    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }}
1151---      while X <> 0 do
1152---        Y := Y - 1;
1153---        X := X - 1
1154---      end
1155---    {{ Y = n - m }}
1156-
1157---  To verify this program, we need to find an invariant `Inv` for the
1158---  loop. As a first step we can leave `Inv` as an unknown and build a
1159---  *skeleton* for the proof by applying the rules for local consistency,
1160---  working from the end of the program to the beginning, as usual, and
1161---  without doing any thinking at all yet.
1162-
1163---  This leads to the following skeleton:
1164-
1165---    (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }}  ->>                   (a)
1166---    (2)    {{ Inv }}
1167---             while X <> 0 do
1168---    (3)              {{ Inv /\ X <> 0 }}  ->>          (c)
1169---    (4)              {{ Inv [X |-> X-1] [Y |-> Y-1] }}
1170---               Y := Y - 1;
1171---    (5)              {{ Inv [X |-> X-1] }}
1172---               X := X - 1
1173---    (6)              {{ Inv }}
1174---             end
1175---    (7)    {{ Inv /\ ~ (X <> 0) }}  ->>                (b)
1176---    (8)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1177-
1178---  Examining this skeleton, we can see that any valid `Inv` will have to
1179---  respect three conditions:
1180-
1181---  - (a) it must be *weak* enough to be implied by the loop's
1182---    precondition, i.e., (1) must imply (2);
1183-
1184---  - (b) it must be *strong* enough to imply the program's postcondition,
1185---    i.e., (7) must imply (8);
1186-
1187---  - (c) it must be *preserved* by a single iteration of the loop,
1188---    assuming that the loop guard also evaluates to true, i.e., (3) must
1189---    imply (4).
1190-
1191---  These conditions are actually independent of the particular program and
1192---  specification we are considering: every loop invariant has to satisfy
1193---  them.
1194-
1195---  One way to find a loop invariant that simultaneously satisfies these
1196---  three conditions is by using an iterative process: start with a
1197---  "candidate" invariant (e.g., a guess or a heuristic choice) and check
1198---  the three conditions above; if any of the checks fails, try to use the
1199---  information that we get from the failure to produce another — hopefully
1200---  better — candidate invariant, and repeat.
1201-
1202---  For instance, in the reduce-to-zero example above, we saw that, for a
1203---  very simple loop, choosing `True` as a loop invariant did the job.
1204---  Maybe it will work here too. To find out, let's try instantiating `Inv`
1205---  with `True` in the skeleton above and see what we get...
1206-
1207---    (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }} ->>                    (a - OK)
1208---    (2)    {{ True }}
1209---             while X <> 0 do
1210---    (3)                   {{ True /\ X <> 0 }} ->>     (c - OK)
1211---    (4)                   {{ True }}
1212---               Y := Y - 1;
1213---    (5)                   {{ True }}
1214---               X := X - 1
1215---    (6)                   {{ True }}
1216---             end
1217---    (7)    {{ True /\ ~(X <> 0) }} ->>                 (b - WRONG!)
1218---    (8)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1219-
1220---  While conditions (a) and (c) are trivially satisfied, (b) is wrong: it
1221---  is not the case that `True /\ X = 0` (7) implies `Y = n - m` (8). In
1222---  fact, the two assertions are completely unrelated, so it is very easy
1223---  to find a counterexample to the implication (say, `Y = X = m = 0` and
1224---  `n = 1`).
1225-
1226---  If we want (b) to hold, we need to strengthen the loop invariant so
1227---  that it implies the postcondition (8). One simple way to do this is to
1228---  let the loop invariant *be* the postcondition. So let's return to our
1229---  skeleton, instantiate `Inv` with `Y = n - m`, and try checking
1230---  conditions (a) to (c) again.
1231-
1232---    (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }} ->>                        (a - WRONG!)
1233---    (2)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1234---             while X <> 0 do
1235---    (3)                     {{ Y = n - m /\ X <> 0 }} ->>  (c - WRONG!)
1236---    (4)                     {{ Y - 1 = n - m }}
1237---               Y := Y - 1;
1238---    (5)                     {{ Y = n - m }}
1239---               X := X - 1
1240---    (6)                     {{ Y = n - m }}
1241---             end
1242---    (7)    {{ Y = n - m /\ ~(X <> 0) }} ->>                (b - OK)
1243---    (8)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1244-
1245---  This time, condition (b) holds trivially, but (a) and (c) are broken.
1246---  Condition (a) requires that (1) `X = m /\ Y = n` implies (2)
1247---  `Y = n - m`. If we substitute `Y` by `n` we have to show that
1248---  `n = n - m` for arbitrary `m` and `n`, which is not the case (for
1249---  instance, when `m = n = 1`). Condition (c) requires that
1250---  `n - m - 1 = n - m`, which fails, for instance, for `n = 1` and
1251---  `m = 0`. So, although `Y = n - m` holds at the end of the loop, it does
1252---  not hold from the start, and it doesn't hold on each iteration; it is
1253---  not a correct loop invariant.
1254-
1255---  This failure is not very surprising: the variable `Y` changes during
1256---  the loop, while `m` and `n` are constant, so the assertion we chose
1257---  didn't have much chance of being a loop invariant!
1258-
1259---  To do better, we need to generalize (7) to some statement that is
1260---  equivalent to (8) when `X` is `0`, since this will be the case when the
1261---  loop terminates, and that "fills the gap" in some appropriate way when
1262---  `X` is nonzero. Looking at how the loop works, we can observe that `X`
1263---  and `Y` are decremented together until `X` reaches `0`. So, if `X = 2`
1264---  and `Y = 5` initially, after one iteration of the loop we obtain
1265---  `X = 1` and `Y = 4`; after two iterations `X = 0` and `Y = 3`; and then
1266---  the loop stops. Notice that the difference between `Y` and `X` stays
1267---  constant between iterations: initially, `Y = n` and `X = m`, and the
1268---  difference is always `n - m`. So let's try instantiating `Inv` in the
1269---  skeleton above with `Y - X = n - m`.
1270-
1271---    (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }} ->>                            (a - OK)
1272---    (2)    {{ Y - X = n - m }}
1273---             while X <> 0 do
1274---    (3)                    {{ Y - X = n - m /\ X <> 0 }} ->>   (c - OK)
1275---    (4)                    {{ (Y - 1) - (X - 1) = n - m }}
1276---               Y := Y - 1;
1277---    (5)                    {{ Y - (X - 1) = n - m }}
1278---               X := X - 1
1279---    (6)                    {{ Y - X = n - m }}
1280---             end
1281---    (7)    {{ Y - X = n - m /\ ~(X <> 0) }} ->>                (b - OK)
1282---    (8)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1283-
1284---  Success! Conditions (a), (b) and (c) all hold now. (To verify (c), we
1285---  need to check that, under the assumption that `X <> 0`, we have
1286---  `Y - X = (Y - 1) - (X - 1)`; this holds for all natural numbers `X` and
1287---  `Y`.)
1288-
1289---  Here is the final version of the decorated program:
1290-
1291-def subtractSlowlyDec (m n : Nat) : Decorated where
1292-  pre := ({{ X = m ∧ Y = n }})
1293-  body := dcom {
1294-    ->> {{ Y - X = n - m }}
1295-    while (X ≠ 0) do
1296-      {{ Y - X = n - m ∧ ¬ X = 0 }}
1297-      ->> {{ (Y - 1) - (X - 1) = n - m }}
1298-      Y := Y - 1 {{ Y - (X - 1) = n - m }};
1299-      X := X - 1 {{ Y - X = n - m }}
1300-    end
1301-      {{ Y - X = n - m ∧ X = 0 }}
1302-    ->> {{ Y = n - m }}
1303-  }
1304-
1305-theorem subtract_slowly_outer_triple_valid (m n : Nat) :
1306-    (subtractSlowlyDec m n).OuterTripleValid := by
1307-  sorry

1311---  ### Exercise (2 stars): slow_assignment ⭐⭐
1312-

1314---  variable `Y` is to start `Y` at `0`, then decrement `X` until it hits
1315---  `0`, incrementing `Y` at each step. Here is a program that implements
1316---  this idea. Fill in decorations and prove the decorated program correct.
1317---  (The proof should be very simple.)

1323-    (->> {{ ({{ Y + X = m }}) }}
1324-      while (X ≠ 0) do
1325-        {{ ({{ Y + X = m ∧ ¬ X = 0 }}) }}
1326-        ->> {{ ({{ Y + (X - 1) + 1 = m }}) }}
1327-        X := X - 1 {{ ({{ Y + X + 1 = m }}) }};

1330-      end
1331-        {{ ({{ Y + X = m ∧ X = 0 }}) }}

1333-  }

1339---  ### Example: Parity
1340-
1341---  Here is a cute way of computing the parity of a value initially stored
1342---  in `X`, due to Daniel Cristofani.
1343-
1344---    {{ X = m }}
1345---      while 2 <= X do
1346---        X := X - 2
1347---      end
1348---    {{ X = parity m }}
1349-
1350---  The `parity` function used in the specification is defined in Lean as
1351---  follows:
1352-
1353-def parity : Nat → Nat
1354-  | 0 => 0
1355-  | 1 => 1
1356-  | Nat.succ (Nat.succ n) => parity n
1357-
1358---  The postcondition does not hold at the beginning of the loop, since
1359---  `m = parity m` does not hold for an arbitrary `m`, so we cannot hope to
1360---  use that as a loop invariant. To find a loop invariant that works,
1361---  let's think a bit about what this loop does. On each iteration it
1362---  decrements `X` by `2`, which preserves the parity of `X`. So the parity
1363---  of `X` does not change, i.e., it is invariant. The initial value of `X`
1364---  is `m`, so the parity of `X` is always equal to the parity of `m`.
1365---  Using `parity X = parity m` as an invariant we obtain the following
1366---  decorated program:
1367-
1368---    {{ X = m }} ->>                                         (a - OK)
1369---    {{ parity X = parity m }}
1370---      while 2 <= X do
1371---                   {{ parity X = parity m /\ 2 <= X }} ->>  (c - OK)
1372---                   {{ parity (X-2) = parity m }}
1373---        X := X - 2
1374---                   {{ parity X = parity m }}
1375---      end
1376---    {{ parity X = parity m /\ ~(2 <= X) }} ->>              (b - OK)
1377---    {{ X = parity m }}
1378-
1379---  With this loop invariant, conditions (a), (b), and (c) are all
1380---  satisfied. For verifying (b), we observe that, when `X < 2`, we have
1381---  `parity X = X` (we can easily see this in the definition of `parity`).
1382---  For verifying (c), we observe that, when `2 <= X`, we have
1383---  `parity X = parity (X-2)`.
1384-
1385---  Note to developers:
1386---      `HIDE: A more complexly phrased loop invariant for the same program
1387---      [[
1388---              {{ X = m }}  ->>                        (a - OK)
1389---              {{ ev X <-> ev m }}
1390---            while 2 <= X do
1391---                {{ ev X <-> ev m /\ 2 <= X }}  ->>    (c - OK)
1392---                {{ ev (X-2) <-> ev m }}
1393---              X := X - 2
1394---                {{ ev X <-> ev m }}
1395---            end
1396---              {{ (ev X <-> ev m) /\ ~(2 <= X) }}  ->>     (b - OK)
1397---              {{ X=0 <-> ev m }}
1398---      ]]`
1399---
1400---      `HIDE: find_parity'_dec; more complicated phrasing of invariant
1401---      there is very little resemblance between the invariant and the
1402---      postcondition -- the implication is also non-obvious, and the
1403---      X <= m condition makes the invariant more complicated
1404---      [[
1405---       {{ X = m }} ->>
1406---       {{ X <= m /\ ev (m - X) }}
1407---      while 2 <= X do
1408---         {{ X <= m /\ ev (m - X) /\ 2 <= X }} ->>
1409---         {{ X - 2 <= m /\ ev (m - (X - 2)) }}

1413---       {{ X <= m /\ ev (m - X) /\ ~(2 <= X) }} ->>

1509-      X := X - 2 {{ inv }}
1510-    end
1511-      {{ exit }}

1513-  }

1680---  WORK IN CLASS
1681-
1682---  The first thing to note is that the loop reads `X` but doesn't change
1683---  its value. As we saw in the previous example, it can be a good idea in
1684---  such cases to add `X = m` to the loop invariant. The other thing that
1685---  we know is often useful in the loop invariant is the postcondition, so
1686---  let's add that too, leading to the candidate loop invariant
1687---  `Z = m * m /\ X = m`.
1688-
1689---    {{ X = m }} ->>                                       (a - WRONG)
1690---    {{ 0 = m*m /\ X = m }}

1692---                   {{ 0 = m*m /\ X = m }};
1693---      Z := 0
1694---                   {{ Z = m*m /\ X = m }};
1695---      while Y <> X do
1696---                   {{ Z = m*m /\ X = m /\ Y <> X }} ->>   (c - WRONG)
1697---                   {{ Z+X = m*m /\ X = m }}

1699---                   {{ Z = m*m /\ X = m }};
1700---        Y := Y + 1
1701---                   {{ Z = m*m /\ X = m }}
1702---      end
1703---    {{ Z = m*m /\ X = m /\ ~(Y <> X) }} ->>               (b - OK)

1707---  starts at `0` and works itself up to `m*m`, we can't expect `Z` to be
1708---  `m*m` from the start. If we look at how `Z` progresses in the loop,
1709---  after the 1st iteration `Z = m`, after the 2nd iteration `Z = 2*m`, and
1710---  at the end `Z = m*m`. Since the variable `Y` tracks how many times we
1711---  go through the loop, this leads us to derive a new loop invariant
1712---  candidate: `Z = Y*m /\ X = m`.
1713-
1714---    {{ X = m }} ->>                                        (a - OK)
1715---    {{ 0 = 0*m /\ X = m }}
1716---      Y := 0
1717---                    {{ 0 = Y*m /\ X = m }};
1718---      Z := 0
1719---                    {{ Z = Y*m /\ X = m }};
1720---      while Y <> X do
1721---                    {{ Z = Y*m /\ X = m /\ Y <> X }} ->>   (c - OK)
1722---                    {{ Z+X = (Y+1)*m /\ X = m }}
1723---        Z := Z + X
1724---                    {{ Z = (Y+1)*m /\ X = m }};
1725---        Y := Y + 1
1726---                    {{ Z = Y*m /\ X = m }}
1727---      end
1728---    {{ Z = Y*m /\ X = m /\ ~(Y <> X) }} ->>                (b - OK)

2034---    X := 0;
2035---      {{ c = X + c /\ 0 = 0 }}
2036---    Y := 0;

2042---        {{ Z + 1 = X + 1 + c /\ Y = 0 }}

2044---        {{ Z + 1 = X + c /\ Y = 0 }}
2045---      Z := Z + 1
2046---        {{ Z = X + c /\ Y = 0 }}
2047---    end;
2048---      {{ Z = X + c /\ Y = 0 /\ ~(X <> a) }} ->>
2049---      {{ Z = a + Y + c }}
2050---    while Y <> b do
2051---        {{ Z = a + Y + c /\ Y <> b }} ->>
2052---        {{ Z + 1 = a + Y + 1 + c }}

2056---        {{ Z = a + Y + c }}

2197---  Note to developers:
2198---      `HIDE: Another (very) good exercise from 09-mid2 -- just needs typeset
2199---
2200---      The notion of weakest precondition has a natural dual : given a
2201---      precondition and a command, we can ask what is the strongest
2202---      postcondition of the command with respect to the
2203---      precondition. Formally, we can define it like this:
2204---
2205---      Q is the strongest postcondition of c for P if:
2206---
2207---      (a) {{P}} c {{Q}}, and
2208---
2209---      (b) if Q′ is an assertion such that {{P}}c{{Q′}},
2210---          then Q st implies Q′ st, for all states st.
2211---
2212---      Q is the strongest (most difficult to satisfy) assertion that is
2213---      guaranteed to hold after c if P holds before. For example, the
2214---      strongest postcondition of the command skip with respect to the
2215---      precondition Y = 1 is Y = 1. Similarly, the postcondition in...
2216---
2217---               {{ Y = y }}
2218---                 if !Y === A0 then X := A0 else Y := !Y *** A2
2219---               {{ (Y = y = X = 0) ∨ (Y = 2*y ∧ y <> 0) }}
2220---
2221---      ...is the strongest one.
2222---
2223---      Complete each of the following Hoare triples with the strongest
2224---      postcondition for the given command and precondition.
2225---
2226---      (a) {{Y=1}} X:=!Y+++A1 {{?}}
2227---      (b) {{True}} X:=A5 {{?}}
2228---      (c) {{ True }} skip {{ ? }}
2229---      (d) {{ True }} while true do skip {{ ? }}
2230---      (e) {{ X = x ∧ Y = y }}
2231---          while BNot (!X === A0) do (
2232---                          Y := !Y +++ A2;
2233---                          X := !X --- A1
2234---                        )
2235---          {{ ? }}`

2442-/- It is easy to go from a `DCom` to a `Com` by erasing all

2445-def DCom.erase (d : DCom) : Com :=
2446-  match d with
2447-  | .skip => .skip
2448-  | .seq d1 d2 => .seq d1.erase d2.erase
2449-  | .asgn x a => .asgn x a

2454-/- We can express what it means for a decorated program to
2455-be correct as follows: -/

2457-def Decorated.OuterTripleValid (dec : Decorated) : Prop :=

2459-
2460-/- This VC generator is derived from Mike Gordon,
2461-"Background reading on Hoare Logic,"
2462-https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/archive/mjcg/HL/Notes/Notes.pdf -/
2463-
2464-def DCom.awp (post : Assertion) (d : DCom) : Assertion :=
2465-  match d with
2466-  | .skip => post
2467-  | .seq d1 d2 => d1.awp (d2.awp post)
2468-  | .asgn x a => {{ post [x ↦ ~a] }}
2469-  | .cond b d1 d2 =>
2470-      fun st =>
2471-        (b.eval st = true ∧ d1.awp post st) ∨
2472-        (b.eval st = false ∧ d2.awp post st)
2473-  | .whileDo _ invariant _ => invariant
2474-  | .assert assertion => fun st => assertion st ∧ post st
2475-
2476-def DCom.VerificationConditions
2477-    (post : Assertion) (d : DCom) : Prop :=
2478-  match d with
2479-  | .seq d1 d2 =>
2480-      d1.VerificationConditions (d2.awp post) ∧
2481-      d2.VerificationConditions post
2482-  | .cond _ d1 d2 =>
2483-      d1.VerificationConditions post ∧
2484-      d2.VerificationConditions post
2485-  | .whileDo b invariant body =>
2486-      (∀ st, invariant st ∧ b.eval st ≠ true → post st) ∧
2487-      (∀ st, invariant st ∧ b.eval st = true →
2488-        body.awp invariant st) ∧
2489-      body.VerificationConditions invariant
2490-  | _ => True
2491-
2492-theorem vc_correct (d : DCom) (post : Assertion)
2493-    (hvc : d.VerificationConditions post) :
2494-    ValidHoareTriple (d.awp post) d.erase post := by
2495-  sorry

2498-    (dec : Decorated) : Prop :=
2499-  (dec.pre ->> dec.body.awp dec.post) ∧
2500-  dec.body.VerificationConditions dec.post

2647-  }
2648-  post := ({{ Z = m * m }})
2649-
2650-theorem square_simpler_outer_triple_valid (m : Nat) :
2651-    (squareSimplerDec m).OuterTripleValid := by
2652-  sorry
2653-
2654-def twoLoopsDec (a b c : Nat) : Decorated where
2655-  pre := ({{ True }})
2656-  body := sdcom {
2657-    X := 0;
2658-    Y := 0;
2659-    Z := ~(Aexp.num c);
2660-    (while (X ≠ ~(Aexp.num a)) do
2661-      {{ Z = X + c ∧ Y = 0 }}
2662-      X := X + 1;
2663-      Z := Z + 1
2664-    end);
2665-    while (Y ≠ ~(Aexp.num b)) do
2666-      {{ Z = a + Y + c }}
2667-      Y := Y + 1;
2668-      Z := Z + 1
2669-    end
2670-  }
2671-  post := ({{ Z = a + b + c }})
2672-
2673-theorem two_loops_correct (a b c : Nat) :
2674-    (twoLoopsDec a b c).OuterTripleValid := by
2675-  sorry
2676-
2677-def subtractSlowlyDec (m p : Nat) : Decorated where
2678-  pre := ({{ X = m ∧ Z = p }})
2679-  body := sdcom {
2680-    while (X ≠ 0) do
2681-      {{ Z - X = p - m }}
2682-      Z := Z - 1;
2683-      X := X - 1
2684-    end
2685-  }
2686-  post := ({{ Z = p - m }})
2687-
2688-theorem subtract_slowly_correct (m p : Nat) :
2689-    (subtractSlowlyDec m p).OuterTripleValid := by
2690-  sorry
2691-
2692-def dpow2Down (n : Nat) : Decorated where
2693-  pre := ({{ True }})
2694-  body := sdcom {
2695-    X := 0;
2696-    Y := 1;
2697-    Z := 1;
2698-    while (X ≠ ~(Aexp.num n)) do
2699-      {{ Y = pow2 (X + 1) - 1 ∧ Z = pow2 X }}
2700-      Z := 2 * Z;
2701-      Y := Y + Z;
2702-      X := X + 1
2703-    end
2704-  }
2705-  post := ({{ Y = pow2 (n + 1) - 1 }})
2706-
2707-theorem dpow2_down_correct (n : Nat) :
2708-    (dpow2Down n).OuterTripleValid := by
2709-  sorry
2710-
2711-def factorialDec (m : Nat) : Decorated where
2712-  pre := ({{ X = m }})
2713-  body := sdcom {
2714-    Y := 1;
2715-    while (X ≠ 0) do
2716-      {{ Y * fact X = fact m }}
2717-      Y := Y * X;
2718-      X := X - 1
2719-    end
2720-  }
2721-  post := ({{ Y = fact m }})
2722-
2723-theorem factorial_outer_triple_valid (m : Nat) :
2724-    (factorialDec m).OuterTripleValid := by
2725-  sorry
2726-
2727-def T : Ident := "T"
2728-
2729-def dfib (n : Nat) : Decorated where
2730-  pre := ({{ True }})
2731-  body := sdcom {
2732-    X := 1;
2733-    Y := 1;
2734-    Z := 1;
2735-    while (X ≠ ~(Aexp.num (1 + n))) do
2736-      {{ Z = fib X ∧ Y = fib (Nat.pred X) ∧ X > 0 }}
2737-      T := Z;
2738-      Z := Z + Y;
2739-      Y := T;
2740-      X := 1 + X
2741-    end
2742-  }
2743-  post := ({{ Y = fib n }})
2744-
2745-theorem dfib_correct (n : Nat) :
2746-    (dfib n).OuterTripleValid := by
2747-  sorry

2751-
2752---  ## Weakest Preconditions (Optional)
2753-
2754---  Note to developers:
2755---      HIDE: BCP 21: We talked about moving this stuff to the HoareAsLogic
2756---      chapter to lighten this chapter, but it fits awkwardly there, so
2757---      I'm leaving it here. It's optional anyway. We might consider
2758---      assigning one of the exercises as advanced-only though.
2759-
2760---  Some preconditions are more interesting than others. For example, the
2761---  Hoare triple
2762-
2763---    {{ False }}  X := Y + 1  {{ X <= 5 }}
2764-
2765---  is *not* very interesting: although it is perfectly valid, it tells us
2766---  nothing useful. Since the precondition isn't satisfied by any state, it
2767---  doesn't describe any situations where we can use the command
2768---  `X := Y + 1` to achieve the postcondition `X <= 5`.
2769-
2770---  By contrast,
2771-
2772---    {{ Y <= 4 /\ Z = 0 }}  X := Y + 1 {{ X <= 5 }}
2773-
2774---  has a useful precondition: it tells us that, if we can somehow create a
2775---  situation in which we know that `Y <= 4 /\ Z = 0`, then running this
2776---  command will produce a state satisfying the postcondition. However,
2777---  this precondition is not as useful as it could be, because the `Z = 0`
2778---  clause in the precondition actually has nothing to do with the
2779---  postcondition `X <= 5`.
2780-
2781---  The *most* useful precondition for this command is this one:
2782-
2783---    {{ Y <= 4 }}  X := Y + 1  {{ X <= 5 }}
2784-
2785---  The assertion `Y <= 4` is called the *weakest precondition* of
2786---  `X := Y + 1` with respect to the postcondition `X <= 5`.
2787-
2788---  Assertion `Y <= 4` is a *weakest precondition* of command `X := Y + 1`
2789---  with respect to postcondition `X <= 5`. Think of *weakest* here as
2790---  meaning "easiest to satisfy": a weakest precondition is one that as
2791---  many states as possible can satisfy.
2792-
2793---  `P` is a weakest precondition of command `c` for postcondition `Q` if
2794-
2795---  - `P` is a precondition, that is, `{{P}} c {{Q}}`; and
2796-
2797---  - `P` is at least as weak as all other preconditions, that is, if
2798---    `{{P'}} c {{Q}}` then `P' ->> P`.
2799-
2800---  Note that weakest preconditions need not be unique. For example,
2801---  `Y <= 4` was a weakest precondition above, but so are the logically
2802---  equivalent assertions `Y < 5`, `Y <= 2 * 2`, etc. It is easy to show
2803---  that any two weakest preconditions `P` and `P'` of a command `c` with
2804---  respect to postcondition `Q` are logically equivalent; that is,
2805---  `P <<->> P'`.
2806-
2807-def IsWp (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
2808-  ValidHoareTriple P c Q ∧
2809-  ∀ P' : Assertion, {{ P' }} ~c {{ Q }} → P' ->> P
2810-
2811---  ### Exercise (1 star): wp (Optional) ⭐
2812-
2813---  What are weakest preconditions of the following commands for the
2814---  following postconditions?
2815-
2816---    1) {{ ? }}  skip  {{ X = 5 }}
2817-
2818---    2) {{ ? }}  X := Y + Z {{ X = 5 }}
2819-
2820---    3) {{ ? }}  X := Y  {{ X = Y }}
2821-
2822---    4) {{ ? }}
2823---     if X = 0 then Y := Z + 1 else Y := W + 2 end
2824---     {{ Y = 5 }}
2825-
2826---    5) {{ ? }}
2827---     X := 5
2828---     {{ X = 0 }}
2829-
2830---    6) {{ ? }}
2831---     while true do X := 0 end
2832---     {{ X = 0 }}
2833-
2834---    1) X = 5
2835---    2) Y + Z = 5
2836---    3) True
2837---    4) (X = 0 /\ Z = 4) \/ (X <> 0 /\ W = 3)
2838---    5) False
2839---    6) True
2840-
2841---  ### Exercise (3 stars): is_wp (Advanced, Optional) ⭐⭐⭐
2842-
2843---  Prove formally, using the definition of `ValidHoareTriple`, that
2844---  `Y <= 4` is indeed a weakest precondition of `X := Y + 1` with respect
2845---  to postcondition `X <= 5`.
2846-
2847-theorem is_wp_example :
2848-    IsWp ({{ Y ≤ 4 }}) (imp {X := Y + 1})
2849-      ({{ X ≤ 5 }}) := by
2850-  sorry
2851-
2852---  ### Exercise (2 stars): hoare_asgn_weakest (Advanced, Optional) ⭐⭐
2853-
2854---  Show that the precondition in the rule `hoare_asgn` is in fact the
2855---  weakest precondition.
2856-
2857-theorem hoare_asgn_weakest
2858-    (Q : Assertion) (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) :
2859-    IsWp ({{ Q [x ↦ ~a] }}) (imp {x := ~a}) Q := by
2860-  refine ⟨hoare_asgn, ?_⟩
2861-  intro P hP
2862-  rw [validHoareTriple_def] at hP
2863-  intro st hst
2864-  rw [Assertion.subst_apply]
2865-  apply hP _ hst
2866-  exact Com.EvalR.asgn rfl
2867-
2868---  ### Exercise (2 stars): hoare_havoc_weakest (Advanced, Optional) ⭐⭐
2869-
2870---  Show that your `havoc_pre` function from the `himp_hoare` exercise in
2871---  the Hoare chapter returns a weakest precondition.
2872-
2873-namespace Himp2
2874-
2875-theorem hoare_havoc_weakest (P Q : Assertion) (x : Ident)
2876-    (h : Himp.ValidHoareTriple P (Himp.Com.havoc x) Q) :
2877-    P ->> Himp.havoc_pre x Q := by
2878-  sorry
2879-
2880-end Himp2

8---  # Imp: Simple Imperative Programs
9-
10---  Note to developers (before next release):
11---      Needs some WORKINCLASSes and some quizzes
12---
