14---      add C-style arrays (i.e., indirect read/write). This sets up some
15---      really nice challenge problems in Hoare (reasoning about arrays /
16---      aliasing / etc.).
17---
18---      SOONER: BCP 25: Maybe we should write / instead of && in
19---      assertions, to save a mismatch in the `dec_minimum` exercise in
20---      Hoare2?
21---
22---      At some point we could consider moving material from the old
23---      HoareLists to this chapter (and into later files, as appropriate).
24---      We haven't done it yet because it's a shame to complicate the nice
25---      simple presentation here when it's used as the basis for
26---      applications like Xavier's static analysis lectures. Also, we now
27---      have a whole volume on real separation logic...
28---
29---      MWH (port note): The Rocq chapter's "Rocq Automation" tour has been
30---      retooled here for Lean. The tactic combinators `try` and `repeat`
31---      (and the custom-tactic `macro`) are introduced in this chapter;
32---      `<;>` and `simp` were already introduced in Logical Foundations
33---      (`<;>` in `Induction`) so we use them freely and the `<;>` section
34---      below is a recap. For linear arithmetic we use `lia`; NOTE that LF
35---      currently introduces `omega`, not `lia`, so this needs to be
36---      reconciled volume-wide (either introduce `lia` in LF, or keep
37---      `omega`).
38-
39---  In this chapter, we take a more serious look at how to use Lean as a
40---  tool to study other things. Our case study is a *simple imperative
41---  programming language* called Imp, embodying a tiny core fragment of
42---  conventional mainstream languages such as C and Java.
43-
44---  Here is a familiar mathematical function written in Imp.
45-
46---    Z := X;
47---    Y := 1;
48---    while (Z ≠ 0) {
49---      Y := Y * Z;
50---      Z := Z - 1;
51---    }
52-
53---  We concentrate here on defining the *syntax* and *semantics* of Imp;
54---  later in this volume we develop a theory of *program equivalence* and
55---  introduce *Hoare Logic*, a popular logic for reasoning about imperative
56---  programs.
57-
58---  We build Imp in three layers. The first — a core language of
59---  *arithmetic and boolean expressions* — is developed in its own chapter,
60---  *Slang*; read that one first. There you meet the abstract syntax of
61---  arithmetic expressions (`Aexp`) and boolean expressions (`Bexp`), their
62---  evaluation both as a recursive *function* and as an inductive
63---  *relation* (proved equivalent), and a small `optimize0plus` program
64---  transformation together with its correctness proof. Those expressions
65---  are *variable-free*.
66-
67---  This chapter picks up from there. First we extend the expressions with
68---  *variables*; then we add a language of *commands* — assignment,
69---  conditionals, sequencing, and loops.
70-
71---  ## Expressions With Variables
72-
73---  Let's return to defining Imp. The next thing we need to do is to enrich
74---  our arithmetic and boolean expressions with variables. To keep things
75---  simple, we'll assume that all variables are global and that they only
76---  hold numbers.
77-
78---  ### States
79-
80---  Since we'll want to look variables up to find out their current values,
81---  we'll use total maps from the `Maps` chapter. A *machine state* (or
82---  just *state*) represents the current values of all variables at some
83---  point in the execution of a program.
84-
85---  For simplicity, we assume that the state is defined for *all*
86---  variables, even though any given program is only able to mention a
87---  finite number of them. Because each variable stores a natural number,
88---  we represent the state as a total map from strings (variable names) to
89---  `Nat`, and will use `0` as the default value in the store.
90-
91---  We give the type of variable identifiers a name, `Ident`. For now it is
92---  just `String`; naming it makes the intent clearer.
93-
94-open scoped MyGetElem
95-
96-abbrev Ident := String
97-abbrev State := TotalMap Ident Nat
98-
99---  ### Syntax
100-
101---  We can add variables to the arithmetic expressions we had before simply
102---  by including one more constructor. (This is a fresh `Aexp`, replacing
103---  the variable-free one from the *Slang* chapter.)
104-
105---  Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
106---      That should be a live chapter link.
107-
108-inductive Aexp where
109-  | num (n : Nat)
110-  | id (x : Ident)                -- NEW
111-  | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
112-  | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp)
113-  | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp)
114-
115---  Note to developers (Chris Henson @chenson2018):
116---      Rather than define identifiers as Ident, a more general approach is
117---      to use a **type variable** with `DecidableEq` (as the `Maps`
118---      chapter does), threaded through `Aexp`/`Bexp`/`Com`/`State`.
119---      Stashed for a future decision; the parameterized version would look
120---      like:
121---
122---      `inductive Aexp (V : Type) where
123---        | num (n : Nat)
124---        | id (x : V)
125---        | plus (a1 a2 : Aexp V)
126---        | minus (a1 a2 : Aexp V)
127---        | mult (a1 a2 : Aexp V)
128---      -- … then `Bexp V`, `Com V`, `abbrev State (V) [DecidableEq V] :=
129---      -- TotalMap V Nat`, and `[DecidableEq V]` wherever a lookup/update is
130---      -- performed.`
131-
132---  The `Bexp` definition is unchanged, except that it now refers to the
133---  new `Aexp`.
134-
135-inductive Bexp where
136-  | bool (b : Bool)
137-  | eq (a1 a2 : Aexp)
138-  | neq (a1 a2 : Aexp)
139-  | le (a1 a2 : Aexp)
140-  | gt (a1 a2 : Aexp)
141-  | not (b : Bexp)
142-  | and (b1 b2 : Bexp)
143-
144---  Defining a few variable names as shorthands will make examples easier
145---  to read.
146-
147-def W : Ident := "W"
148-def X : Ident := "X"
149-def Y : Ident := "Y"
150-def Z : Ident := "Z"
151-
152---  ### Notations
153-
154---  To make Imp programs easier to read and write, we introduce some
155---  notations.
156-
157---  You do not need to understand exactly what these declarations do.
158---  Briefly, though, here is how the two blocks below fit together:
159-
160---  - The `declare_syntax_cat` directive adds a new non-terminal to Lean's
161---    grammar, called `imp_aexp`. We'll add additional non-terminals
162---    further below.
163-
164---  - Each `syntax` directive defines a grammar production, of which there
165---    are eight in total. The first two define literals, `num` and `ident`,
166---    as `imp_aexp`s. The next several directives define productions for
167---    building larger expressions, with some annotations to define
168---    precedence, etc.
169-
170---  - Finally, `macro_rules` is used to translate each production of the
171---    `imp_aexp` nonterminal into a Lean expression.
172-
173---  Boolean expressions and, later, commands follow this same pattern
174---  exactly, so their declarations are collapsed where they appear: open
175---  one if you want to see the pattern repeated, and skip them otherwise.
176-
177-/-- Arithmetic expressions of Imp -/
178-declare_syntax_cat imp_aexp
179-/-- Numeric literal -/
180-syntax:max num : imp_aexp
181-/-- Variable reference -/
182-syntax:max ident : imp_aexp
183-/-- Addition -/
184-syntax:65 imp_aexp:65 " + " imp_aexp:66 : imp_aexp
185-/-- Subtraction -/
186-syntax:65 imp_aexp:65 " - " imp_aexp:66 : imp_aexp
187-/-- Multiplication -/
188-syntax:70 imp_aexp:70 " * " imp_aexp:71 : imp_aexp
189-/-- Parentheses for grouping -/
190-syntax "(" imp_aexp ")" : imp_aexp
191-/-- Escape to Lean -/
192-syntax:max "~" term:max : imp_aexp
193-
194-/-- Embed an Imp arithmetic expression into a Lean term -/
195-syntax:min "aexp " "{" imp_aexp "}" : term
196-
197-open Lean in
198-macro_rules
199-  | `(aexp { $n:num }) => `(Aexp.num $(quote n.getNat))
200-  | `(aexp { $x:ident }) => `(Aexp.id $x)
201-  | `(aexp { ~$e }) => pure e
202-  | `(aexp { $a + $b }) => `(Aexp.plus (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
203-  | `(aexp { $a - $b }) => `(Aexp.minus (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
204-  | `(aexp { $a * $b }) => `(Aexp.mult (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
205-  | `(aexp { ($a) }) => `(aexp {$a})
206-
207---  THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: boolean expressions
208-
209-/-- Boolean expressions of Imp -/
210-declare_syntax_cat imp_bexp
211-/-- Boolean literal (`true` or `false`) -/
212-syntax:max ident : imp_bexp
213-/-- Equality of arithmetic expressions -/
214-syntax:50 imp_aexp:51 " = " imp_aexp:51 : imp_bexp
215-/-- Disequality of arithmetic expressions -/
216-syntax:50 imp_aexp:51 " ≠ " imp_aexp:51 : imp_bexp
217-/-- Less than or equal -/
218-syntax:50 imp_aexp:51 " ≤ " imp_aexp:51 : imp_bexp
219-/-- Greater than -/
220-syntax:50 imp_aexp:51 " > " imp_aexp:51 : imp_bexp
221-/-- Boolean negation -/
222-syntax:70 "¬ " imp_bexp:70 : imp_bexp
223-/-- Boolean conjunction -/
224-syntax:35 imp_bexp:36 " ∧ " imp_bexp:35 : imp_bexp
225-/-- Parentheses for grouping -/
226-syntax "(" imp_bexp ")" : imp_bexp
227-/-- Escape to Lean -/
228-syntax:max "~" term:max : imp_bexp
229-
230-/-- Embed an Imp boolean expression into a Lean term -/
231-syntax:min "bexp " "{" imp_bexp "}" : term
232-
233---  END DETAILS
234-
235---  THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: boolean expressions, macro rules
236-
237-open Lean in
238-macro_rules
239-  | `(bexp { $x:ident }) =>
240-    match x.getId with
241-    | `true  => `(Bexp.bool true)
242-    | `false => `(Bexp.bool false)
243-    | _      => Macro.throwErrorAt x s!"expected 'true' or 'false', got '{x.getId}'"
244-  | `(bexp { ~$e }) => pure e
245-  | `(bexp { $a:imp_aexp = $b:imp_aexp }) => `(Bexp.eq (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
246-  | `(bexp { $a:imp_aexp ≠ $b:imp_aexp }) => `(Bexp.neq (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
247-  | `(bexp { $a:imp_aexp ≤ $b:imp_aexp }) => `(Bexp.le (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
248-  | `(bexp { $a:imp_aexp > $b:imp_aexp }) => `(Bexp.gt (aexp {$a}) (aexp {$b}))
249-  | `(bexp { ¬ $b:imp_bexp }) => `(Bexp.not (bexp {$b}))
250-  | `(bexp { $b1:imp_bexp ∧ $b2:imp_bexp }) => `(Bexp.and (bexp {$b1}) (bexp {$b2}))
251-  | `(bexp { ($b:imp_bexp) }) => `(bexp {$b})
252-
253---  END DETAILS
254-
255-#check aexp { 3 + (X * 2) }
256-#check bexp { true ∧ ¬(X ≤ 4) }
257-
258---  ### Delaborators
259-
260---  The notations above are *input* only: they teach Lean how to **read**
261---  `aexp
262---  { … }` and `bexp { … }`, but Lean still **prints** an expression
263---  using its raw constructors -- `example_aexp` shows up as
264---  `Aexp.plus (Aexp.num 3) …` rather than `aexp { 3 + X * 2 }`. A
265---  *delaborator* closes the loop. Where a `macro` turns surface syntax
266---  into a term (*elaboration*), a delaborator does the reverse: it turns
267---  an elaborated term back into surface syntax so that Lean's own output
268---  uses our concrete Imp notation.
269-
270---  Each delaborator walks a term of the given type and rebuilds the
271---  matching piece of `imp_aexp`/`imp_bexp` syntax; a subterm Lean doesn't
272---  recognize is printed with the `~` escape. The `@[delab …]` attribute
273---  registers the top-level function to fire whenever Lean is about to
274---  display a term headed by one of those constructors -- unless notation
275---  printing has been switched off with `set_option pp.notation false`,
276---  which lets us fall back to the raw constructors when debugging (see
277---  *Desugaring Notations* below). The companion *category parenthesizer*
278---  re-inserts the parentheses the grammar's precedences demand, so that,
279---  e.g., `(1 + 2) * 3` prints with its parentheses intact.
280-
281---  You do not need to understand the details, and the code is collapsed
282---  below for that reason. The result is that a `#check`, an `#eval`, or a
283---  proof goal mentioning an Imp expression is displayed in readable Imp
284---  syntax rather than as a pile of constructors.
285-
286---  THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: printing expressions back
287-
288-namespace Imp.Delab
289-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Parenthesizer
290-
291-/-- Re-inserts parentheses in `imp_aexp` output according to the grammar's precedences. -/
292-@[category_parenthesizer imp_aexp]
293-def imp_aexp.parenthesizer : CategoryParenthesizer | prec => do
294-  maybeParenthesize `imp_aexp true wrapParens prec <|
295-    parenthesizeCategoryCore `imp_aexp prec
296-where
297-  wrapParens (stx : Syntax) : Syntax := Unhygienic.run do
298-    let pstx ← `(($(⟨stx⟩)))
299-    return pstx.raw.setInfo (SourceInfo.fromRef stx)
300-
301-/-- Re-inserts parentheses in `imp_bexp` output according to the grammar's precedences. -/
302-@[category_parenthesizer imp_bexp]
303-def imp_bexp.parenthesizer : CategoryParenthesizer | prec => do
304-  maybeParenthesize `imp_bexp true wrapParens prec <|
305-    parenthesizeCategoryCore `imp_bexp prec
306-where
307-  wrapParens (stx : Syntax) : Syntax := Unhygienic.run do
308-    let pstx ← `(($(⟨stx⟩)))
309-    return pstx.raw.setInfo (SourceInfo.fromRef stx)
310-
311-/-- Tag freshly built syntax with the term info that Lean's pretty printer expects. -/
312-def annAsTerm {any} (stx : TSyntax any) : DelabM (TSyntax any) :=
313-  (⟨·⟩) <$> annotateTermInfo ⟨stx.raw⟩
314-
315-/-- Rebuild `imp_aexp` concrete syntax from an `Aexp` term. -/
316-partial def delabAexpInner : DelabM (TSyntax `imp_aexp) := do
317-  let e ← getExpr
318-  let stx ←
319-    match_expr e with
320-    | Aexp.num _ =>
321-      match (← withAppArg getExpr).nat? with
322-      | some v => pure ⟨Syntax.mkNumLit (toString v) |>.raw⟩
323-      | none   => `(imp_aexp| ~$(← withAppArg delab))
324-    | Aexp.id _ =>
325-      -- A variable reference like aexp { X } elaborates to Aexp.id X where X is the
326-      -- declared Ident constant, so the delaborators print the constant's name as a
327-      -- bare identifier (and also handle the .id "X" string-literal form).
328-      match ← withAppArg getExpr with
329-      | .const nm _      => `(imp_aexp| $(mkIdent nm):ident)
330-      | .lit (.strVal s) => `(imp_aexp| $(mkIdent (.mkSimple s)):ident)
331-      | _                => `(imp_aexp| ~$(← withAppArg delab))
332-    | Aexp.plus _ _ =>
333-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
334-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
335-      `(imp_aexp| $s1 + $s2)
336-    | Aexp.minus _ _ =>
337-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
338-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
339-      `(imp_aexp| $s1 - $s2)
340-    | Aexp.mult _ _ =>
341-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
342-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
343-      `(imp_aexp| $s1 * $s2)
344-    | _ => `(imp_aexp| ~$(← delab))
345-  annAsTerm stx
346-
347-/-- Rebuild `imp_bexp` concrete syntax from a `Bexp` term. -/
348-partial def delabBexpInner : DelabM (TSyntax `imp_bexp) := do
349-  let e ← getExpr
350-  let stx ←
351-    match_expr e with
352-    | Bexp.bool _ =>
353-      match ← withAppArg getExpr with
354-      | .const ``Bool.true _  => `(imp_bexp| $(mkIdent `true):ident)
355-      | .const ``Bool.false _ => `(imp_bexp| $(mkIdent `false):ident)
356-      | _                     => `(imp_bexp| ~$(← withAppArg delab))
357-    | Bexp.eq _ _ =>
358-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
359-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
360-      `(imp_bexp| $s1:imp_aexp = $s2:imp_aexp)
361-    | Bexp.neq _ _ =>
362-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
363-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
364-      `(imp_bexp| $s1:imp_aexp ≠ $s2:imp_aexp)
365-    | Bexp.le _ _ =>
366-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
367-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
368-      `(imp_bexp| $s1:imp_aexp ≤ $s2:imp_aexp)
369-    | Bexp.gt _ _ =>
370-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpInner
371-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
372-      `(imp_bexp| $s1:imp_aexp > $s2:imp_aexp)
373-    | Bexp.not _ =>
374-      let s ← withAppArg delabBexpInner
375-      `(imp_bexp| ¬ $s)
376-    | Bexp.and _ _ =>
377-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabBexpInner
378-      let s2 ← withAppArg delabBexpInner
379-      `(imp_bexp| $s1 ∧ $s2)
380-    | _ => `(imp_bexp| ~$(← delab))
381-  annAsTerm stx

392-@[delab app.Aexp.num, delab app.Aexp.id, delab app.Aexp.plus,
393-  delab app.Aexp.minus, delab app.Aexp.mult]
394-partial def delabAexp : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
395-  -- This delaborator only understands `Aexp`'s constructors -- bail otherwise.
396-  guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
397-    | Aexp.num _ => true
398-    | Aexp.id _ => true
399-    | Aexp.plus _ _ => true
400-    | Aexp.minus _ _ => true
401-    | Aexp.mult _ _ => true
402-    | _ => false
403-  match ← delabAexpInner with
404-  | `(imp_aexp| ~$e) => pure e
405-  | e => `(term| aexp { $e })

408-  delab app.Bexp.gt, delab app.Bexp.not, delab app.Bexp.and]
409-partial def delabBexp : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
410-  guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
411-    | Bexp.bool _ => true
412-    | Bexp.eq _ _ => true
413-    | Bexp.neq _ _ => true
414-    | Bexp.le _ _ => true
415-    | Bexp.gt _ _ => true
416-    | Bexp.not _ => true
417-    | Bexp.and _ _ => true
418-    | _ => false
419-  match ← delabBexpInner with
420-  | `(imp_bexp| ~$e) => pure e
421-  | e => `(term| bexp { $e })

426-
427---  With these delaborators in place, Lean pretty-prints Imp expressions
428---  with the higher-level notations rather than their raw constructors.
429-
430---  The pretty-printed version of an expression might not exactly match its
431---  original form. For example, the parentheses around `X * 2` in
432---  `aexp { 3 + (X * 2) }` are not printed because they are redundant --
433---  which the parenthesizer knows.
434-
435-/-- info: aexp {3 + X * 2} : Aexp -/
436-#guard_msgs in
437-#check aexp { 3 + (X * 2) }
438-
439-/-- info: bexp {true ∧ ¬ (X ≤ 4)} : Bexp -/
440-#guard_msgs in
441-#check bexp { true ∧ ¬(X ≤ 4) }

443---  ### Evaluation
444-
445---  The arithmetic and boolean evaluators must now be extended to handle
446---  variables, taking a state `st` as an extra argument. A variable is
447---  looked up in the state with the map-indexing notation `st[x]` from the
448---  `Typeclasses` chapter. For the notation to work, we used
449---  `open scoped MyGetElem` earlier, which opens only the scoped items like
450---  notation from the module.
451-
452-def Aexp.eval (st : State) (a : Aexp) : Nat :=
453-  match a with
454-  | num   n     =>  n
455-  | id    x     =>  st[x]                    -- NEW
456-  | plus  a1 a2 =>  a1.eval st + a2.eval st
457-  | minus a1 a2 =>  a1.eval st - a2.eval st
458-  | mult  a1 a2 =>  a1.eval st * a2.eval st
459-
460-def Bexp.eval (st : State) (b : Bexp) : Bool :=
461-  match b with
462-  | bool b      =>  b
463-  | eq   a1 a2  =>  a1.eval st == a2.eval st
464-  | neq  a1 a2  =>  a1.eval st != a2.eval st
465-  | le   a1 a2  =>  a1.eval st ≤  a2.eval st
466-  | gt   a1 a2  =>  a1.eval st >  a2.eval st
467-  | not  b1     =>  !b1.eval st
468-  | and  b1 b2  =>  b1.eval st && b2.eval st
469-
470-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_num (st : State) (n : Nat) : (num n).eval st = n := rfl
471-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_id (st : State) (x : Ident) : (Aexp.id x).eval st = st[x] := rfl
472-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_plus (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
473-    (plus a1 a2).eval st = a1.eval st + a2.eval st := rfl
474-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_minus (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
475-    (minus a1 a2).eval st = a1.eval st - a2.eval st := rfl
476-@[simp] theorem Aexp.eval_mult (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
477-    (mult a1 a2).eval st = a1.eval st * a2.eval st := rfl
478-
479-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_bool (st : State) (b : Bool) : (bool b).eval st = b := rfl
480-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_eq (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
481-    (eq a1 a2).eval st = (a1.eval st == a2.eval st) := rfl
482-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_neq (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
483-    (neq a1 a2).eval st = (a1.eval st != a2.eval st) := rfl
484-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_le (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
485-    (le a1 a2).eval st = (a1.eval st ≤ a2.eval st : Bool) := rfl
486-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_gt (st : State) (a1 a2 : Aexp) :
487-    (gt a1 a2).eval st = (a1.eval st > a2.eval st : Bool) := rfl
488-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_not (st : State) (b : Bexp) : (not b).eval st = !b.eval st := rfl
489-@[simp] theorem Bexp.eval_and (st : State) (b1 b2 : Bexp) :
490-    (and b1 b2).eval st = (b1.eval st && b2.eval st) := rfl
491-
492---  We reuse the total-map notation (`x →ₜ v ; ∅` etc.) for states.
493-
494-example : aexp { 3 + (X * 2) }.eval (X →ₜ 5 ; ∅) = 13 := by rfl
495-
496-example : aexp { Z + (X * Y) }.eval (X →ₜ 5 ; Y →ₜ 4 ; ∅) = 20 := by rfl
497-
498-example : bexp { true ∧ ¬(X ≤ 4) }.eval (X →ₜ 5 ; ∅) = true := by rfl
499-

507---  ## Commands
508-
509---  Now we are ready to define the syntax and behavior of Imp *commands*
510---  (or *statements*). Informally, commands `c` are described by the
511---  following BNF grammar:
512-
513---  c ::= skip
514---      | x := a
515---      | c ; c
516---      | if b then c else c end
517---      | while b do c end
518-
519---  Here is the formal definition of the abstract syntax of commands.
520-
521-inductive Com where
522-  | skip
523-  | asgn (x : Ident) (a : Aexp)
524-  | seq (c1 c2 : Com)
525-  | cond (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com)
526-  | whileDo (b : Bexp) (c : Com)
527-
528---  THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: commands, macro rules
529-
530-/-- Imp commands -/
531-declare_syntax_cat imp_com
532-/-- The command that does nothing (`skip`) -/
533-syntax ident : imp_com
534-/-- Sequencing: one command after another -/
535-syntax imp_com ";" ppDedent(ppLine imp_com) : imp_com
536-/-- Assignment -/
537-syntax ident " := " imp_aexp : imp_com
538-/-- Conditional -/
539-syntax "if " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine imp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}" ppHardSpace "else" ppHardSpace "{") ppLine imp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : imp_com
540-/-- Loop -/
541-syntax "while " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine imp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : imp_com
542-/-- Escape to Lean -/
543-syntax:max "~" term:max : imp_com
544-
545-/-- Include an Imp command in Lean code -/
546-syntax:min "imp" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine imp_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : term
547-
548-namespace Com
549-
550-open Lean in
551-scoped macro_rules
552-  | `(imp { $x:ident }) =>
553-    if x.getId == `skip then `(Com.skip)
554-    else Macro.throwErrorAt x s!"expected 'skip', got '{x.getId}'"
555-  | `(imp { $c1 ; $c2 }) =>
556-    `(Com.seq (imp {$c1}) (imp {$c2}))
557-  | `(imp { $x:ident := $a }) =>
558-    `(Com.asgn $x (aexp {$a}))
559-  | `(imp { if ($b) {$c1} else {$c2} }) =>
560-    `(Com.cond (bexp {$b}) (imp {$c1}) (imp {$c2}))
561-  | `(imp { while ($b) {$c} }) =>
562-    `(Com.whileDo (bexp {$b}) (imp {$c}))
563-  | `(imp { ~$c }) =>
564-    pure c
565-
566-end Com
567-
568-open scoped Com

570---  END DETAILS
571-
572---  Just as we did for expressions, we add a delaborator so that Lean
573---  prints commands back in the `imp { … }` concrete syntax (see the
574---  Delaborators section above). It reuses the expression delaborators for
575---  the condition of an `if`/`while` and for the right-hand side of an
576---  assignment, and prints an unrecognized subcommand with the `~` escape.
577-
578---  THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: printing commands back
579-
580-namespace Imp.Delab
581-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr
582-
583-partial def delabComInnerFor (ns : Name) (extra : DelabM (TSyntax `imp_com)) :
584-    DelabM (TSyntax `imp_com) := do
585-  let e ← getExpr
586-  let stx ←
587-    -- Using `(imp_com| skip)` would delaborate as `skip✝`. `mkIdent` fixes this.
588-    if e.isConstOf (ns ++ `skip) then
589-      `(imp_com| $(mkIdent `skip):ident)
590-    else if e.isAppOfArity (ns ++ `asgn) 2 then
591-      match ← withAppFn <| withAppArg getExpr with
592-      | .lit (.strVal s) =>
593-        let a ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
594-        `(imp_com| $(mkIdent (.mkSimple s)):ident := $a)
595-      | _ =>
596-        let `($x:ident) ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delab | failure
597-        let a ← withAppArg delabAexpInner
598-        `(imp_com| $x:ident := $a)
599-    else if e.isAppOfArity (ns ++ `seq) 2 then
600-      let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg (delabComInnerFor ns extra)
601-      let s2 ← withAppArg (delabComInnerFor ns extra)
602-      `(imp_com| $s1; $s2)
603-    else if e.isAppOfArity (ns ++ `cond) 3 then
604-      let b  ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg delabBexpInner
605-      let c1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg (delabComInnerFor ns extra)
606-      let c2 ← withAppArg (delabComInnerFor ns extra)
607-      `(imp_com| if ($b) {$c1} else {$c2})
608-    else if e.isAppOfArity (ns ++ `whileDo) 2 then
609-      let b ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabBexpInner
610-      let c ← withAppArg (delabComInnerFor ns extra)
611-      `(imp_com| while ($b) {$c})
612-    else
613-      extra <|> `(imp_com| ~$(← delab))
614-  annAsTerm stx
615-
616-/-- Rebuild `imp_com` concrete syntax from a `Com` term. -/
617-partial def delabComInner : DelabM (TSyntax `imp_com) :=
618-  delabComInnerFor ``Com failure
619-
620-@[delab app.Com.skip, delab app.Com.asgn, delab app.Com.seq,
621-  delab app.Com.cond, delab app.Com.whileDo]
622-partial def delabCom : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
623-  guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
624-    | Com.skip => true
625-    | Com.asgn _ _ => true
626-    | Com.seq _ _ => true
627-    | Com.cond _ _ _ => true
628-    | Com.whileDo _ _ => true
629-    | _ => false
630-  match ← delabComInner with
631-  | `(imp_com| ~$e) => pure e
632-  | e => `(term| imp { $e })
633-
634-end Imp.Delab

637-
638---  As an example, here is the factorial function again, written as a
639---  formal definition. When this command terminates, the variable `Y` will
640---  contain the factorial of the initial value of `X`. (Compare this to the
641---  concrete Imp program at the very start of the chapter.)
642-
643-def fact_in_lean : Com := imp {
644-  Z := X;
645-  Y := 1;
646-  while (Z ≠ 0) {
647-    Y := Y * Z;
648-    Z := Z - 1
649-  }
650-}
651-
652---  Because we registered a delaborator, we can inspect a defined program
653---  with `#print`, which pretty prints the stored definition using the same
654---  syntax:
655-
656-/--
657-info: def fact_in_lean : Com :=
658-imp {
659-  Z := X;
660-  Y := 1;
661-  while (Z ≠ 0) {
662-    Y := Y * Z;
663-    Z := Z - 1
664-  }
665-}
666--/
667-#guard_msgs in
668-#print fact_in_lean
669-
670---  ### Desugaring Notations
671-
672---  The `imp { … }` notation, together with the delaborators, is purely a
673---  convenience for reading and writing programs. Occasionally, such as
674---  when debugging a definition or a stuck proof, the concrete syntax
675---  `hide`s the underlying structure we want to see. For those moments we
676---  can switch the Imp notation off in Lean's output with
677---  `set_option pp.notation false`, which our delaborators honor.
678-
679---  Note that unlike a `def`, `imp { … }` is a `macro` which is expanded
680---  during elaboration, **before** the resulting term is type-checked. So
681---  `fact_in_lean` is not a program hidden behind a layer of notation that
682---  a proof must first peel back; it simply **is** the underlying tree of
683---  `Com`, `Aexp`, and `Bexp` constructors. Consequently, when a proof goal
684---  mentions an Imp program, tactics such as `cases`, `injection`, and
685---  `simp` already act on those constructors directly -- there is nothing
686---  to "unfold". The delaborators affect only how that tree is
687---  **displayed**. Nevertheless, seeing the raw constructors is sometimes
688---  very helpful!
689-
690-/-- info: imp {
691-  X := X + 1
692-} : Com -/
693-#guard_msgs in
694-#check imp { X := X + 1 }
695-
696-/-- info: Com.asgn X ((Aexp.id X).plus (Aexp.num 1)) : Com -/
697-#guard_msgs in
698-set_option pp.notation false in
699-#check imp { X := X + 1 }
700-
701---  ### More Examples
702-
703---  A few more examples.
704-
705---  Assignment:
706-
707-def plus2 : Com := imp { X := X + 2 }
708-def XtimesYinZ : Com := imp { Z := X * Y }
709-
710---  Loops:
711-
712-def subtract_slowly_body : Com := imp {
713-  Z := Z - 1;
714-  X := X - 1
715-}
716-
717-def subtract_slowly : Com := imp {
718-  while (X ≠ 0) {
719-    ~subtract_slowly_body
720-  }
721-}
722-
723-def subtract_3_from_5_slowly : Com := imp {
724-  X := 3;
725-  Z := 5;
726-  ~subtract_slowly
727-}

729---  An infinite loop:
730-
731-def loop : Com := imp { while (true) { skip } }
732-
733---  ## Evaluating Commands
734-
735---  Next we need to define what it means to evaluate an Imp command. The
736---  fact that `while` loops don't necessarily terminate makes defining an
737---  evaluation function tricky.
738-
739---  ### Evaluation as a Function (Failed Attempt)
740-
741---  Here's an attempt at defining an evaluation function for commands (with
742---  a bogus `while` case).
743-
744-def Com.ceval_fun_no_while (st : State) (c : Com) : State :=
745-  match c with
746-  | imp {skip} => st
747-  | imp {x := ~a} => (x →ₜ a.eval st ; st)
748-  | imp {~c1; ~c2} =>
749-      let st' := ceval_fun_no_while st c1
750-      ceval_fun_no_while st' c2
751-  | imp {if (~b) {~c1} else {~c2}} =>
752-      if b.eval st then ceval_fun_no_while st c1
753-      else ceval_fun_no_while st c2
754-  | imp {while (~_) {~_}} => st     -- bogus
755-
756---  In a more conventional functional language like OCaml or Haskell we
757---  could add the `while` case as follows:
758-
759---  | .whileDo b c =>
760---      if b.eval st then ceval_fun st (.seq c (.whileDo b c))
761---      else st
762-
763---  Lean doesn't accept such a definition ("fail to show termination")
764---  because the function we want to define is not guaranteed to terminate.
765---  Indeed, it *doesn't* always terminate: the full `ceval_fun` applied to
766---  the `loop` program above would run forever. Since Lean aims to be not
767---  just a programming language but also a consistent logic, any
768---  potentially non-terminating function must be rejected. Here is what
769---  would go wrong if Lean allowed non-terminating recursive functions:
770-
771---  def loop_false (n : Nat) : False := loop_false n
772-
773---  That is, propositions like `False` would become provable
774---  (`loop_false 0` would be a proof of `False`), a disaster for logical
775---  consistency.
776-
777---  Thus, because it doesn't terminate on all inputs, the full `ceval_fun`
778---  cannot be written in Lean -- at least not without additional tricks and
779---  workarounds.
780-
781---  Note to developers:
782---      Perhaps that discussion should be moved to -- or previewed in --
783---      Logic.v? MRC'20: It's already in ProofObjects (which not everyone
784---      sees).
785-
786---  ### Evaluation as a Relation
787-
788---  Here's a better way: define `ceval` as a *relation* rather than a
789---  *function* -- i.e., make its result a `Prop` rather than a `State`,
790---  similar to what we did for `Aexp.EvalR` above.
791-
792---  This is an important change. Besides freeing us from awkward
793---  workarounds, it gives us more flexibility in the definition. For
794---  example, if we add nondeterministic features like `any` to the
795---  language, we want the definition of evaluation to be nondeterministic
796---  -- i.e., not only will it not be total, it will not even be a function!
797-
798---  Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1):
799---      I kind of hate this notation. Is there something more standard in
800---      Lean? CSLib precedent maybe?
801-
802---  We'll use the notation `st =[ c ]=> st'` for the `Com.EvalR` relation:
803---  `st =[ c ]=> st'` means that executing program `c` in a starting state
804---  `st` results in an ending state `st'`. This can be pronounced "`c`
805---  takes state `st` to `st'`".
806-
807---  Operational Semantics
808-
809---  Note to developers (before next release):
810---      BCP 21: I wonder if `seq` would be easier to work with if st' and
811---      st'' were swapped...
812-
813---  Here is an informal definition of evaluation, presented as inference
814---  rules for readability:
815-
816---                          -----------------                  (skip)
817---                          st =[ skip ]=> st
818-
819---                          a.eval st = n
820---                  --------------------------------           (asgn)
821---                  st =[ x := a ]=> (x →ₜ n ; st)
822-
823---                          st  =[ c1 ]=> st'
824---                          st' =[ c2 ]=> st''
825---                        ---------------------                (seq)
826---                        st =[ c1;c2 ]=> st''

1018---  ### Determinism of Evaluation
1019-
1020---  Changing from a computational to a relational definition of evaluation
1021---  is a good move because it frees us from the artificial requirement that
1022---  evaluation be a total function. But it raises a question: is the
1023---  relational definition really a partial *function*? Could the same
1024---  command, from the same state, evaluate to two different final states?
1025---  In fact this cannot happen: `ceval` *is* a partial function.
1026-
1027-theorem ceval_deterministic (c : Com) (st st1 st2 : State)
1028-    (e1 : st =[ c ]=> st1) (e2 : st =[ c ]=> st2) : st1 = st2 := by
1029-  induction e1 generalizing st2 with
1030-  | @skip st =>
1031-      inversion e2
1032-      rfl
1033-  | @asgn st a n x h =>
1034-      inversion e2 with
1035-      | asgn h' => subst h; subst h'; rfl
1036-  | @seq c1 c2 st st' st'' h1 h2 ih1 ih2 =>
1037-      inversion e2 with
1038-      | seq st2' h1' h2' =>
1039-          have hst : st' = st2' := ih1 _ h1'
1040-          subst hst
1041-          exact ih2 _ h2'
1042-  | @ifTrue st st' b c1 c2 hb hc ih =>
1043-      inversion e2 with
1044-      | ifTrue hb' hc' => exact ih _ hc'
1045-      | ifFalse hb' hc' => simp_all
1046-  | @ifFalse st st' b c1 c2 hb hc ih =>
1047-      inversion e2 with
1048-      | ifTrue hb' hc' => simp_all
1049-      | ifFalse hb' hc' => exact ih _ hc'
1050-  | @whileFalse b st c hb =>
1051-      inversion e2 with
1052-      | whileFalse hb' => rfl
1053-      | whileTrue hb' hc' hl' => simp_all
1054-  | @whileTrue st st' st'' b c hb hc hloop ih1 ih2 =>
1055-      inversion e2 with
1056-      | whileFalse hb' => simp_all
1057-      | whileTrue st2' _ hc' hl' =>
1058-          have hst : st' = st2' := ih1 _ hc'
1059-          subst hst
1060-          exact ih2 _ hl'

1071-  imp {

1080-    (X →ₜ 2 ; ∅) =[ pup_to_n ]=>

1096---  ## Reasoning About Imp Programs
1097-
1098---  We'll get into more systematic and powerful techniques for reasoning
1099---  about Imp programs in the next chapter, but we can already do a few
1100---  things (albeit in a somewhat low-level way) just by working with the
1101---  bare definitions. This section explores some examples.
1102-
1103-theorem plus2_spec (st : State) (n : Nat) (st' : State)
1104-    (hx : st[X] = n) (heval : st =[ plus2 ]=> st') :
1105-    st'[X] = n + 2 := by
1106-  -- Inverting `heval` forces one step of the `ceval` computation: since
1107-  -- `plus2` is an assignment, `st'` must be `st` extended at `X`.
1108-  unfold plus2 at heval
1109-  inversion heval with
1110-  | asgn m h =>
1111-      simp only [Aexp.eval_plus, Aexp.eval_id, Aexp.eval_num] at h
1112-      rw [TotalMap.update_eq]
1113-      lia
1114-

1161-        intro heq; unfold loop at heq; injection heq with e1 _

1165-    | @skip s0 => intro heq; simp [loop] at heq
1166-    | @asgn s0 a n x h => intro heq; simp [loop] at heq

1172---  ### Exercise (3 stars): no_whiles_eqv ⭐⭐⭐
1173-
1174---  The following function yields `true` just on programs with no while
1175---  loops. Using `inductive`, write a property `Com.NoWhilesR` that holds
1176---  exactly when `c` is while-free, then prove it equivalent to
1177---  `Com.no_whiles`.
1178-
1179-def Com.no_whiles (c : Com) : Bool :=
1180-  match c with
1181-  | imp {skip} => true
1182-  | imp {_x := ~_a} => true
1183-  | imp {~c1; ~c2} => no_whiles c1 && no_whiles c2
1184-  | imp {if (~_) {~ct} else {~cf}} => no_whiles ct && no_whiles cf
1185-  | imp {while (~_) {~_}} => false
1186-
1187-inductive Com.NoWhilesR : Com → Prop where
1188-  | skip : Com.NoWhilesR (imp { skip })
1189-  | asgn (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) : Com.NoWhilesR (imp { x := ~a })
1190-  | seq (c1 c2 : Com) (h1 : Com.NoWhilesR c1) (h2 : Com.NoWhilesR c2) :
1191-      Com.NoWhilesR (imp { ~c1; ~c2 })
1192-  | cond (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com) (h1 : Com.NoWhilesR c1) (h2 : Com.NoWhilesR c2) :
1193-      Com.NoWhilesR (imp { if (~b) { ~c1 } else { ~c2 } })
1194-
1195-theorem no_whiles_eqv (c : Com) : c.no_whiles = true ↔ Com.NoWhilesR c := by
1196-  constructor
1197-  · induction c with
1198-    | skip => intro _; exact .skip
1199-    | asgn x a => intro _; exact .asgn x a
1200-    | seq c1 c2 ih1 ih2 =>
1201-        intro h; simp only [Com.no_whiles, Bool.and_eq_true] at h
1202-        exact .seq _ _ (ih1 h.1) (ih2 h.2)
1203-    | cond b c1 c2 ih1 ih2 =>
1204-        intro h; simp only [Com.no_whiles, Bool.and_eq_true] at h
1205-        exact .cond _ _ _ (ih1 h.1) (ih2 h.2)
1206-    | whileDo b c ih => intro h; simp [Com.no_whiles] at h
1207-  · intro h
1208-    induction h with
1209-    | skip => rfl
1210-    | asgn x a => rfl
1211-    | seq c1 c2 h1 h2 ih1 ih2 => simp [Com.no_whiles, ih1, ih2]
1212-    | cond b c1 c2 h1 h2 ih1 ih2 => simp [Com.no_whiles, ih1, ih2]

1214---  ### Exercise (4 stars): no_whiles_terminating ⭐⭐⭐⭐
1215-
1216---  Imp programs that don't involve while loops always terminate. State and
1217---  prove a theorem `no_whiles_terminating` that says this. Use either
1218---  `Com.no_whiles` or `Com.NoWhilesR`, as you prefer.
1219-
1220-theorem no_whiles_terminating (c : Com) (st : State) (h : Com.NoWhilesR c) :
1221-    ∃ st', st =[ c ]=> st' := by
1222-  induction h generalizing st with
1223-  | @skip => exact ⟨st, .skip⟩
1224-  | @asgn x a => exact ⟨(x →ₜ a.eval st ; st), .asgn rfl⟩
1225-  | @seq c1 c2 h1 h2 ih1 ih2 =>
1226-      obtain ⟨st', hc1⟩ := ih1 st
1227-      obtain ⟨st'', hc2⟩ := ih2 st'
1228-      exact ⟨st'', .seq hc1 hc2⟩
1229-  | @cond b c1 c2 h1 h2 ih1 ih2 =>
1230-      cases hb : b.eval st with
1231-      | true =>
1232-          obtain ⟨st', hc1⟩ := ih1 st
1233-          exact ⟨st', .ifTrue hb hc1⟩
1234-      | false =>
1235-          obtain ⟨st', hc2⟩ := ih2 st
1236-          exact ⟨st', .ifFalse hb hc2⟩
1237-

1241-theorem no_whiles_terminating' (c : Com) (st1 : State)
1242-    (hb : c.no_whiles = true) : ∃ st2, st1 =[ c ]=> st2 := by
1243-  induction c generalizing st1 with
1244-  | @skip => exact ⟨st1, .skip⟩
1245-  | @asgn x a => exact ⟨(x →ₜ a.eval st1 ; st1), .asgn rfl⟩
1246-  | @seq c1 c2 ih1 ih2 =>
1247-      simp only [Com.no_whiles, Bool.and_eq_true] at hb
1248-      obtain ⟨st1', hc1⟩ := ih1 st1 hb.1
1249-      obtain ⟨st1'', hc2⟩ := ih2 st1' hb.2
1250-      exact ⟨st1'', .seq hc1 hc2⟩
1251-  | @cond b ct cf ih1 ih2 =>

1253-      cases hbev : b.eval st1 with
1254-      | true =>

1257-      | false =>

1292---        already be defined and in scope at that point in the document, or {name} fails
1293---        to build).
1294---      * {ref "tag"} cross-references link "see the X section" phrasings; add a
1295---        `%%% tag := "…" %%%` block under a heading to make it a target. Done for the
1296---        Notations and Delaborators sections; more internal "above/below" phrasings
1297---        could get the same treatment.
1298---      * {tactic}`simp` — link tactic names in the automation/tactics prose (`try`,
1299---        `repeat`, `<;>`, `simp`, `lia`, `cases`, `induction`).
1300---      * {deftech}/{tech} — a small glossary: define Imp's core terms once with
1301---        {deftech} (abstract syntax, state, big-step, relation, partial function, …)
1302---        and link later uses with {tech}.
1303---      * {lean}`expr` — inline elaborated expressions/types where a whole expression,
1304---        not just a single name, reads better with hover types (e.g. the
1305---        `Coe Ident Aexp` / `OfNat Aexp n` bullets in the Notations section).`

HL/Slang.lean

1-import SFLCompat
2-
3---  # Slang: Arithmetic and Boolean Expressions
4-
5---  Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
6---      We need to figure out our approach to text width, especially for
7---      proofs. Quite a few proofs here don't render into the chosen page
8---      width, and for terse mode it will be worse.
9-
10---  In **Logical Foundations** (LF) we went through the basics of how to
11---  use Lean to prove theorems and write functional programs. Now, we begin
12---  to shift gears to using it to reason about properties of programs and
13---  programming languages. We begin by looking at a language we call
14---  **Slang** (for *simple language*). Despite its simplicity, Slang lets
15---  us introduce key concepts for specifying the *syntax* and *semantics*
16---  of programming languages and show how those concepts are realized in
17---  Lean.
18-
19---  (This chapter is shared, word for word, between two volumes: **Type
20---  Systems** (TS) and **Hoare Logic** (HL). If you have already worked
21---  through it in the other volume, you can safely skip ahead to the next
22---  chapter of this one.)
23-
24---  ## Arithmetic and Boolean Expressions
25-
26---  Slang is a simple core language of *arithmetic and boolean expressions*
27---  sufficient to express simple computations and logical predicates.
28-
29---  ### Syntax
30-
31-namespace Slang
32-
33---  These two definitions specify the *abstract syntax* of arithmetic and
34---  boolean expressions.
35-
36-inductive Aexp where
37-  | num (n : Nat)
38-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
39-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
40-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
41-
42-inductive Bexp where
43-  | bool (b : Bool)
44-  | eq (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
45-  | neq (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
46-  | le (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
47-  | gt (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
48-  | not (b : Bexp)
49-  | and (b₁ b₂ : Bexp)
50-
51---  In this chapter, we'll ignore the translation from the *concrete
52---  syntax* that a programmer would actually write to these abstract syntax
53---  trees -- the process that, for example, would translate the string
54---  `"1 + 2 * 3"` to the AST `.plus (.num 1) (.mult (.num 2) (.num 3))`.
55-
56---  For comparison, here's a conventional BNF (Backus-Naur Form) grammar
57---  defining the same abstract syntax:
58-
59---  a ::= nat
60---      | a + a
61---      | a − a
62---      | a * a
63---  b ::= bool
64---      | a = a
65---      | a ≠ a
66---      | a ≤ a
67---      | a > a
68---      | ¬ b
69---      | b ∧ b
70-
71---  Compared to the Lean version above...
72-
73---  - The BNF is more informal -- for example, it gives some suggestions
74---    about the surface syntax of expressions (like the fact that the
75---    addition operation is written with an infix `+`) while leaving other
76---    aspects of lexical analysis and parsing (like the relative precedence
77---    of `+`, `-`, and `*`, the use of parens to group subexpressions,
78---    etc.) unspecified. Some additional information -- and human
79---    intelligence -- would be required to turn this description into a
80---    formal definition, e.g., for implementing a compiler. The Lean
81---    version consistently omits all this information and concentrates on
82---    the abstract syntax only.
83-
84---  - Conversely, the BNF version is lighter and easier to read. Its
85---    informality makes it flexible, a big advantage in situations like
86---    discussions at the blackboard, where conveying general ideas is more
87---    important than nailing down every detail precisely.
88-
89---    Indeed, there are dozens of BNF-like notations and people switch
90---    freely among them -- usually without bothering to say which kind of
91---    BNF they're using, because there is no need to: a rough-and-ready
92---    informal understanding is all that's important.
93-
94---  It's good to be comfortable with both sorts of notations: informal ones
95---  for communicating between humans and formal ones for carrying out
96---  implementations and proofs.
97-
98---  ### Evaluation
99-
100---  *Evaluating* an arithmetic expression produces a number.
101-
102-namespace Aexp
103-def eval (a : Aexp) : Nat :=
104-  match a with
105-  | num   n     =>  n
106-  | plus  a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval + a₂.eval
107-  | minus a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval - a₂.eval
108-  | mult  a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval * a₂.eval
109-
110-@[simp] theorem eval_num (n : Nat) : (num n).eval = n := rfl
111-@[simp] theorem eval_plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (plus a₁ a₂).eval = a₁.eval + a₂.eval := rfl
112-@[simp] theorem eval_minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (minus a₁ a₂).eval = a₁.eval - a₂.eval := rfl
113-@[simp] theorem eval_mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (mult a₁ a₂).eval = a₁.eval * a₂.eval := rfl
114-
115-example : eval (.plus (.num 2) (.num 2)) = 4 := by simp
116-end Aexp
117-
118---  Similarly, evaluating a boolean expression yields a boolean.
119-
120-namespace Bexp
121-def eval (b : Bexp) : Bool :=
122-  match b with
123-  | bool b     =>  b
124-  | eq   a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval == a₂.eval
125-  | neq  a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval != a₂.eval
126-  | le   a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval ≤ a₂.eval
127-  | gt   a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval > a₂.eval
128-  | not  b₁    =>  !eval b₁
129-  | and  b₁ b₂ =>  eval b₁ && eval b₂
130-
131-@[simp] theorem eval_bool (b : Bool) : (bool b).eval = b := rfl
132-@[simp] theorem eval_eq (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (eq a₁ a₂).eval = (a₁.eval == a₂.eval) := rfl
133-@[simp] theorem eval_neq (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (neq a₁ a₂).eval = (a₁.eval != a₂.eval) := rfl
134-@[simp] theorem eval_le (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (le a₁ a₂).eval = (a₁.eval ≤ a₂.eval : Bool) := rfl
135-@[simp] theorem eval_gt (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (gt a₁ a₂).eval = (a₁.eval > a₂.eval : Bool) := rfl
136-@[simp] theorem eval_not (b : Bexp) : (not b).eval = !b.eval := rfl
137-@[simp] theorem eval_and (b₁ b₂ : Bexp) : (and b₁ b₂).eval = (b₁.eval && b₂.eval) := rfl
138-end Bexp
139-
140---  It's worth noting that `≤` and `>` are `Prop`-valued, i.e.
141---  `a₁.eval st ≤ a₂.eval st` is a proposition, but `Bexp.eval` returns a
142---  `Bool`, so Lean implicitly inserts a `decide` coercion. You can observe
143---  the call to `decide` by hovering over `Bexp.eval_le` and
144---  `Bexp.eval_gt`.
145-
146---  _Quiz:_
147-
148---  What does the following expression evaluate to?
149-
150---  Aexp.eval (.plus (.num 3) (.minus (.num 4) (.num 1)))
151-
152---  (A) true (B) false (C) 0 (D) 3 (E) 6
153-
154---  ### Optimization
155-
156---  We can now start to get some mileage out of these definitions. Suppose
157---  we define a function that takes an arithmetic expression and slightly
158---  simplifies it, changing every occurrence of `0 + e` (i.e.,
159---  `.plus (.num 0) e`) into just `e`.
160-
161-def Aexp.optimize0plus (a : Aexp) : Aexp :=
162-  match a with
163-  | num   n          => num n
164-  | plus  (num 0) e₂ => optimize0plus e₂
165-  | plus  e₁      e₂ => plus  (optimize0plus e₁) (optimize0plus e₂)
166-  | minus e₁      e₂ => minus (optimize0plus e₁) (optimize0plus e₂)
167-  | mult  e₁      e₂ => mult  (optimize0plus e₁) (optimize0plus e₂)
168-
169---  To gain confidence that our optimization is doing the right thing, we
170---  can test it on some examples and see if the output looks OK.
171-
172-example :
173-    Aexp.optimize0plus (.plus (.num 2)
174-                               (.plus (.num 0)
175-                                      (.plus (.num 0) (.num 1))))
176-      = .plus (.num 2) (.num 1) := by rfl
177-
178---  But if we want to be certain the optimization is correct -- that
179---  evaluating an optimized expression *always* gives the same result as
180---  the original -- we should prove it!
181-
182---  Here is a first, deliberately explicit, proof, by induction on `a`. The
183---  interesting case is `Aexp.plus`: because `Aexp.optimize0plus` treats
184---  `plus (num 0) e` specially, we case-split on the left operand `a₁` --
185---  and, when it is a numeral, on whether that numeral is `0` -- to line
186---  the proof up with the function's own branches. Once the constructors
187---  are exposed, each case is discharged by essentially the same
188---  incantation: unfold `Aexp.optimize0plus`, rewrite `Aexp.eval` by its
189---  characterizing lemmas, then finish with the induction hypotheses.
190---  Notice how repetitive that makes the proof.
191-
192-theorem optimize0plus_sound (a : Aexp) :
193-    a.optimize0plus.eval = a.eval := by
194-  induction a with
195-  | num n => rfl
196-  | plus a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
197-    cases a₁ with
198-    | num n =>
199-      cases n with
200-      | zero =>
201-        simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus, Aexp.eval_num, Nat.zero_add]
202-        exact ih₂
203-      | succ n =>
204-        simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus, Aexp.eval_num]
205-        rw [ih₂]
206-    | plus b₁ b₂ =>
207-      simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus] at ih₁ ⊢
208-      rw [ih₁, ih₂]
209-    | minus b₁ b₂ =>
210-      simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus] at ih₁ ⊢
211-      rw [ih₁, ih₂]
212-    | mult b₁ b₂ =>
213-      simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_plus] at ih₁ ⊢
214-      rw [ih₁, ih₂]
215-  | minus a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
216-    simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_minus]
217-    rw [ih₁, ih₂]
218-  | mult a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
219-    simp only [Aexp.optimize0plus, Aexp.eval_mult]
220-    rw [ih₁, ih₂]
221-
222---  We can do much better. The case analysis we performed by hand --
223---  peeling `plus` apart to reach the `plus (num 0) e` branch -- is exactly
224---  the case analysis that `Aexp.optimize0plus` itself performs.
225-
226---  The `fun_induction` tactic inducts along a function's **own** recursion
227---  structure: `fun_induction
228---  Aexp.optimize0plus a` hands us one goal per
229---  branch of `optimize0plus` -- the special `plus (num 0) e` branch
230---  included -- so the nested `cases` disappear.
231-
232---  Before applying `fun_induction` to a function as complex as
233---  `Aexp.optimize0plus`, let's see how it works on somthing simpler.
234---  Recall the definition of `Nat.even` and `Nat.odd`:
235-
236-def Nat.even (n : Nat) :=
237-  match n with
238-  | 0 => true
239-  | 1 => false
240-  | n' + 2 => even n'
241-
242-def Nat.odd (n : Nat) := Nat.even (n + 1)
243-
244---  Normally, if we perform induction on `n`, we get two cases - `0` and
245---  `n' + 1` - one for each of the cases in the inductive definition of
246---  natural numbers. Functional induction on `Nat.even`, however, gives us
247---  three cases - `0`, `1`, and `n' + 2` - corresponding to each of the
248---  cases of its definition.
249-
250-example (n : Nat) (h : Nat.even n = true) : Nat.odd n = false := by
251-  fun_induction Nat.even n
252-  . rfl
253-  . contradiction
254-  . simp [Nat.odd, Nat.even] at *
255-    lia
256-
257---  Now let's try using `fun_induction` on `Aexp.optimize0plus`. When we do
258---  this, every goal has the same shape, so we can attack them uniformly
259---  with the `<;>` combinator and a single tactic, `simp_all`, which
260---  rewrites `Aexp.eval` by the `@[simp]` characterizing lemmas and uses
261---  the induction hypotheses -- which it picks up from the local context
262---  automatically -- to close each goal. The whole proof collapses to two
263---  lines.
264-
265-theorem optimize0plus_sound' (a : Aexp) :
266-    a.optimize0plus.eval = a.eval := by
267-  fun_induction Aexp.optimize0plus a <;> simp_all
268-
269---  ### Exercise (3 stars): optimize0plusB_sound ⭐⭐⭐
270-
271---  Since the `Aexp.optimize0plus` transformation doesn't change the value
272---  of an `Aexp`, we should be able to apply it to all the `Aexp`s that
273---  appear in a `Bexp` without changing the `Bexp`'s value. Write a
274---  function that performs this transformation on `Bexp`s and prove it
275---  sound. Use the combinators we've just seen to make the proof as short
276---  and elegant as possible.
277-
278-def Bexp.optimize0plusB (b : Bexp) : Bexp := (
279-  match b with
280-  | bool b    =>  bool b
281-  | eq a₁ a₂  =>  eq a₁.optimize0plus a₂.optimize0plus
282-  | neq a₁ a₂ =>  neq a₁.optimize0plus a₂.optimize0plus
283-  | le a₁ a₂  =>  le a₁.optimize0plus a₂.optimize0plus
284-  | gt a₁ a₂  =>  gt a₁.optimize0plus a₂.optimize0plus
285-  | not b₁    =>  not (optimize0plusB b₁)
286-  | and b₁ b₂ =>  and (optimize0plusB b₁) (optimize0plusB b₂))
287-
288-theorem optimize0plusB_test1 :
289-    Bexp.optimize0plusB
290-        (.not (.gt (.plus (.num 0) (.num 4)) (.num 8)))
291-      = (.not (.gt (.num 4) (.num 8))) := (by rfl)
292-
293-theorem optimize0plusB_test2 :
294-    Bexp.optimize0plusB
295-        (.and (.le (.plus (.num 0) (.num 4)) (.num 5)) (.bool true))
296-      = (.and (.le (.num 4) (.num 5)) (.bool true)) := (by rfl)
297-
298-theorem optimize0plusB_sound (b : Bexp) :
299-    b.optimize0plusB.eval = b.eval := by
300-  induction b <;>
301-  simp_all [Bexp.optimize0plusB, optimize0plus_sound]
302-
303---  ### Exercise (4 stars): optimize (Optional) ⭐⭐⭐⭐
304-
305---  The optimization implemented by our `Aexp.optimize0plus` is only one of
306---  many possible optimizations on arithmetic and boolean expressions.
307---  Write a more sophisticated optimizer and prove it correct. (You will
308---  probably find it easiest to start small -- add just a single, simple
309---  optimization and its correctness proof -- and build up incrementally to
310---  something more interesting.)
311-
312---  ## Evaluation as a Relation
313-
314---  We have presented `Aexp.eval` and `Bexp.eval` as functions defined by
315---  recursion. Another way to think about evaluation -- one that is often
316---  more flexible -- is as a *relation* between expressions and their
317---  values. This perspective leads to inductive definitions like the
318---  following.
319-
320-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
321-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
322-  | plus {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
323-      EvalR (.plus a₁ a₂) (n₁ + n₂)
324-  | minus {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
325-      EvalR (.minus a₁ a₂) (n₁ - n₂)
326-  | mult {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
327-      EvalR (.mult a₁ a₂) (n₁ * n₂)
328-
329---  One comment on the style of this definition. We could instead have
330---  presented this relation with **positional** hypotheses -- no names for
331---  the premises.
332-
333-namespace ArithUnnamed
334-
335-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
336-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
337-  | plus {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} : EvalR a₁ n₁ → EvalR a₂ n₂ → EvalR (.plus a₁ a₂) (n₁ + n₂)
338-  | minus {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} : EvalR a₁ n₁ → EvalR a₂ n₂ → EvalR (.minus a₁ a₂) (n₁ - n₂)
339-  | mult {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} : EvalR a₁ n₁ → EvalR a₂ n₂ → EvalR (.mult a₁ a₂) (n₁ * n₂)
340-
341-end ArithUnnamed
342-
343---  The version above makes the rules somewhat easier to read, but gives
344---  less control over naming the hypotheses during proofs involving the
345---  relation. For this reason we adopt the named style.
346-
347---  It will be convenient to have an infix notation for `Aexp.EvalR`. We'll
348---  write `e ⇓ n` to mean that arithmetic expression `e` evaluates to value
349---  `n`. The `⇓` symbol is typed `\Downarrow`.
350-
351-scoped notation:55 e:56 " ⇓ " n:56 => Aexp.EvalR e n
352-
353---  The `notation` is declared right after the inductive. The `scoped`
354---  keyword allows us to scope the notation to the present namespace so it
355---  doesn't collide with other evaluation relations later.
356-
357---  ### Inference Rule Notation
358-
359---  In informal discussions, it is convenient to write the rules for
360---  `Aexp.EvalR` and similar relations in the more readable graphical form
361---  of *inference rules*, where the premises above the line justify the
362---  conclusion below the line. For example, the constructor `plus` can be
363---  written like this as an inference rule:
364-
365---  a₁ ⇓ n₁
366---                           a₂ ⇓ n₂
367---                      ------------------          (plus)
368---                      plus a₁ a₂ ⇓ n₁ + n₂
369-
370---  Notice the structural correspondence between this rule and our version
371---  of the inductive type with unnamed hypotheses:
372-
373---  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) :
374---          EvalR a₁ n₁ →
375---          EvalR a₂ n₂ →
376---          EvalR (.plus a₁ a₂) (n₁ + n₂)
377-
378---  Formally, there is nothing deep about inference rules: they are just an
379---  informal notation for implications. You can read the rule name on the
380---  right as the name of the constructor and read each of the linebreaks
381---  between the premises above the line (as well as the line itself) as
382---  `→`. All the variables mentioned in the rule (`a₁`, `n₁`, etc.) are
383---  implicitly bound by universal quantifiers at the beginning. (Such
384---  variables are often called *metavariables* to distinguish them from the
385---  variables of whatever language we are defining. At the moment, our
386---  arithmetic expressions don't include variables, but we'll soon be
387---  adding them.) The whole collection of rules is understood as being
388---  wrapped, implicitly, in an inductive declaration. In informal prose,
389---  this is sometimes indicated by saying something like "Let `Aexp.EvalR`
390---  be the smallest relation closed under the following rules...".
391-
392---  To summarize: a group of inference rules corresponds to a single
393---  inductive definition; each rule's name corresponds to a constructor
394---  name; above the line are the premises, below the line the conclusion;
395---  metavariables like `a₁` and `n₁` are implicitly universally quantified.
396---  The whole collection of rules defines `⇓` as the smallest relation
397---  closed under them:
398-
399---  ---------                (num)
400---                          num n ⇓ n
401-
402---                           a₁ ⇓ n₁
403---                           a₂ ⇓ n₂
404---                      ------------------           (plus)
405---                      plus a₁ a₂ ⇓ n₁ + n₂
406-
407---                           a₁ ⇓ n₁
408---                           a₂ ⇓ n₂
409---                     -------------------           (minus)
410---                     minus a₁ a₂ ⇓ n₁ - n₂
411-
412---                           a₁ ⇓ n₁
413---                           a₂ ⇓ n₂
414---                      ------------------           (mult)
415---                      mult a₁ a₂ ⇓ n₁*n₂
416-
417---  _Quiz:_
418-
419---  Which rules are needed to prove the following?
420-
421---  .mult (.plus (.num 3) (.num 1)) (.num 0) ⇓ 0
422-
423---  (A) `num` and `plus` (B) `num` only (C) `num` and `mult` (D) `mult` and
424---  `plus` (E) `num`, `mult`, and `plus`

436---  ### Exercise (1 star): beval_rules (Optional) ⭐
437-
438---  Here, again, is the definition of the `Bexp.eval` function:
439-
440---    def Bexp.eval (b : Bexp) : Bool :=
441---      match b with
442---      | bool b     => b
443---      | eq   a₁ a₂ => a₁.eval == a₂.eval
444---      | neq  a₁ a₂ => a₁.eval != a₂.eval
445---      | le   a₁ a₂ => a₁.eval ≤ a₂.eval
446---      | gt   a₁ a₂ => a₁.eval > a₂.eval
447---      | not  b₁    => !eval b₁
448---      | and  b₁ b₂ => eval b₁ && eval b₂
449-
450---  Write out a corresponding definition of boolean evaluation as a
451---  relation in inference rule notation.
452-
453---  Answer (`⇓` is defined below):
454-
455---                    -------------                (bool)
456---                     bool bv ⇓ bv
457-
458---                          a₁ ⇓ n₁
459---                          a₂ ⇓ n₂
460---                    ---------------------        (eq)
461---                    eq a₁ a₂ ⇓ (n₁ == n₂)
462-
463---                          a₁ ⇓ n₁
464---                          a₂ ⇓ n₂
465---                  ---------------------          (neq)
466---                   neq a₁ a₂ ⇓ n₁ != n₂
467-
468---                          a₁ ⇓ n₁
469---                          a₂ ⇓ n₂
470---                    --------------------------   (le)
471---                    le a₁ a₂ ⇓ (Nat.ble n₁ n₂)
472-
473---                          a₁ ⇓ n₁
474---                          a₂ ⇓ n₂
475---                    ---------------------------  (gt)
476---                    gt a₁ a₂ ⇓ !(Nat.ble n₁ n₂)
477-
478---                           b ⇓ bv
479---                       -----------               (not)
480---                       not b ⇓ !bv
481-
482---                          b₁ ⇓ bv₁
483---                          b₂ ⇓ bv₂
484---                   ----------------------        (and)
485---                   and b₁ b₂ ⇓ bv₁ && bv₂

487---  ### Equivalence of the Definitions
488-
489---  It is straightforward to prove that the relational and functional
490---  definitions of evaluation agree.
491-
492-theorem Aexp.evalR_iff_eval (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) :
493-    a ⇓ n ↔ a.eval = n := by
494-  constructor
495-  · intro h
496-    induction h with
497-    | num n => rfl
498-    | plus h₁ h₂ ih₁ ih₂ => simp only [Aexp.eval_plus]; rw [ih₁, ih₂]
499-    | minus h₁ h₂ ih₁ ih₂ => simp only [Aexp.eval_minus]; rw [ih₁, ih₂]
500-    | mult h₁ h₂ ih₁ ih₂ => simp only [Aexp.eval_mult]; rw [ih₁, ih₂]
501-  · intro h
502-    subst h
503-    induction a with
504-    | num n => exact .num n
505-    | plus a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ => exact .plus ih₁ ih₂
506-    | minus a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ => exact .minus ih₁ ih₂
507-    | mult a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ => exact .mult ih₁ ih₂
508-
509---  We can make the proof quite a bit shorter using more automation like we
510---  did in the previous section.
511-
512-theorem Aexp.evalR_iff_eval' (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) :
513-    a ⇓ n ↔ a.eval = n := by
514-  constructor <;> intro h
515-  · induction h <;> simp_all
516-  · subst h; induction a <;> constructor <;> assumption

531-      EvalR (.and b₁ b₂) (bv₁ && bv₂)

536-    b ⇓ bv ↔ b.eval = bv := by
537-  constructor <;> intro h
538-  · induction h <;> simp_all [Aexp.evalR_iff_eval]

540-    induction b <;> constructor <;> simp_all [Aexp.evalR_iff_eval]

542-end Slang
543-
544---  ### Computational vs. Relational Definitions
545-
546---  For the definitions of evaluation for arithmetic and boolean
547---  expressions, the choice of whether to use functional or relational
548---  definitions is mainly a matter of taste. However, there are situations
549---  where relational definitions work much better than functional ones.
550-
551-namespace Slang.AevalRDivision
552-
553---  For example, suppose that we wanted to extend the arithmetic operations
554---  with division:
555-
556-inductive Aexp where
557-  | num (n : Nat)
558-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
559-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
560-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
561-  | div (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)             -- NEW
562-
563---  Extending the definition of `Aexp.eval` to handle this new operation
564---  would not be straightforward due to division being a *partial*
565---  operation; i.e., what should we return as the result of
566---  `.div (.num 5) (.num 0)`? One option would be to lift the definition of
567---  `Aexp.eval` to return an option:
568-
569-namespace Aexp
570-
571-def eval (a : Aexp) : Option Nat :=
572-  match a with
573-  | num   n     =>  some n
574-  | plus  a₁ a₂ =>  match a₁.eval, a₂.eval with
575-                    | some n₁, some n₂ => some (n₁ + n₂)
576-                    | _, _ => none
577-  | minus a₁ a₂ =>  match a₁.eval, a₂.eval with
578-                    | some n₁, some n₂ => some (n₁ - n₂)
579-                    | _, _ => none
580-  | mult  a₁ a₂ =>  match a₁.eval, a₂.eval with
581-                    | some n₁, some n₂ => some (n₁ * n₂)
582-                    | _, _ => none
583-  | div   a₁ a₂ =>  match a₁.eval, a₂.eval with
584-                    | _, some 0 => none
585-                    | some n₁, some n₂ => some (n₁ * n₂)
586-                    | _, _ => none
587-end Aexp
588-
589---  This definition is a lot wordier than the earlier version. There are
590---  tools to reduce this overhead, namely monads, but we will not discuss
591---  these in Software Foundations in Lean. Curious readers can learn more
592---  about them from [Functional Programming in
593---  Lean](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Monads/).
594-
595---  By contrast, partiality is no problem for the relational version of the
596---  definition.
597-
598-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
599-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
600-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
601-      EvalR (.plus a₁ a₂) (n₁ + n₂)
602-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
603-      EvalR (.minus a₁ a₂) (n₁ - n₂)
604-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
605-      EvalR (.mult a₁ a₂) (n₁ * n₂)
606-  | div (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ n₃ : Nat)             -- NEW
607-      (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) (hpos : n₂ > 0) (hdiv : n₂ * n₃ = n₁) :
608-      EvalR (.div a₁ a₂) n₃
609-
610---  Notice that there are some inputs (those with a divisor of 0) for which
611---  this relation does not specify an output.
612-
613-end Slang.AevalRDivision
614-
615-namespace Slang.AevalRExtended
616-
617---  As another example, suppose that we want to extend the arithmetic
618---  operations by a nondeterministic number generator `any` that, when
619---  evaluated, may yield any number. (This is not the same as making a
620---  *probabilistic* choice among all numbers -- we only say which results
621---  are *possible*.)
622-
623-inductive Aexp where
624-  | any                            -- NEW
625-  | num (n : Nat)
626-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
627-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
628-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
629-
630---  Again, extending `Aexp.eval` would be tricky, since evaluation is now
631---  *not* a deterministic function from expressions to numbers; but
632---  extending the relation is no problem.
633-
634---  h₂
635-
636-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
637-  | any (n : Nat) : EvalR .any n                   -- NEW
638-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
639-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
640-      EvalR (.plus a₁ a₂) (n₁ + n₂)
641-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
642-      EvalR (.minus a₁ a₂) (n₁ - n₂)
643-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
644-      EvalR (.mult a₁ a₂) (n₁ * n₂)
645-
646-end Slang.AevalRExtended
647-
648---  At this point you may be wondering: which of these styles should I use
649---  by default?
650-
651---  Where the thing being defined is not easy to express as a function,
652---  definitions are often simpler. When both styles are workable,
653---  relational definitions can be more elegant and easier to understand,
654---  and Lean generates useful inversion and induction principles from them.
655---  On the other hand, functional definitions are automatically
656---  deterministic and total -- whereas, for a relation, we must *prove*
657---  these if we need them -- and we can use Lean's computation mechanism to
658---  simplify them during proofs.
659-
660---  In large developments it is common to give a definition in *both*
661---  styles plus a lemma that the two coincide, allowing later proofs to
662---  switch between points of view at will -- exactly what we did above in
663---  `Slang.Aexp.evalR_iff_eval` and `Slang.Bexp.evalR_iff_eval`.
664-

13-/-- Internal syntactic representation of a single inversion alternative. -/
14-declare_syntax_cat invAlt
15-syntax " | " caseArg " => " tacticSeq : invAlt
16-
17-/-- An inversion alternative matching one or more goal tags,
18-  expanding to multiple single [invAlt]s. -/
19-declare_syntax_cat invAlts
20-syntax (" | " caseArg)+ " => " tacticSeq : invAlts
21-
22-/--
23-  `inversion h` behaves like `cases h` except that where `cases` would fail with
24-  > "Dependent elimination failed: Failed to solve equation ...",
25-
26-  `inversion` instead leaves behind those unsolveable equations in the context.
27-  These equations arise from generalizing the indices of `h`'s type.
28-  In such cases, `h` itself is generalized with a heterogenenous equality `heq`
29-  to the corresponding constructor in each branch.
30-
31-  For instance, given a hypothesis `h : f n ≤ 0`,
32-  `inversion h` will produce one goal for the case `Nat.le.refl {n} : n ≤ n`
33-  with the equations `eq : f n = 0` and `heq : h ≍ Nat.le.refl`,
34-  rather than failing to solve `f n = 0`.
35-
36-  * If `inversion +clear h` is set, then `heq` will be `clear`ed from the context if present,
37-    along with `h` if there are no dependencies on it.
38-    This is the usual behavior of `cases`.
39-  * The form `inversion t with (tac ...) | tag₁ x ... => tac ... | ... | tagₙ z ... => tac ...`
40-    is supported, similar to that of `cases` and `induction`.
41--/
42-syntax (name := inversion)
43-  "inversion " optConfig ident (" with " (tacticSeq)? (colGe invAlts)*)? : tactic
44-
45-end Lean.Parser

49-/-- Get the user-facing name for the given metavariable. -/
50-def _root_.Lean.MVarId.getUserName (mvarId : MVarId) : MetaM Name := do
51-  let decl ← mvarId.getDecl
52-  return decl.userName
53-
54-/-- Get the string suffix of a name as a name -/
55-def _root_.Lean.Name.getSuffix : Name → Name
56-| .anonymous => .anonymous
57-| .str _ s => .str .anonymous s
58-| .num n _ => n.getSuffix
59-
60-/--
61-  This function is similar to `forallMetaTelescopeReducing`: Given `e` of the
62-  form `forall ..xs, A`, this combinator will create a new metavariable for
63-  each `x` in `xs` until it reaches an `x` whose type is defeq to `t`,
64-  and instantiate `A` with these, while also reducing `A` if needed.
65-  It uses `forallMetaTelescopeReducing`.
66-
67-  This function returns a triple `(mvs, bis, out)` where
68-  - `mvs` is an array containing the new metavariables.
69-  - `bis` is an array containing the binder infos for the `mvs`.
70-  - `out` is `e` but instantiated with the `mvs`.
71-
72-  Lifted from [https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Lean/Meta/Basic.lean#L41].
73--/
74-def forallMetaTelescopeReducingUntilDefEq
75-    (e t : Expr) (kind : MetavarKind := MetavarKind.natural) :
76-    MetaM (Array Expr × Array BinderInfo × Expr) := do
77-  let (ms, bs, tp) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducing e (some 1) kind
78-  unless ms.size == 1 do
79-    if ms.size == 0 then throwError m!"Failed: {← ppExpr e} is not the type of a function."
80-    else throwError m!"Failed"
81-  let mut mvs := ms
82-  let mut bis := bs
83-  let mut out : Expr := tp
84-  while !(← isDefEq (← inferType mvs.toList.getLast!) t) do
85-    let (ms, bs, tp) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducing out (some 1) kind
86-    unless ms.size == 1 do
87-      throwError m!"Failed to find {← ppExpr t} as the type of a parameter of {← ppExpr e}."
88-    mvs := mvs ++ ms
89-    bis := bis ++ bs
90-    out := tp
91-  return (mvs, bis, out)
92-
93-/-- Given equations `eqs` in the local context of `mvarId`,
94-  unify them using [Lean.Meta.unifyEq?],
95-  but if unification fails, leave the equation in the context.
96-  This means we should never get a "Dependent elimination failed" error.
97-  While marked partial, this _should_ always terminate,
98-  decreasing on the sum of the sizes of the terms of each equation.
99-
100-  Lifted from [Lean.Meta.Cases.unifyEqs]. -/
101-partial def unifyEqs (eqs : List FVarId) (mvarId : MVarId) (subst : FVarSubst) (caseName? : Option Name) : MetaM (MVarId × FVarSubst) := withIncRecDepth do
102-  match eqs with
103-  | [] => return (mvarId, subst)
104-  | eq :: eqs =>
105-    let some { mvarId, subst, numNewEqs } ← Option.join <$> (observing? $ unifyEq? mvarId eq subst MVarId.acyclic caseName?)
106-      | unifyEqs eqs mvarId subst caseName?
107-    let (newEqs, mvarId) ← mvarId.introN numNewEqs
108-    let eqs := eqs.map (Expr.fvarId! ∘ subst.get)
109-    unifyEqs (newEqs.toList ++ eqs) mvarId subst caseName?
110-
111-/-- Lifted from [Lean.Meta.Cases.unifyCasesEqs]. -/
112-def unifyCasesEqs (eqs : List FVarId) (subgoals : Array CasesSubgoal) : MetaM (Array CasesSubgoal) :=
113-  subgoals.filterMapM fun s => do
114-    let eqs := eqs.filterMap (Expr.fvarId? ∘ s.subst.get)
115-    let (mvarId, subst) ← unifyEqs eqs s.mvarId s.subst s.ctorName
116-    if (← mvarId.isAssignedOrDelayedAssigned) then return none
117-    else return some { s with
118-      mvarId := mvarId,
119-      subst  := subst,
120-      fields := s.fields.map (subst.apply ·)
121-    }
122-
123-/-- Try to clear the given fvars from the local context of each subgoal,
124-  using the subgoals' substitution mappings to find the fvars.
125-
126-  As with [MVarId.tryClearMany], the fvars must be in the order they appear in the context.  -/
127-def casesClearMany (subgoals : Array CasesSubgoal) (fvarIds : Array FVarId) : MetaM (Array CasesSubgoal) :=
128-  subgoals.mapM fun s => do
129-    let fvarIds := fvarIds.filterMap (Expr.fvarId? ∘ s.subst.get)
130-    let mvarId ← s.mvarId.tryClearMany fvarIds
131-    return { s with mvarId }
132-
133-end Lean.Meta

143-/--
144-  `apply t at i` uses forward reasoning with `t` at the hypothesis `i`.
145-  Explicitly, if `t : α₁ → ⋯ → αᵢ → ⋯ → αₙ` and `i` has type `αᵢ`, then this tactic adds
146-  metavariables/goals for any terms of `αⱼ` for `j = 1, …, i-1`,
147-  then replaces the type of `i` with `αᵢ₊₁ → ⋯ → αₙ` by applying those metavariables and the
148-  original `i`.
149-
150-  Lifted from [https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Tactic/ApplyAt.lean].
151--/
152-elab "apply " t:term " at " i:ident : tactic => withSynthesize <| withMainContext do
153-  let f ← elabTermForApply t
154-  let some ldecl := (← getLCtx).findFromUserName? i.getId
155-    | throwErrorAt i m!"Identifier {i} not found"
156-  let (mvs, bis, _) ← forallMetaTelescopeReducingUntilDefEq (← inferType f) ldecl.type
157-  for (m, b) in mvs.zip bis do
158-    if b.isInstImplicit && !(← m.mvarId!.isAssigned) then
159-      try m.mvarId!.inferInstance
160-      catch _ => continue
161-  let (_, mainGoal) ← (← getMainGoal).note ldecl.userName
162-    (← mkAppOptM' f (mvs.pop.push ldecl.toExpr |>.map some))
163-  let mainGoal ← mainGoal.tryClear ldecl.fvarId
164-  replaceMainGoal <| [mainGoal] ++ mvs.pop.toList.map (·.mvarId!)

166-structure InversionConfig where
167-  clear : Bool := false

169-declare_config_elab elabInversionConfig InversionConfig

171-open Cases in
172-/-- Perform inversion on the given variable in the context of the given goal.
173-  Behaves like [Lean.Meta.Cases.cases] and generalizes indices if they aren't independent,
174-  except instead of calling [Lean.Meta.Cases.unifyEqs], which may fail
175-  if the generalizing equations can't all be destructed and substituted away,
176-  it calls our [unifyCasesEqs] above, which keeps unsolvable equations in the context. -/
177-def _root_.Lean.MVarId.inversion (mvarId : MVarId) (h : FVarId) (config : InversionConfig)
178-    (givenNames : Array AltVarNames := #[]) (interestingCtors? : Option (Array Name) := none) :
179-    TacticM (Array CasesSubgoal) := mvarId.withContext do
180-  let goal ← getMainGoal
181-  goal.withContext do
182-    let some ctx ← mkCasesContext? h
183-    | throwTacticEx `inversion goal "Target {Expr.fvar h} does not belong to an inductive type"
184-    -- If the target's type isn't a predicate with indices, behave like `cases`
185-    if ← hasIndepIndices ctx then
186-      let subgoals ← inductionCasesOn goal h givenNames ctx (interestingCtors? := interestingCtors?)
187-      let subgoals ← if config.clear
188-        then casesClearMany subgoals #[h]
189-        else pure subgoals
190-      return subgoals
191-    -- Otherwise, use custom [unifyEqs] to not fail on unifying HEqs
192-    else
193-      let gis@⟨newGoal, _, newTarget, numEqs⟩ ← generalizeIndices goal h
194-      let (newEqs, newGoal) ← newGoal.introN numEqs
195-      let some targetEq := newEqs.back?
196-      | throwTacticEx `inversion newGoal "Failed to generalize target"
197-      let subgoals ← inductionCasesOn newGoal newTarget givenNames ctx (interestingCtors? := interestingCtors?)
198-      let subgoals ← elimAuxIndices gis subgoals
199-      let subgoals ← unifyCasesEqs newEqs.toList subgoals
200-      let subgoals ← if config.clear
201-        then casesClearMany subgoals #[h, targetEq]
202-        else pure subgoals
203-      return subgoals
204-
205-/-- Given an inversion alternative and a list of goals,
206-  solve the tagged goal with the provided tactics,
207-  throwing an error if the goal cannot be found or solved. -/
208-def evalInvAlt (goals : List MVarId) (alt : TSyntax `invAlt) : TacticM (List MVarId) :=
209-  match alt with
210-  | `(invAlt| | $tag:ident $vars:binderIdent* => $tactics:tacticSeq) => do
211-    if let some goal ← goals.findM? (matchTag tag.getId <$> ·.getUserName) then
212-      return [← trySolveGoal vars tactics goal]
213-    else throwError m!"Invalid alternative name `{tag.getId}`: {← errorMsg}"
214-  | `(invAlt| | _ $vars:binderIdent* => $tactics:tacticSeq) => do
215-    if !goals.isEmpty then
216-      goals.mapM (trySolveGoal vars tactics)
217-    else throwErrorAt alt m!"Invalid wildcard alternative: {← errorMsg}"
218-  | _ => throwErrorAt alt "Could not parse inversion alternative"
219-where
220-  matchTag tag name : Bool :=
221-    tag == name || tag.isPrefixOf name || tag.isSuffixOf name
222-  trySolveGoal vars tactics goal : TacticM MVarId := do
223-    let goals ← renameInaccessibles goal vars >>= evalTacticAt tactics
224-    unless goals.isEmpty do
225-      reportUnsolvedGoals goals
226-    return goal
227-  errorMsg : TacticM MessageData := do
228-    let goalMsgs ← goals.mapM (.ofName <$> ·.getUserName)
229-    return if goals.isEmpty
230-      then m!"There are no unhandled alternatives"
231-      else m!"Expected {.orList goalMsgs}"
232-
233-@[tactic Lean.Parser.inversion, inherit_doc Lean.Parser.inversion]
234-public meta def evalInversion : Tactic
235-  | `(tactic| inversion $config $h:ident $[with $[$tactics?:tacticSeq]? $[$alts?:invAlts]*]?) => do
236-    let casesSubgoals ← (← getMainGoal).inversion (← getFVarId h) (← elabInversionConfig config)
237-    let mut goals ← casesSubgoals.toList.mapM setUserName
238-    if let some tactics := tactics?.join then
239-      let subgoals ← goals.mapM (evalTacticAt tactics)
240-      goals ← subgoals.flatten.filterM (not <$> ·.isAssignedOrDelayedAssigned)
241-    if let some alts := alts? then
242-      let expandedAlts ← Array.flatten <$> alts.mapM expandInvAlts
243-      for alt in expandedAlts do
244-        let solvedGoals ← evalInvAlt goals alt
245-        goals := goals.removeAll solvedGoals
246-      unless goals.isEmpty do
247-        reportUnsolvedGoals goals
248-    replaceMainGoal goals
249-  | stx => throwErrorAt stx "Could not parse inversion tactic"
250-where
251-  setUserName subgoal : TacticM MVarId := do
252-    if let some name := subgoal.ctorName then
253-      subgoal.mvarId.setUserName name.getSuffix
254-    return subgoal.mvarId
255-  expandInvAlts
256-    | `(invAlts| $[| $args:caseArg]* => $tactics:tacticSeq) =>
257-      args.mapM (`(invAlt| | $(·) => $tactics))
258-    | stx => throwErrorAt stx "Could not parse inversion alternatives"
259-
260-end Lean.Elab.Tactic
261-
262-end -- meta section
