264-namespace Tests
265-open Nat
266-
267-set_option autoImplicit false
268-set_option pp.proofs true
269-set_option pp.fieldNotation false
270-
271-/-! # `inversion` tests -/
272-
273-/-- In Lean, "inversion" on `leq : f n ≤ 0`, where `f : Nat → Nat`,
274-  requires `generalizing e : f n = m`, since Lean does not perform
275-  the dependent case analysis automatically. `cases leq` will fail here.
276-  We want to keep the style of reasoning familiar to PL:
277-  "I know `h`; what must have been true for `h` to be true?"
278-  The technicality of needing to generalize hinders teaching and learning
279-  this style of reasoning for audiences new to proof assistants and logic.
280-  To solve this, we introduce and use the `inversion` tactic,
281-  which automatically generalizes varaibles, performs case analysis,
282-  and eliminates impossible subcases. -/
283-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ 0) : 0 = f n := by
284-  -- cases leq /- Dependent elimination failed: Failed to solve equation 0 = f n -/
285-  inversion leq; assumption
286-
287-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ 0) : 0 = f n := by
288-  inversion +clear leq; assumption
289-
290-/-- error: Unknown identifier `leq` -/
291-#guard_msgs(error) in
292-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ 0) : 0 = f n := by
293-  inversion +clear leq
294-  guard_hyp leq
295-
296-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ 0) : 0 = f n := by
297-  inversion leq with
298-  | refl heq eq =>
299-    guard_hyp heq : leq ≍ le.refl
300-    guard_hyp eq : 0 = f n
301-    assumption
302-
303-/-- warning: declaration uses `sorry` -/
304-#guard_msgs(warning) in
305-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n m : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ f m) : f n = 0 := by
306-  inversion leq with
307-  | refl e _ | step k _ e _ =>
308-    try rw [← e]
309-    sorry
310-
311-/-- error: Invalid wildcard alternative: There are no unhandled alternatives -/
312-#guard_msgs(error) in
313-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n m : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ f m) : f n = 0 := by
314-  inversion +clear leq with
315-  | refl e | step k _ e =>
316-    try rw [← e]
317-    sorry
318-  | _ => sorry
319-
320-/-- error: Invalid alternative name `step`: There are no unhandled alternatives -/
321-#guard_msgs(error) in
322-example (f : Nat → Nat) (n m : Nat) (leq : f n ≤ f m) : f n = 0 := by
323-  inversion +clear leq with
324-  | _ e | step k _ e =>
325-    try rw [← e]
326-    sorry
327-
328-inductive The : ∀ {α}, α → Prop where
329-  | mk : The zero
330-
331-/-- sfl#40: Case names should be the constructors' names -/
332-example {x : Nat} (h : The x) : x = zero := by
333-  inversion h with
334-  | mk => rfl
335-
336-example {α} {n m k : α} : [n, m] = [k, k] → [n] = [m] := by
337-  intro h
338-  inversion h; rfl
339-
340-example {n : Nat} : n + 1 = 1 + n := by
341-  induction n with try rfl
342-  | succ => lia
343-
344-inductive NoStutter {α : Type} : List α → Prop where
345-  | nostutter0: NoStutter []
346-  | nostutter1 {n} : NoStutter (n :: [])
347-  | nostutter2 {x y l} (hneq : x ≠ y) (h : NoStutter (y :: l)) : NoStutter (x :: y :: l)
348-
349-/-- The last (only) case name need not be provided -/
350-example : ¬ (NoStutter [3, 1, 1, 4]) := by
351-  intro contra
352-  inversion contra with | _ contra =>
353-  inversion contra with | _ h _ =>
354-  apply h
355-  rfl
356-
357-/-- Inversion may optionally take a sequence of tactics on all goals -/
358-example {α x y} {l : List α} (h : NoStutter l) (hl : l = x :: y :: []) : x ≠ y := by
359-  inversion h with
360-    injections
361-    try subst_vars
362-  | nostutter2 => assumption
363-
364-/-- `with` acts similarly to `<;>` on the optional sequence of tactics -/
365-example {α x y} {l : List α} (h : NoStutter l) (hl : l = x :: y :: []) : x ≠ y := by
366-  inversion h with
367-    injections
368-    try (subst_vars; assumption)
369-
370-example {x y} {l : List Nat} (h : NoStutter l) (hl : l = x :: y :: []) : x ≠ y := by
371-  inversion h with
372-    injections
373-    try cases x
374-  | nostutter2.zero => subst_vars; assumption
375-  | nostutter2.succ => subst_vars; assumption
376-
377-inductive Vec α : Nat → Type where
378-  | nil : Vec α 0
379-  | cons {n} : α → Vec α n → Vec α (n + 1)
380-
381-/-- Inversion should work on indexed `Type`s as well -/
382-example {α} (n : Nat) (v : Vec α (n + 1)) : ∃ hd tl, v = Vec.cons hd tl := by
383-  inversion v with
384-  | cons hd tl => exists hd, tl
385-
386-inductive Wec α : Nat → Type where
387-  | nil : Wec α 0
388-  | cons {n} (f : Nat → Nat) : α → Wec α n → Wec α (f n)
389-
390-/-- warning: declaration uses `sorry` -/
391-#guard_msgs(warning) in
392-example {α} (n : Nat) (v : Wec α (succ n)) :
393-    ∃ hd tl, v = Wec.cons succ hd tl := by
394-  inversion v with
395-  | cons m f hd tl eq heq =>
396-    guard_hyp eq : succ n = f m
397-    guard_hyp heq : v ≍ Wec.cons f hd tl
398-    sorry
399-
400-inductive EmptyRelation : Nat → Nat → Prop where
401-
402-/-- sfl#52: Inversion should still work on nonindexed `Prop`s -/
403-example n m : ¬ EmptyRelation n m := by
404-  intro contra; inversion contra
405-
406-/-- With `inductive.autoPromoteIndices` true (the default),
407-  this is also a nonindexed `Prop`... -/
408-inductive silly : Nat → Prop where
409-| silly1 n (h : n > 1) : silly n
410-| silly2 n (h : exists m, m * 2 = n) : silly n
411-| silly3 n (h : exists m, n = m + 2) : silly n
412-
413-/-- ...and inversion should continue to work -/
414-example {n} (h : silly n) : n ≠ 1 := by
415-  inversion h <;> omega
416-
417-/-- Inversion should also work on nonindexed `Type`s -/
418-example (n : Nat) : Nat := by
419-  inversion n with
420-  | zero => exact zero
421-  | succ n' => exact n'
422-
423-/-! # `lemma` tests -/
424-
425-lemma doubleNegation : ∀ P, P → ¬ ¬ P := by
426-  intro P p np; exact (np p)
427-
428-/-! # `apply` tests -/
429-
430-example (H : Bool → Nat → False) (n : Nat) : False := by
431-  apply H at n; apply n; exact true
432-
433-end Tests

LF/Typeclasses.lean

1-import SFLCompat
2-
3---  # Typeclasses
4-
5---  Chapter Poly introduced **parametric polymorphism**, declaring a type
6---  variable with no constraint on it.
7-
8---  Note to developers (Michael Hicks @mwhicks1):
9---      Students will run across universes, though. When looking at List
10---      lemmas, for example, they will see things like:
11---
12---      `List.reverse.{u} {α : Type u} (as : List α) : List α`
13---
14---      Are we explaining these things somewhere, maybe in Poly ?
15-
16---  Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
17---      Yes, in Poly!
18-
19---  This lets us work with a type like `List α`, writing functions like
20---  `List.reverse` and `List.length` and proofs like `List.length_reverse`,
21---  which use only the list's structure and never inspect any particular
22---  `a : α`.
23-
24---  Sometimes, though, we want less freedom: rather than leaving `α`
25---  completely generic, we want to partially specify its behavior. In Lean,
26---  this is done through a form of "ad hoc polymorphism" called
27---  **typeclasses**. The concept originated in Haskell and is analogous to
28---  features you may know from other languages, such as traits in Rust.
29-
30---  ## Why We Need Typeclasses
31-
32---  Consider the following function, which checks whether a natural number
33---  occurs in a list:
34-
35-def List.elem_nat (a : Nat) (xs : List Nat) : Bool :=
36-  match xs with
37-  | [] => false
38-  | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_nat a tl
39-
40-theorem List.elem_nat_nil (a : Nat) : [].elem_nat a = false := rfl
41-
42-theorem List.elem_nat_cons (a b : Nat) (xs : List Nat) :
43-    (b :: xs).elem_nat a = bif a == b then true else elem_nat a xs := rfl
44-
45-#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 0
46-#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 1
47-#eval [0, 1].elem_nat 2
48-
49---  What if we want this to work for lists of *any* element type, not just
50---  `Nat`? Parametric polymorphism suggests simply replacing `Nat` with a
51---  type variable `α`, but that produces a puzzling error:
52-
53-sf_expect_failure_in
54-  def List.elem_poly {α : Type} (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
55-    match xs with
56-    | [] => false
57-    | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl
58-
59---  failed to synthesize instance of type class
60---    BEq α
61-
62---  Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
63-
64---  Lean is trying to use typeclasses to work out how `==` should behave on
65---  a value of type `α`. We'll see exactly why shortly; for now, here's one
66---  way to sidestep the problem: have the caller supply the equality test
67---  to use.
68-
69-def List.elem_poly_eq {α : Type} (eq : α → α → Bool) (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
70-  match xs with
71-  | [] => false
72-  | b :: tl => bif eq a b then true else elem_poly_eq eq a tl
73-
74-#eval [0, 1].elem_poly_eq Nat.beq 0
75-
76---  This works, but it's tedious: every caller has to know, and remember to
77---  supply, the right equality function.
78-
79---  Typeclasses automate this — instead of the programmer passing the
80---  function explicitly, Lean searches for one and provides it on its own.
81---  We specify something we want Lean to search for by declaring a `class`
82---  with the needed function as a field; a `class` is like an interface in
83---  Java or a trait in Rust. Particular implementations of that class are
84---  called *instance*; each type can have its own instance of a class. For
85---  functions that would use such instances, we specify the name of the
86---  class in a *instance implicit* on the polymorphic variable that the
87---  instance's function applies to. This directs Lean to rely on the class
88---  inside the function, and to find and fill in the appropriate instance
89---  when the function is called.
90-
91---  Here is what this looks like for `List.elem_poly`:
92-
93-def List.elem_poly {α : Type} [BEq α] (a : α) (xs : List α) : Bool :=
94-  match xs with
95-  | [] => false
96-  | b :: tl => bif a == b then true else elem_poly a tl
97-
98-theorem List.elem_poly_nil {α : Type} [BEq α] (a : α) : [].elem_poly a = false := rfl
99-
100-theorem List.elem_poly_cons {α : Type} [BEq α] (a b : α) (xs : List α) :
101-    (b :: xs).elem_poly a = bif a == b then true else elem_poly a xs := rfl
102-
103-#eval [0, 1].elem_poly 0
104-
105---  Comparing `List.elem_poly_eq` with `List.elem_poly`, we see three
106---  differences. First, `List.elem_poly_eq` takes an *explicit* parameter
107---  `eq`, whereas `List.elem_poly` specifies an instance implicit
108---  `[BEq α]`. The instance implicit indicates that an instance of `BEq`
109---  must be provided at call sites for the particular type `α` that is
110---  used. Second, whereas `List.elem_poly_eq` invokes parameter `eq` to
111---  test equality, `List.elem_poly` uses `==` instead. As Lists noted when
112---  we first used it, `==` on `Nat` comes from the `BEq` typeclass.
113---  Finally, whereas `[0, 1].elem_poly_eq Nat.beq 0` passes the equality
114---  function `Nat.beq` explicitly, in `[0, 1].elem_poly 0` Lean fills it in
115---  automatically based on the type `Nat` of the `List`.
116-
117---  Note to developers (xhalo32):
118---      This is technically incorrect, the instance `BEq Nat`, which comes
119---      from `DecidableEq`, does not contain `Nat.beq`. You can see in
120---      proofs of `List.elem_nat` versus `List.elem_poly_eq` versus
121---      `List.elem_poly` and how `Nat.beq` and `==` play different roles.
122-
123---  Going back to the earlier version of `List.elem_poly`, without the
124---  instance implicit, we can now understand the error message: `α` was
125---  fully generic — so the `==` in its body would have needed to work for
126---  *every* type `α`, and no single `BEq` instance can do that. So Lean's
127---  search failed.
128-
129---  Now it is time to dig into the details of what we have seen so far.
130---  We'll see exactly how `[BEq α]` gets filled in below, starting with how
131---  to define a typeclass in the first place.
132-
133---  ## Defining Your Own Typeclasses
134-
135---  `BEq` comes from Lean's standard library. Let's define a typeclass of
136---  our own, to see the mechanism — classes, instances, and synthesis —
137---  that made `==` resolve automatically above.
138-
139---  Suppose we want a function that returns the first element of a list,
140---  defaulting to a given value if the list is empty. As with
141---  `List.elem_poly_eq` above, here is a version that makes the default
142---  value an explicit parameter:
143-
144-def List.headOr_ex {α : Type} (defaultValue : α) (xs : List α) : α :=
145-  match xs with
146-  | [] => defaultValue
147-  | hd :: _ => hd
148-
149-#eval [1, 2, 3].headOr_ex 0
150-#eval ([] : List Nat).headOr_ex 0
151-
152---  This works, but again it's tedious: every caller has to supply an
153---  element of `α` to default to, even when there's an obvious choice based
154---  on the type of the things in the list, like `0` for `Nat`.
155-
156---  Getting Lean to fill in `defaultValue` automatically takes two things.
157---  One is marking the parameter as "searchable," rather than something the
158---  caller always supplies explicitly. The other is giving Lean some
159---  information about what it should search *for*.
160-
161---  Considering the second problem first: the way to provide this
162---  information is to *name* the data we're after — the **default value**
163---  of a type. In particular, a `structure` (chapter Lists) is a good way
164---  to give this information a name; structures can also bundle together
165---  more than one piece of data, which will come in handy later, though we
166---  only need a single field here.
167-
168---  To address the first problem, we need to mark this particular structure
169---  as one Lean should search for automatically — not every
170---  `structure`-typed argument should be.
171-
172---  Let's build up to what we want in two steps: first the naming, as a
173---  plain `structure`; then the marking, by upgrading it to a `class`.
174---  Here's the structure — we'll put it in its own namespace so we can
175---  reuse the name `DefaultValue` for the class version below:
176-
177-namespace DefaultValueScratch
178-
179-structure DefaultValue (α : Type) where
180-  value : α
181-
182---  A value of type `DefaultValue Nat` picks out a particular `Nat` to
183---  serve as the type's default: it's built the same way any structure is,
184---  by supplying a `Nat` for the `value` field:
185-
186-def natDefault : DefaultValue Nat where
187-  value := 0
188-
189-end DefaultValueScratch
190-
191---  Now for the marking: we need to tell Lean that `DefaultValue` is the
192---  sort of structure it should search for automatically, the way it needs
193---  to for `List.headOr_ex`'s `defaultValue` argument. We do this by
194---  writing `class` in place of `structure`:
195-
196-class DefaultValue (α : Type) where
197-  value : α
198-
199---  We then provide values of this type a bit differently. Instead of
200---  `def`, we use `instance`:
201-
202-instance instDefaultValueNat : DefaultValue Nat where
203-  value := 0
204-
205---  Lean can now find this instance on its own, via *typeclass synthesis*
206---  (or *typeclass inference*) — the same process that found `BEq Nat`
207---  earlier. That means we can rewrite `List.headOr_ex` the same way we
208---  rewrote `List.elem_poly_eq` into `List.elem_poly` above, replacing the
209---  explicit `defaultValue` parameter with an instance implicit:
210-
211-def List.headOr {α : Type} [DefaultValue α] (xs : List α) : α :=
212-  match xs with
213-  | [] => DefaultValue.value
214-  | hd :: _ => hd
215-
216-#eval [1, 2, 3].headOr
217-#eval ([] : List Nat).headOr
218-
219-example : DefaultValue.value = (0 : Nat) := by rfl
220-
221---  Notice that we refer to `DefaultValue.value` alone, with no instance
222---  named. Because the expression equates `DefaultValue.value` with the
223---  `Nat` `0`, Lean selects `instDefaultValueNat`, the instance for
224---  `DefaultValue Nat`. We know this because we are able to prove that
225---  `DefaultValue.value` is equal to `0`.
226-
227---  Let's declare a second instance, for `Int`, the type of integers
228---  `... -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ...`:
229-
230-instance instDefaultValueInt : DefaultValue Int where
231-  value := -1
232-
233---  We can also create instances for polymorphic types, like `Option α`,
234---  whose default is `none`, by giving the instance declaration a
235---  parameter:
236-
237-instance instDefaultValueOption {α : Type} : DefaultValue (Option α) where
238-  value := none
239-
240---  Now, Lean can infer instances for all these types, including inside
241---  `List.headOr`:
242-
243-example : DefaultValue.value = (0 : Nat) := by rfl
244-example : DefaultValue.value = (-1 : Int) := by rfl
245-example : DefaultValue.value = (none : Option Bool) := by rfl
246-example : DefaultValue.value = (none : Option (List Nat)) := by rfl
247-example : ([] : List Nat).headOr = 0 := by rfl
248-example : ([] : List Int).headOr = -1 := by rfl
249-example : ([] : List (Option Bool)).headOr = none := by rfl
250-example : ([] : List (Option Bool)).headOr = none := by rfl
251-
252---  Synthesis infers instances we could have specified explicitly:
253-
254-example : instDefaultValueNat.value = (0 : Nat) := by rfl
255-example : instDefaultValueInt.value = (-1 : Int) := by rfl
256-example : instDefaultValueOption.value = (none : Option Nat) := by rfl
257-
258---  The option `pp.all` shows which instance Lean picked:
259-
260-set_option pp.all true in
261-#check (DefaultValue.value : Nat)
262-
263---  @DefaultValue.value Nat instDefaultValueNat : Nat
264-
265-set_option pp.all true in
266-#check (DefaultValue.value : Int)
267-
268---  @DefaultValue.value Int instDefaultValueInt : Int
269-
270---  This reveals `instDefaultValueNat` and `instDefaultValueInt` as the
271---  instances Lean picked. The `#synth` command runs the same search
272---  directly:
273-
274-#synth DefaultValue Nat
275-
276---  instDefaultValueNat
277-
278---  For a typeclass like `DefaultValue` that carries data — a term, such as
279---  the `1` above, rather than only proofs (which we will see below) — we
280---  expect at most one instance per type, so this search has a unique
281---  answer.
282-
283---  We'll put `DefaultValue`'s standard-library equivalent, `Inhabited`, to
284---  work later in this chapter, when we define maps that need a default
285---  value for a generic type. First, though, let's go back to
286---  `List.elem_poly` and see how its `[BEq α]` argument actually gets
287---  resolved.
288-
289---  ## Using Typeclasses
290-
291---  Let's check what `==` meant for `List.elem_nat`, with notation display
292---  turned off:
293-
294-set_option pp.notation false in
295-#check 1 == 2
296-
297---  BEq.beq 1 2 : Bool
298-
299---  Rather than `Nat.beq`, `==` turns out to be notation for `BEq.beq`, a
300---  field of exactly the kind of typeclass we just learned to define:
301-
302-sf_recall_source
303-  /--
304-    `BEq α` is a typeclass for supplying a boolean-valued equality relation on
305-    `α`, notated as `a == b`. Unlike `DecidableEq α` (which uses `a = b`), this
306-    is `Bool` valued instead of `Prop` valued, and it also does not have any
307-    axioms like being reflexive or agreeing with `=`. It is mainly intended for
308-    programming applications. See `LawfulBEq` for a version that requires that
309-    `==` and `=` coincide.
310-  
311-    Typically we prefer to put the "more variable" term on the left,
312-    and the "more constant" term on the right.
313-    -/
314-    class BEq (α : Type u) where
315-      /-- Boolean equality, notated as `a == b`. -/
316-      beq : α → α → Bool
317-
318---  Writing `a == b` makes Lean search for an **instance** of `BEq` for the
319---  type of `a` and `b`, the same way it searched for a `DefaultValue`
320---  instance above. For `Nat`, that instance is:
321-
322-instance (priority := low) : BEq Nat where
323-  beq := Nat.beq
324-
325---  This is the instance Lean supplies for `[BEq α]` when `List.elem_poly`
326---  is called on a `List Nat` — no different from Lean choosing
327---  `instDefaultValueNat` for `DefaultValue.value` earlier when it was
328---  equated with `(1 : Nat)`.
329-
330---  ### Exercise (1 star): List.elem_poly_eq_elem_nat ⭐
331-
332---  Prove that `List.elem_poly` agrees with `List.elem_nat` when
333---  specialized to natural numbers.
334-
335-theorem List.elem_poly_eq_elem_nat (xs : List Nat) (n : Nat) : xs.elem_poly n = xs.elem_nat n := by
336-  (
337-  induction xs with
338-  | nil =>
339-    rewrite [List.elem_poly_nil, List.elem_nat_nil]
340-    rfl
341-  | cons hd tl ih =>
342-    rewrite [List.elem_poly_cons, List.elem_nat_cons, ih]
343-    rfl)

345---  ## Proof-Carrying Typeclasses
346-
347---  The above examples enforce no conditions on the data an instance may
348---  carry — any value of the right type will do. But sometimes enforcing
349---  constraints on data is useful. For example, suppose we want to specify
350---  that a type has not just a single element, but two. Here is a first
351---  attempt:
352-
353-sf_experiment
354-  class HasTwoIncomplete (α : Type) where
355-    one : α
356-    two : α
357-
358---  Unfortunately, this specification isn't precise because it allows `one`
359---  and `two` to refer to the same term. Fortunately, Lean's typeclasses
360---  can carry proofs along with data, so we can write the following to
361---  enforce that `one` and `two` are distinct.
362-
363-class HasTwo (α : Type) where
364-  one : α
365-  two : α
366-  one_neq_two : one ≠ two
367-
368---  Declaring instances works in much the same way as before, except that
369---  now the `HasTwo.one_neq_two` field requires a proof:
370-
371-instance : HasTwo Nat where
372-  one := 1
373-  two := 2
374-  one_neq_two := by intro contra; contradiction
375-
376---  In most languages that support typeclasses (or traits) it is not
377---  possible to formally enforce laws such as `one_neq_two`. Thus it falls
378---  to the author to check, informally, that any required invariants are
379---  satisfied, which can lead to bugs.
380-
381---  Note to developers (Niklas Halonen @xhalo32):
382---      HasThree needs either grading attributes or manual grading
383-
384---  ### Exercise (1 star): HasThree ⭐
385-
386---  Following the pattern of `DefaultValue` and `HasTwo`, define a class
387---  `HasThree` that specifies a type with at least three distinct elements,
388---  and give an instance of it for `Nat`.
389-
390-class HasThree (α : Type) where
391-  one : α
392-  two : α
393-  three : α
394-  one_neq_two : one ≠ two
395-  one_neq_three : one ≠ three
396-  two_neq_three : two ≠ three
397-
398-instance : HasThree Nat where
399-  one := 1
400-  two := 2
401-  three := 3
402-  one_neq_two := (by intro contra; contradiction)
403-  one_neq_three := (by intro contra; contradiction)
404-  two_neq_three := (by intro contra; contradiction)
405-
406-namespace Algebra
407-
408---  This facility is very powerful, and is used extensively in Lean to
409---  define mathematical structures that carry both operators and laws about
410---  how those operators interact. As a simple example, let's use a
411---  typeclass to define a *monoid*, a simple algebraic structure that
412---  includes four things:
413-
414---  - an underlying set of data, represented by a type `α`,
415-
416---  - an operator (which we'll write `⊗`, typed otimes) that combines two
417---    elements of type `α` into one,
418-
419---  - a particular element `id` of type `α`, which we call the "identity
420---    element", and
421-
422---  - some laws about the interaction of `⊗` and `id`, namely that:
423-
424---    - `∀ x, id ⊗ x = x = x ⊗ id`, and
425-
426---    - `∀ x y z, x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z` (i.e., that `⊗` is
427---      associative)
428-
429---  We can express these requirements in the form of a typeclass:
430-
431--- first we define a notation typeclass for our operator ⊗
432-class OpSet (α : Type) where
433-  op : α → α → α
434-
435-infixr:70 " ⊗ " => OpSet.op
436-
437-class Monoid (α : Type) extends (OpSet α) where
438-  id : α
439-  left_id : ∀ (x : α), id ⊗ x = x
440-  right_id : ∀ (x : α), x ⊗ id = x
441-  assoc : ∀ (x y z : α), x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z
442-
443---  The `extends` keyword indicates that the `Monoid` typeclass extends the
444---  `OpSet` typeclass, which just defines a set with an operator and some
445---  notation for it. The `Monoid` typeclass "inherits" the fields of
446---  `OpSet`, similar to how a class would in an object-oriented language.
447-
448---  As one might expect, the `+` operator over `Nat`s forms a monoid, where
449---  `0` is the identity element. Note that we don't have to define `Nat`'s
450---  `OpSet` instance separately, we can define a single instance that
451---  implements both classes.
452-
453-instance : Monoid Nat where
454-  op := Nat.add
455-  id := 0
456-  left_id := by lia
457-  right_id := by lia
458-  assoc := by lia
459-
460---  Note to developers (Niklas Halonen @xhalo32):
461---      Need to come up with a way to grade the data-carrying instances.
462---      What makes this more complicated is that the `op` is fixed but the
463---      `id` is not.
464-
465---  ### Exercise (1 star): NatMonoidMul ⭐
466-
467---  However, multiplication on `Nat`s *also* forms a monoid. What is its
468---  identity element?
469-
470-instance : Monoid Nat where
471-  op := Nat.mul
472-  id := (1)
473-  left_id := (by lia)
474-  right_id := (by lia)
475-  assoc := (by lia)
476-
477---  ### Exercise (1 star): ListMonoidAppend ⭐
478-
479---  There are also many monoids over other types. Most usefully in computer
480---  science, lists of any type also form a monoid, with `List.append` as
481---  the operator in question:
482-
483-instance {α : Type} : Monoid (List α) where
484-  op := List.append
485-  id := ([])
486-  left_id := (by simp)
487-  right_id := (by simp)
488-  assoc := (by simp)
489-
490---  In addition to defining instances of `Monoid`, we can also prove some
491---  properties about monoids in general, just based on the laws defined on
492---  the typeclass. One simple theorem about monoids is that the identity
493---  element of a monoid is unique. That is, if we have two monoids over the
494---  same set with the same operator, their identity elements must also be
495---  the same:
496-
497-theorem id_unique {α : Type} {m₁ m₂ : Monoid α} (h : m₁.op = m₂.op) : m₁.id = m₂.id := by
498-  obtain @⟨op₁, id₁, left_id₁, right_id₁, assoc₁⟩ := m₁
499-  obtain @⟨op₂, id₂, left_id₂, right_id₂, assoc₂⟩ := m₂
500-  have h' : id₁ = id₂ := by
501-    -- this introduces a use of m₁'s operator
502-    rw [← left_id₁ id₂]
503-    -- we use our hypothesis to rewrite m₁'s operator into m₂'s
504-    rw [h]
505-    -- then, we can use m₂'s right id
506-    rw [right_id₂]
507-  -- the goal `m₁.id = m₂.id` is equivalent with `id₁ = id₂` even though it displays `Monoid.id = Monoid.id`
508-  exact h'
509-
510---  In the above proof, we can destructure the monoid instances `m₁` and
511---  `m₂` with the `obtain` tactic we saw in the Logic chapter. When we do
512---  so however, because these are class instances instead of normal
513---  structures, we preface our tuple with the `@` symbol. When stepping
514---  through the above proof, if the notation is confusing to you, remember
515---  that you can set `set_option pp.all true` or
516---  `set_option pp.explicit true` to make Lean show you more clearly what
517---  is going on. For example, the goal is displayed as
518---  `Monoid.id = Monoid.id` since the instances `m₁` and `m₂` are implicit
519---  arguments to `Monoid.id`. Setting `pp.explicit true` displays the goal
520---  as `@Eq α (@Monoid.id α m₁) (@Monoid.id α m₂)`.
521-
522---  A *group* is a special kind of monoid with an *inverse* operation
523---  `inv`, which has the property that `∀ x, inv x ⊗ x = id = x ⊗ inv x`.
524---  We can extend the definition of a `Monoid` to capture this new feature:
525-
526-class Group (α : Type) extends (Monoid α) where
527-  inv : α → α
528-  left_inv : ∀ (x : α), inv x ⊗ x = id
529-  right_inv: ∀ (x : α), x ⊗ inv x = id
530-
531---  Now, the monoids we described earlier are not groups: there is no
532---  inverse operation on the natural numbers such that
533---  `∀ x, x + inv x = 0 = inv x + x`, for example. However, addition does
534---  form a group over the integers:
535-
536---  ### Exercise (1 star): IntGroupAdd ⭐
537-
538-instance : Group Int where
539-  op := Int.add
540-  id := (0)
541-  inv := (Int.neg)
542-  left_id := (by lia)
543-  right_id := (by lia)
544-  assoc := (by lia)
545-  left_inv := (by lia)
546-  right_inv := (by lia)
547-
548---  The study of groups is called *group theory* and is a rich area of
549---  mathematics. Here, we will only prove a handful of its simplest
550---  results:
551-
552---  Note to developers (Daniel Sainati @dsainati1):
553---      This also prints weird.
554-
555---  ### Exercise (1 star): InverseUnique ⭐
556-
557---  Two groups defined with the same operation over the same set must have
558---  the same inverse as well.
559-
560-theorem inv_unique {α : Type} {g₁ g₂ : Group α} (h : g₁.op = g₂.op) : g₁.inv = g₂.inv := by
561-  ext a
562-  rw [←g₁.right_id (Group.inv a), ←g₁.right_inv a]
563-  rw [g₁.assoc, h, g₂.left_inv a, g₂.left_id]
564-
565---  Note to developers (Daniel Sainati @dsainati1):
566---      Taking suggestions for additional simple group theory theorems to
567---      prove here.
568-
569-end Algebra
570-
571---  ## Maps
572-
573---  *Maps* (or "dictionaries") are ubiquitous data structures both in
574---  ordinary programming and in the theory of programming languages; we're
575---  going to need them in many places in later volumes.
576-
577---  We'll define two flavors of maps: *total maps*, which include a
578---  "default" element to be returned when a key being looked up doesn't
579---  exist, and *partial maps*, which instead return an option to indicate
580---  success or failure. Partial maps are defined in terms of total maps,
581---  using `none` as the default element.
582-
583---  ### Key and Value Types
584-
585---  To define maps, we first need a type for the keys that we will use to
586---  index into our maps and a type for the values the maps return. In this
587---  section, we'll use the type variable `α` for the type of keys and `β`
588---  for values. In addition to `BEq`, which we have already seen, our key
589---  type `α` requires instances of the `ReflBEq` and `LawfulBEq`
590---  typeclasses:
591-
592-sf_recall_source
593-  /-- `ReflBEq α` says that the `BEq` implementation is reflexive. -/
594-    class ReflBEq (α) [BEq α] : Prop where
595-      /-- `==` is reflexive, that is, `(a == a) = true`. -/
596-      protected rfl {a : α} : a == a
597-
598-sf_recall_source
599-  /--
600-    A Boolean equality test coincides with propositional equality.
601-  
602-    In other words:
603-     * `a == b` implies `a = b`.
604-     * `a == a` is true.
605-    -/
606-    class LawfulBEq (α : Type u) [BEq α] : Prop extends ReflBEq α where
607-      /-- If `a == b` evaluates to `true`, then `a` and `b` are equal in the logic. -/
608-      eq_of_beq : {a b : α} → a == b → a = b
609-
610---  These classes refine `BEq`, specifying that (`==`) is reflexive and
611---  coincides with proposition equality `=`.
612-
613---  In general, we place no constraints on the value type `β`.
614-
615---  ### Total Maps
616-
617---  The Lists chapter introduced a partial map abstraction, `PartialMap`,
618---  with a `find` function for lookup, based on lists of key-value pairs.
619---  Here, we are going to build a map abstraction using functions instead.
620---  The advantage of this representation is that it offers a more
621---  *extensional* view of maps, as we saw with functions in the Logic
622---  chapter: two maps that respond to every query in the same way will be
623---  represented as exactly the same function, rather than just as
624---  "equivalent" list structures. This simplifies proofs that use maps.
625-
626---  Instead of using functions directly, we encapsulate them inside a
627---  `structure` which we call `TotalMap`. Intuitively, a total map just
628---  contains a function `inner` from a key of type `α` to a value of type
629---  `β`.
630-
631-structure TotalMap (α : Type) (β : Type) where
632-  inner : α → β
633-
634-namespace TotalMap
635-
636---  In order to declare a default value of `β` we will use the `Inhabited`
637---  typeclass, which is the standard library's implementation of our
638---  `DefaultValue` example from above:
639-
640---  The function `TotalMap.empty` yields an empty total map, given a
641---  default element; this map always returns the default element when
642---  applied to any key.
643-
644-def empty {α β : Type} [Inhabited β] : TotalMap α β where
645-  inner := fun _ ↦ default
646-
647---  These types and implicit instances are now available automatically to
648---  all the definitions in this section.
649-
650---  Just as declaring `BEq`/`DefaultValue` instances above hooked `==` and
651---  `DefaultValue.value` up to our types, we can declare an instance of the
652---  standard library's `EmptyCollection` typeclass to associate `∅` with
653---  this empty map.
654-
655-instance {α β : Type} [Inhabited β] : EmptyCollection (TotalMap α β) where
656-  emptyCollection := TotalMap.empty
657-
658-theorem empty_def {α β : Type} [Inhabited β] : (∅ : TotalMap α β) = { inner := fun _ ↦ default } := by rfl
659-
660---  Here, for example, is an empty map that takes `Nat` keys to `Nat`
661---  values:
662-
663-def emptyNatMap : TotalMap Nat Nat := ∅
664-
665---  #### Getting Elements
666-
667---  While `TotalMap`s happen to be implemented as functions under the hood,
668---  we would prefer not to expose this fact in its public interface.
669---  Accordingly, we define new operations for querying and updating
670---  mappings. We define a function `get` for getting the value associated
671---  with a key playing the role that `find` played for the Lists chapter's
672---  list-based maps,
673-
674-def get {α β : Type} (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) := m.inner a
675-
676-/-- This exposes implementation-specific details of `TotalMap`.
677-Avoid using this outside the `TotalMap` namespace. -/
678-theorem get_def {α β : Type} {m : TotalMap α β} {a : α} : m.get a = m.inner a := by rfl
679-
680-example : emptyNatMap.get 2 = 0 := by rfl
681-
682---  Here is an example that uses the API lemmas `empty_def` and `get_def`:
683-
684-example {n : Nat} : emptyNatMap.get n = 0 := by
685-  rewrite [get_def, emptyNatMap, empty_def, Nat.default_eq_zero]
686-  rfl
687-
688---  In the above example, we use `rewrite` and `rfl` instead of the usual
689---  `rw` to highlight something interesting. After the rewrites in this
690---  proof, we end up with a goal that looks like
691---  `{ inner := fun x => 0 }.inner n = 0`, which we can solve with `rfl`.
692---  This is because the projection `.inner` on a structure of the form
693---  `{ inner := x }` is definitionally equal to `x`.
694-
695---  `get` is the public API counterpart to `inner` which is an
696---  implementation-specific detail of `TotalMap`. Because `get_def` "peeks"
697---  through the abstraction, it should be used sparingly, and only inside
698---  the `TotalMap` namespace.
699-
700---  To make element-getting more convenient, let's define notation so we
701---  can write `emptyNatMap[2]` rather than `emptyNatMap.get`. We could
702---  notate `get` directly — we'll do exactly that for `update` below — but
703---  here we'll instead make "getting an element" its own typeclass,
704---  `MyGetElem`, and notate it. Doing so means `m[a]` resolves to
705---  `MyGetElem.getElem m a` for any type with a `MyGetElem` instance, not
706---  just `TotalMap`.
707-
708---  Using typeclasses to define notation is typical in Lean when the same
709---  notation is useful for many different types. We have seen the approach
710---  already with `==`: writing `a == b` is notation for `BEq.beq`, resolved
711---  by instance search for whatever type `a` and `b` have. We also just saw
712---  overloaded notation for `EmptyCollection` above, where `∅` is notation
713---  for `EmptyCollection.emptyCollection`. Our typeclass `MyGetElem` is a
714---  simpler version of the standard library's `GetElem` typeclass, which
715---  has many instances such as `Array`, `List`, and `Vector`. We develop it
716---  to illustrate the notation-as-typeclass approach.
717-
718---  Note to developers (Niklas Halonen @xhalo32):
719---      A reason I can come up with why we use a notation typeclass (in
720---      library code) over a plain notation is that it makes it possible
721---      (for a downstream consumer) to write `open scoped MyGetElem`
722---      instead of writing `open scoped TotalMap` and
723---      `open scoped PartialMap` individually. This wouldn't be a good sell
724---      if `→ₜ` and `→ₚ` are scoped notations, but they're currently
725---      global.
726-
727-end TotalMap
728-
729---  The `MyGetElem` typeclass takes three type parameters: the map
730---  implementation, its keys, and its values.
731-
732-class MyGetElem (coll : Type) (idx : Type) (elem : outParam Type) where
733-  getElem (xs : coll) (i : idx) : elem
734-
735---  (Don't worry about the `outParam` qualifier; it is a hint to Lean that
736---  helps typeclass inference.)
737-
738---  The appropriate instance of `MyGetElem` for our `TotalMap` is:
739-
740-instance {α β : Type} : MyGetElem (TotalMap α β) α β where
741-  getElem m a := m.get a
742-
743---  Now we can associate the bracket syntax with `MyGetElem.getElem`. We've
744---  defined custom notation before — `::` and `[...]` for lists (chapter
745---  Lists, including an `app_unexpander` for printing `[...]`-notation
746---  lists back out), or `+`/`*`/`==` for arithmetic — but always with
747---  `infixl`/`infixr` or `scoped macro`; this is the first time we reach
748---  for the more general `notation`/`macro_rules` forms for getting the
749---  `m[a]` syntax to work.
750-
751---  Don't worry about following the mechanism in detail — the `macro_rules`
752---  and the `app_unexpander` below are minor technicalities. However, if
753---  you do wish to learn more, Chapter 5 and 6 of [Metaprogramming in Lean
754---  4](https://leanprover-community.github.io/lean4-metaprogramming-book/)
755---  contain more detail.
756-
757-namespace MyGetElem
758-
759-scoped macro_rules | `($xs[$i]) => ``(getElem $xs $i)
760-
761-@[app_unexpander getElem]
762-def unexpandGetElem : Lean.PrettyPrinter.Unexpander
763-  | `($_ $xs $i) => `($xs[$i])
764-  | _ => throw ()
765-end MyGetElem
766-
767-open scoped MyGetElem
768-
769---  Since the standard library already declares the `x[i]` syntax for
770---  `GetElem`, we only need to define the `macro_rules`, not the `notation`
771---  as we have done previously. It's scoped since we don't want to override
772---  the default `GetElem` everywhere, but only when `open scoped MyGetElem`
773---  is in force.
774-
775---  Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
776---      Make sure we've really explained `open scoped` somewhere...
777-
778---  Since we provided a `MyGetElem` instance for `TotalMap`, we can now use
779---  the notation `m[a]` to access elements of a map `m`.
780-
781-namespace TotalMap
782-
783-theorem getElem_def {α β : Type} (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) : m[a] = m.get a := by rfl
784-
785-example : emptyNatMap[1] = default := by rfl
786-
787-example {n : Nat} : emptyNatMap[n] = 0 := by
788-  rw [getElem_def, get_def, emptyNatMap, empty_def, Nat.default_eq_zero]
789-
790---  We want the public API of `TotalMap` to use the `m[a]` notation instead
791---  of `m.get a` so we provide the reverse direction of `getElem_def` as a
792---  `simp` lemma; the `m[a]` notation is the `TotalMap` API's `simp` normal
793---  form.
794-
795-@[simp]
796-theorem get_eq_getElem {α β : Type} (m : TotalMap α β) (a : α) : m.get a = m[a] := rfl
797-
798-example {n : Nat} : emptyNatMap.get n = emptyNatMap[n] := by
799-  simp
800-
801---  This design minimizes the need to use `getElem_def` outside concrete
802---  examples (which are typically solvable with `rfl` anyways).
803-
804---  #### Updating Elements
805-
806---  Now we turn to the `update` function, which takes a map `m`, a key `a`,
807---  and a value `b` and returns a new map that takes `a` to `b` and takes
808---  every other key to whatever `m` does. We do this by wrapping a new map
809---  function around the old one.
810-
811-def update {α β : Type} (m : TotalMap α β) [BEq α] (a : α) (b : β) : TotalMap α β where
812-  inner := fun a' => bif a == a' then b else m[a']
813-
814---  For example, we can build a map taking `String` to `Bool`, where
815---  `"foo"` and `"bar"` are mapped to `true` and every other key is mapped
816---  to `false`, like this:
817-
818-def exampleMap :=
819-  (∅ : TotalMap String Bool)
820-    |>.update "foo" true
821-    |>.update "bar" true
822-
823---  Here `|>` is Lean's **pipe** notation: `x |>.f y` means `x.f y`,
824---  letting us chain a sequence of function or method calls left to right
825---  without nested parentheses.
826-
827---  Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
828---      Should we introduce this notation earlier? (Are there good places
829---      to use it earlier?)
830-
831---  We also introduce a notation for updating maps — this time, rather than
832---  going through a typeclass and its own `notation`/`macro_rules`
833---  machinery as we did for `MyGetElem`, we write a `notation` that

1071---  ### Notation for Concrete Maps
1072-
1073---  Wouldn't it be nice if we could use a more natural notation for
1074---  concrete maps like `{ "bar" ↦ true, "foo" ↦ true }`? To accomplish this
1075---  we define a simple structure that consists of a key and a value along
1076---  with `↦` notation for it.
1077-
1078-/--
1079-A key-value pair with `↦` syntax.
1080--/
1081-@[ext]
1082-structure KVPair (K : Type) (V : Type) where
1083-  key : K
1084-  value : V
1085-
1086-namespace KVPair
1087-scoped notation k " ↦ " v => KVPair.mk k v
1088-end KVPair
1089-
1090-open scoped KVPair
1091-
1092---  Next, we declare `Insert` and `Singleton` instances — the
1093---  standard-library typeclasses behind the `{x, y, ...}` and `{x}`
1094---  collection-literal notation that `List`, `Finset`, and other stdlib
1095---  containers already support — so that `TotalMap` can use it too.
1096-
1097-namespace TotalMap
1098-
1099-instance {α β : Type} [BEq α] : Insert (KVPair α β) (TotalMap α β) where
1100-  insert kv m := kv.key →ₜ kv.value ; m
1101-
1102-instance {α β : Type} [BEq α] [Inhabited β] : Singleton (KVPair α β) (TotalMap α β) where
1103-  singleton kv := insert kv ∅
1104-
1105-instance {α β : Type} [BEq α] [Inhabited β] : LawfulSingleton (KVPair α β) (TotalMap α β) where
1106-  insert_empty_eq _ := rfl
1107-
1108-end TotalMap

1148-structure PartialMap (α : Type) (β : Type) where

1151-  use `PartialMap.toTotal` instead, so there's exactly one sanctioned way to get at it. -/

1305---  One last thing: for partial maps, it's convenient to introduce a notion
1306---  of map inclusion, stating that all the entries in one map are also
1307---  present in another. Lean already has notation for this — `m₁ ⊆ m₂` —
1308---  which we get by supplying a `HasSubset` instance.

1310-def Subset {α β : Type} (m₁ m₂ : PartialMap α β) : Prop :=
1311-  ∀ {a : α} {b : β}, m₁[a] = some b → m₂[a] = some b

1314-  Subset := PartialMap.Subset

1317-    m₁ ⊆ m₂ ↔ (∀ {a : α} {b : β}, m₁[a] = some b → m₂[a] = some b) := .rfl

1320-
1321-theorem update_subset {α β : Type} [BEq α] [LawfulBEq α] (m₁ m₂ : PartialMap α β) (a : α) (b : β)
1322-    (h : m₁ ⊆ m₂) : (a →ₚ b ; m₁) ⊆ (a →ₚ b ; m₂) := by
1323-  rw [subset_def] at h ⊢
1324-  intro a' b' hb
1325-  by_cases ha : a = a'
1326-  · subst ha
1327-    rw [update_eq] at hb ⊢
1328-    exact hb
1329-  · rw [update_neq ha] at hb ⊢
1330-    exact h hb
1331-
1332-end PartialMap

1336---  will see in *Type Systems*, where maps are used to keep track of which

1339---  ## Reflection
1340-
1341-namespace Reflection
1342-
1343---  In this section, we will make use of some definitions and theorems
1344---  about natural numbers that we discussed and proved in previous
1345---  chapters; copy your solutions to those problems here:
1346-
1347-namespace Nat
1348-
1349-def even (n : Nat) :=
1350-  match n with
1351-  | 0     => true
1352-  | 1     => false
1353-  | n + 2 => even n
1354-
1355-theorem even_zero : even 0 = true := by rfl
1356-
1357-theorem even_succ (n : Nat) :
1358-    even (n + 1) = !(even n) := by
1359-  induction n with
1360-  | zero =>
1361-    rfl
1362-  | succ n' ih =>
1363-    rw [even, ih, Bool.not_not]
1364-
1365-def double (n : Nat) : Nat :=
1366-  match n with
1367-  | 0    => 0
1368-  | n' + 1 => double n' + 2
1369-
1370-theorem double_zero : double 0 = 0 := by rfl
1371-
1372-theorem double_succ (n : Nat) : double (n + 1) = double n + 2 := by rfl
1373-
1374-def Even x := ∃ n : Nat, x = Nat.double n
1375-
1376-end Nat
1377-
1378---  We've seen two different ways of expressing logical claims in Lean:
1379---  with booleans (of type `Bool`), and with propositions (of type `Prop`).
1380-
1381---  Here are the key differences between `Bool` and `Prop`:
1382-
1383---  Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
1384---      Check formatting:
1385-
1386---  - ⠀
1387---  - `Bool`
1388---  - `Prop`
1389---  - decidable?
1390---  - yes
1391---  - no
1392---  - useable with `match`?
1393---  - yes
1394---  - no
1395---  - works with `rewrite` tactic?
1396---  - no
1397---  - yes
1398-
1399---  The crucial difference between the two worlds is decidability. Every
1400---  (closed) Lean expression of type `Bool` can be simplified in a finite
1401---  number of steps to either `true` or `false` — i.e., there is a
1402---  terminating mechanical procedure for deciding whether or not it is
1403---  true.
1404-
1405---  This means that, for example, the type `Nat → Bool` is inhabited only
1406---  by functions that, given a `Nat`, always yield either `true` or `false`
1407---  in finite time; and this, in turn, means (by a standard computability
1408---  argument) that there is no function in `Nat → Bool` that checks whether
1409---  a given number is the code of a terminating Turing machine.
1410-
1411---  By contrast, the type `Prop` includes both decidable and undecidable
1412---  mathematical propositions; in particular, the type `Nat → Prop` does
1413---  contain functions representing properties like "the nth Turing machine
1414---  halts." The second row in the table follows directly from this
1415---  essential difference. To evaluate a pattern match (or conditional) on a
1416---  boolean, we need to know whether the scrutinee evaluates to `true` or
1417---  `false`; this only works for `Bool`, not `Prop`.
1418-
1419---  The third row highlights an important practical difference: equality
1420---  functions like `Nat.beq` that return a boolean cannot be used directly
1421---  to justify rewriting with the rewrite tactic; propositional equality is
1422---  required for this. Since `Prop` includes both decidable and undecidable
1423---  properties, we have two options when we want to formalize a property
1424---  that happens to be decidable: we can express it either as a boolean
1425---  computation or as a function into Prop.
1426-
1427---  As an example, we can write
1428-
1429-example : Nat.even 42 := rfl
1430-
1431---  or that there exists some `k` such that `42 = double k`.
1432-
1433-example : Nat.Even 42 := by exists 21
1434-
1435---  Of course, it would be deeply strange if these two characterizations of
1436---  evenness did not describe the same set of natural numbers!
1437-
1438---  Fortunately, they do! To prove this, we first need two helper lemmas.
1439-
1440-theorem even_double (k : Nat) : Nat.even (Nat.double k) = true := by
1441-  induction k with
1442-  | zero =>
1443-    rewrite [Nat.double_zero, Nat.even_zero]
1444-    rfl
1445-  | succ n ih =>
1446-    rewrite [Nat.double_succ, Nat.even_succ, Nat.even_succ, Bool.not_not]
1447-    exact ih
1448-
1449---  ### Exercise (3 stars): even_double_exists ⭐⭐⭐
1450-
1451-theorem even_double_exists (n : Nat) :
1452-    ∃ (k : Nat), n = bif Nat.even n then Nat.double k else Nat.double k + 1 := by (
1453-  induction n with
1454-  | zero =>
1455-    exists 0
1456-  | succ n ih =>
1457-    obtain ⟨k, ih⟩ := ih
1458-    rewrite [Nat.even_succ]
1459-    by_cases h : Nat.even n
1460-    · exists k
1461-      rewrite [h] at ih ⊢
1462-      subst ih
1463-      rfl
1464-    · exists k + 1
1465-      rewrite [Bool.not_eq_true] at h
1466-      rewrite [h] at ih ⊢
1467-      subst ih
1468-      rewrite [cond_false, Bool.not_false, cond_true]
1469-      rfl)
1470-
1471---  Now the main theorem:
1472-
1473-theorem even_iff_Even {n : Nat} : Nat.even n = true ↔ Nat.Even n where
1474-  mp h := by
1475-    have ⟨k, hk⟩ := even_double_exists n
1476-    rewrite [h, cond_true] at hk
1477-    subst hk
1478-    exists k
1479-  mpr h := by
1480-    obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ := h
1481-    subst hk
1482-    exact even_double k
1483-
1484---  In view of this theorem, we can say that the boolean computation
1485---  `n.even` is reflected in the truth of the proposition
1486---  `∃ (k : Nat), n = k.double`.
1487-
1488---  Similarly, to state that two numbers n and m are equal, we can say
1489---  either
1490-
1491---  - that `n == m` returns `true`, or
1492---  - that `n = m`
1493-
1494---  Again, these two notions are equivalent:
1495-
1496---  Note to developers:
1497---      This proof is from the typeclass version, which makes more sense if
1498---      maps are included — CGH
1499-
1500-example (n₁ n₂ : Nat) : n₁ == n₂ ↔ n₁ = n₂ := beq_iff_eq
1501-
1502---  So what should we do in situations where some claim could be formalized
1503---  as either a proposition or a boolean computation? Which should we
1504---  choose?
1505-
1506---  In general, both can be useful. Which we choose has to do with the
1507---  *computational* nature of Lean's core language, which is designed so
1508---  that every function it expresses is total, and by default computable
1509---  unless we explicit indicate otherwise. As an example, consider trying
1510---  to write a function `α → α → Bool` checking for equality on an
1511---  arbitrary type:
1512-
1513---  Note to developers:
1514---      dsainati12 days ago We use regular if for the first time here. It
1515---      is probably necessary to explain at this point what if is and how
1516---      it differs from bif.
1517---
1518---      👍 1 berberman1 day ago Should we clarify the difference between =
1519---      and ==? Observably if and bif can possibly accept both as the
1520---      condition because of Coe or DecidableEq instances, which IMO could
1521---      be confusing.
1522---
1523---      Probably we can talk a bit about the coercion system in this file
1524---      as well, since Coe could be an example of typeclasses, so long as
1525---      if we ignore the outParam thing...
1526---
1527---      chenson20181 day ago I definitely intended for this to cover =
1528---      versus ==. Maps uses LawfulBEq (which says = and == coincide). If
1529---      that will now appear here it's a good place to give some more
1530---      detail?
1531---
1532---      rogerburtonpatel1 day ago I think right after this part on
1533---      decidability is good. It's a hefty chunk of information already, so
1534---      keeping distinct ideas distinct is more likely than not a good
1535---      call.
1536-
1537---  Note to developers:
1538---      @dsainati - commenting this out for the same reason as above
1539---
1540---      `def eq {α : Type} (a₁ a₂ : α) : Bool := if a₁ = a₂ then true else false`
1541---
1542---      `def eq {α : Type} (a₁ a₂ : α) : Bool := if a₁ = a₂ then true else false`
1543---
1544---      `def eq {α : Type} (a₁ a₂ : α) : Bool := if a₁ = a₂ then true else false`
1545-
1546---  Lean will complain here that it cannot find an instance of `Decidable`.
1547---  This typeclass
1548-
1549-sf_experiment
1550-  class inductive Decidable (p : Prop) where
1551-    /-- Proves that `p` is decidable by supplying a proof of `¬p` -/
1552-    | isFalse (h : Not p) : Decidable p
1553-    /-- Proves that `p` is decidable by supplying a proof of `p` -/
1554-    | isTrue (h : p) : Decidable p
1555-
1556---  is the way that we express in Lean that a given proposition is
1557---  decidable. This is the generalization of our observation that
1558---  `even_iff_Even` was reflecting a proof between boolean and
1559---  propositional equality. In fact, we can use this theorem to directly
1560---  construct a `Decidable` instance
1561-
1562-instance (n : Nat) : Decidable (Nat.Even n) := decidable_of_decidable_of_iff even_iff_Even
1563-
1564---  Now we are able to complete such proofs by computation using the
1565---  `decide` tactic:
1566-
1567-example : Nat.Even 2 := by decide
1568-example : Nat.Even 4 := by decide
1569-example : Nat.Even 6 := by decide
1570-example : Nat.Even 100 := by decide
1571-example : ¬ Nat.Even 101 := by decide
1572-example : ∀ n < 10, Nat.Even (2 * n) := by decide
1573-example : ∀ n < 10, Nat.Even (2 * n) ∧ ¬ Nat.Even (2 * n + 1) := by decide
1574-
1575---  In general, Lean will try to use typeclass synthesis with `Decidable`
1576---  in order to determine when it is appropriate to use `Prop` and `Bool`
1577---  interchangeably. For instance, while our example `eq` failed above
1578---  while trying to use propositional equality `=` in the condition of an
1579---  `if` statement, we are allowed to write
1580-
1581-def nat_eq (m n : Nat) : Bool := if m = n then true else false
1582-
1583---  Why is this allowed? It is precisely because equality of natural
1584---  numbers is decidable, and Lean makes use of this fact. If we print this
1585---  definition with notation unset, we would find that it is using
1586---  `instDecidableEqNat`
1587-
1588-set_option pp.all true in
1589-#print nat_eq
1590-
1591---  which proves that this equality is decidable.
1592-
1593---  This is only half the story however: while Lean's core theory enables
1594---  this computation, Lean is also often used in applications where we
1595---  don't care about computability, such as pure mathematics. In
1596---  particular, it is possible to write a function for arbitrary equality:
1597-
1598-sf_experiment
1599-  open scoped Classical in
1600-  noncomputable def eq {α : Type} (a₁ a₂ : α) := if a₁ = a₂ then true else false
1601-  
1602-  set_option pp.all true in
1603-  #print eq
1604-
1605---  But we have indicated to Lean, using the `noncomputable` keyword and
1606---  `Classical` namespace, that we are *not* interested in computation.
1607---  What is happening in the background is that this allows typeclass
1608---  synthesis to find the scoped instance `Classical.propDecidable`, which
1609---  makes use of the axiom of choice to provide a proof that all
1610---  propositions are *classically* decidable. This sort of definition is
1611---  suitable for use with proofs, but is not allowed to be used in
1612---  conjunction with computational features of Lean such as the `decide`
1613---  tactic or the `#eval` command.

11--- Copied from `SubVerso.Compat` to avoid making generated projects depend on verso.
12--- We want to have info state and messages available right after the elaboration,
13--- so we need to disable `Elab.async` which would let diagnostics produced asynchronously
14--- through spanshot tasks.
15-private def commandWithoutAsync (act : CommandElabM Unit) : CommandElabM Unit := do
16-  match (← get).scopes with
17-  | [] => act
18-  | h :: t =>
19-    let mut orig : Option Bool := none
20-    try
21-      orig := h.opts.get? `Elab.async
22-      modify fun s => { s with scopes := { h with opts := h.opts.setBool `Elab.async false } :: t }
23-      act
24-    finally
25-      if let h :: t := (← get).scopes then
26-        let opts := orig.map (h.opts.setBool `Elab.async) |>.getD (h.opts.erase `Elab.async)
27-        modify fun s => { s with scopes := { h with opts := opts } :: t }
28-
29-private def withRestoringState (keepMsgs : Bool) (m : CommandElabM Unit) : CommandElabM Unit := do
30-  let savedState ← get
31-  try
32-    m
33-  finally
34-    let state ← get
35-    set { savedState with
36-      -- Preserve the info tree
37-      infoState := state.infoState
38-      messages := if keepMsgs then state.messages else savedState.messages }
39-
40-namespace IndentedCommands
41-
42-/-! # Block Commands Parser
43-  Parse an indented command block. Commands are separated by new lines.
44-  Since we want to capture parsing errors in `sf_expect_failure_in`,
45-  we can't use Lean command parser directly in our command's syntax,
46-  because any parsing error occurred would fail `sf_expect_failure_in` itself.
47-  One possible solution is to first parse the whole indented body as raw syntax,
48-  and then run Lean's command parser followed by command elaboration.
49--/
50-
51-open Parser
52-
53-private def rawLineEndFn : ParserFn :=
54-  eoiFn <|> satisfyFn (· == '\n') "line break"
55-
56-/-- Consumes everything until the next newline and then consumes the newline itself. -/
57-private def rawLineFn : ParserFn :=
58-  takeUntilFn (· == '\n') >> rawLineEndFn
59-
60-/- For each line after the first body line, consumes leading whitespaces.
61-  If it's blank, consumes the newline; otherwise consumes the line
62-  requiring the indentation.
63--/
64-private def rawIndentedLineFn : ParserFn := atomicFn <|
65-  takeWhileFn (· == ' ') >>
66-  (satisfyFn (· == '\n') "line break" <|>
67-    (checkColGeFn "indented command sequence" >> rawLineFn))
68-
69-private def rawCommandBlockFn : ParserFn :=
70-  rawFn (rawLineFn >> manyFn rawIndentedLineFn) (trailingWs := true)
71-
72-private def rawCommandBlock : Parser := { fn := rawCommandBlockFn }
73-
74-@[combinator_parenthesizer rawCommandBlock]
75-private def rawCommandBlock.parenthesizer := PrettyPrinter.Parenthesizer.visitToken
76-
77-@[combinator_formatter rawCommandBlock]
78-private def rawCommandBlock.formatter := PrettyPrinter.Formatter.visitAtom Name.anonymous
79-
80-private partial def runRawCmdsAux
81-    (ictx : InputContext) (pstate : ModuleParserState) : CommandElabM Unit := do
82-  let state ← get
83-  let scope := state.scopes.head!
84-  let pctx :=  {
85-      env := state.env
86-      options := scope.opts
87-      currNamespace := scope.currNamespace
88-      openDecls := scope.openDecls : ParserModuleContext
89-    }
90-  let (cmd, pstate, messages) := parseCommand ictx pctx pstate state.messages
91-  modify fun state => { state with messages }
92-  unless cmd.isOfKind ``Command.eoi do
93-    elabCommand cmd
94-    runLinters cmd
95-    unless isTerminalCommand cmd do
96-      runRawCmdsAux ictx pstate
97-
98-/- Recovers the source info and elaborates the commands -/
99-private def runRawCmds (body : Syntax) : CommandElabM Unit := do
100-  let some source := body.getSubstring? (withLeading := false) (withTrailing := false)
101-    | throwErrorAt body "command sequence has no source range"
102-  let fileName ← getFileName
103-  let fileMap ← getFileMap
104-  -- Recall that `rawIndentedLineFn` may consume whitespaces after the newline.
105-  -- Here we move the ending back to the last non-whitespace character to produce
106-  -- correctly positioned diagnostics.
107-  let stopPos := source.trimRight.stopPos
108-  if h : stopPos ≤ fileMap.source.rawEndPos then
109-    let ictx := InputContext.mk fileMap.source fileName
110-      (fileMap := fileMap) (endPos := stopPos) (endPos_valid := h)
111-    runRawCmdsAux ictx { pos := source.startPos, recovering := false, hasLeading := false }
112-  else
113-    throwErrorAt body "invalid command-sequence source range"
114-
115-end IndentedCommands
116-
117-end
118-
119-public meta section
120-
121-open Parser IndentedCommands
122-
123-/--
124-Elaborates the enclosed commands and reports their diagnostics,
125-but discards their effects afterwards.
126-
127-Example:
128-```lean
129-sf_experiment
130-  def hidden : Nat := 1
131-  #check hidden
132--- `hidden` is not available here.
133-```
134--/
135-def experimentTk := leading_parser
136-  "sf_experiment"
137-
138-@[command_parser] def experimentCmd := leading_parser
139-  experimentTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
140-    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
141-
142-/--
143-Succeeds only if the enclosed commands fail.
144-Diagnostics from the expected failure are suppressed.
145-
146-Example:
147-```lean
148-sf_expect_failure_in
149-  example : 1 = 2 := rfl
150-```
151--/
152-def expectFailureTk := leading_parser
153-  "sf_expect_failure_in"
154-
155-/-
156-  Like `sf_expect_failure_in` but reports the diagnostics.
157--/
158-def expectFailureInfoTk := leading_parser
159-  "sf_expect_failure_in?"
160-
161-@[command_parser] def expectFailureCmd := leading_parser
162-  expectFailureTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
163-    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
164-
165-@[command_parser] def expectFailureInfoCmd := leading_parser
166-  expectFailureInfoTk >> checkLinebreakBefore "indented command sequence" >>
167-    checkColGt "indented command sequence" >> withPosition rawCommandBlock
168-
169-@[command_elab experimentCmd]
170-def elabExperimentCmd : CommandElab := fun stx => do
171-  let body := stx.getArgs.back!
172-  commandWithoutAsync <| withRestoringState true do
173-    runRawCmds body
174-
175-@[command_elab expectFailureCmd, command_elab expectFailureInfoCmd]
176-def elabExpectFailureCmd : CommandElab := fun stx => do
177-  let keepMsgs := stx.isOfKind ``expectFailureInfoCmd
178-  unless keepMsgs || stx.isOfKind ``expectFailureCmd do
179-    throwUnsupportedSyntax
180-  let tk := stx[0]
181-  let body := stx.getArgs.back!
182-  commandWithoutAsync <| withRestoringState keepMsgs do
183-    withRef tk <| failIfSucceeds <| runRawCmds body
184-
185-end

1-module
2-
3--- For testing cases in this file
4-meta import all Init.Prelude
5-public meta import SFLCompat.Recall.Common
6-
7-/-!
8-# Recall, checked by elaboration
9-
10-`sf_recall` lets a chapter restate a definition from earlier in the
11-development while the build checks that the restatement means the same
12-thing. The restated declaration is elaborated for real, inside a hidden
13-namespace, and compared with the original up to definitional equality; the
14-temporary declaration is then rolled back.
15-
16-Two forms:
17-
18-```
19-sf_recall
20-  def twice (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) : Nat := f <| f n
21-
22-sf_recall statement twice_id : twice id 3 = 3
23-```
24-
25-What is compared:
26-
27-* types, always;
28-* a `def`'s value, safety, and abbreviation status;
29-* an inductive's constructors, one by one (names, parameter and index
30-  counts, and each constructor's type);
31-* a structure's fields, field defaults, and type-class registration;
32-* a theorem's statement, never its proof.
33-
34-So a recalled definition may be reformatted or rephrased into something
35-definitionally equal, and a theorem may be reproved differently or, with
36-the `statement` form, restated without any proof. The command is global and
37-available wherever this module is imported.
38--/
39-
40-
41-namespace SFLCompat.Recall.Check
42-
43-open Lean Elab Command Meta
44-
45-meta section
46-
47-structure DeclId where
48-  /-- This could be a private name. -/
49-  actual : Name
50-  display : Name
51-
52-def DeclId.ofActual (actual : Name) : DeclId :=
53-  { actual, display := privateToUserName actual }
54-
55-/-- Look up the actual name in temp elaboration namespace -/
56-def tempDeclId (userName : Name) : CommandElabM DeclId := do
57-  let env ← getEnv
58-  let privateName := mkPrivateName env userName
59-  let actual ←
60-    if env.contains privateName then pure privateName
61-    else if env.contains userName then pure userName
62-    else throwError "the re-elaborated declaration '{userName}' was not found"
63-  return .ofActual actual
64-
65-def renameBackName (chk orig n : Name) : Name :=
66-  if chk.isPrefixOf n then n.replacePrefix chk orig
67-  else
68-    let chk := privateToUserName chk
69-    if chk.isPrefixOf n then n.replacePrefix chk orig else n
70-
71-/--
72-Replaces the name prefix `chk` with `orig` in every constant that `e`
73-mentions: `chk` itself becomes `orig`, and a longer name such as a hidden
74-constructor `chk.mk` becomes `orig.mk`. Constructor types mention the
75-hidden inductive type's name in argument and resulting positions, so this
76-rewrite is what makes a re-elaborated declaration comparable with the
77-original.
78--/
79-def renameBack (chk orig : DeclId) (e : Expr) : Expr :=
80-  e.replace fun
81-    | .const n us =>
82-      let n' := renameBackName chk.actual orig.actual n
83-      if n == n' then none else some (.const n' us)
84-    | _ => none
85-
86-/--
87-Applies `renameBack` to the expressions recorded in an info tree. The info
88-recorded while elaborating the hidden copy mentions the hidden constants,
89-so hovers over a recalled declaration would otherwise display the hidden
90-names; rewriting before the trees are stored makes them display the
91-originals, which also exist after the hidden copy is rolled back.
92--/
93-partial def renameBackInfoTree (chk orig : DeclId) (t : InfoTree) : InfoTree :=
94-  match t with
95-  | .context (.parentDeclCtx n) t' =>
96-    .context (.parentDeclCtx (renameBackName chk.actual orig.actual n))
97-      (renameBackInfoTree chk orig t')
98-  | .context ctx t' => .context ctx (renameBackInfoTree chk orig t')
99-  | .node i children =>
100-    let i := match i with
101-      | .ofTermInfo ti => .ofTermInfo (reTerm ti)
102-      | .ofDelabTermInfo dti => .ofDelabTermInfo { dti with toTermInfo := reTerm dti.toTermInfo }
103-      | other => other
104-    .node i (children.map (renameBackInfoTree chk orig))
105-  | .hole m => .hole m
106-where
107-  reTerm (ti : TermInfo) : TermInfo :=
108-    { ti with
109-      expr := renameBack chk orig ti.expr
110-      expectedType? := ti.expectedType?.map (renameBack chk orig) }
111-
112-/--
113-Checks that the types of the original constant `x` and its re-elaborated
114-counterpart `chk` agree, definitionally. The restated type is first
115-rewritten by `renameBack renChk renOrig`; the defaults compare a
116-declaration against its own hidden copy, and the constructor check
117-overrides them with the enclosing inductive types, whose names the
118-constructor types mention. The restatement's universe parameters are
119-instantiated with the original's.
120--/
121-def checkTypesMatch (x chk : DeclId) (ref : Syntax)
122-    (renChk : DeclId := chk) (renOrig : DeclId := x) (hint : MessageData := .nil) :
123-    TermElabM Unit := do
124-  let origInfo ← getConstInfo x.actual
125-  let chkInfo ← getConstInfo chk.actual
126-  unless origInfo.levelParams.length == chkInfo.levelParams.length do
127-    throwErrorAt ref (m!"universe parameters of '{x.display}' do not match" ++ hint)
128-  let chkType := (renameBack renChk renOrig chkInfo.type).instantiateLevelParams
129-    chkInfo.levelParams (origInfo.levelParams.map .param)
130-  unless ← isDefEq chkType origInfo.type do
131-    throwErrorAt ref
132-      (m!"the statement of '{x.display}' does not match.\n\
133-          Original:{indentD origInfo.type}\nRestated:{indentD chkType}" ++ hint)
134-
135-/--
136-All constructor syntax nodes of a command, in source order: an inductive
137-type's `| name : ...` alternatives and a structure's `name ::` header.
138--/
139-partial def ctorStxs (stx : Syntax) : Array Syntax :=
140-  let inner := stx.getArgs.flatMap ctorStxs
141-  if stx.isOfKind ``Lean.Parser.Command.ctor
142-      || stx.isOfKind ``Lean.Parser.Command.structCtor then
143-    #[stx] ++ inner
144-  else inner
145-
146-/-- Does the syntax contain a doc comment? -/
147-def hasDocComment (stx : Syntax) : Bool :=
148-  (stx.find? (·.isOfKind ``Lean.Parser.Command.docComment)).isSome
149-
150-/--
151-Suggestions localized to a mismatched constructor, returned as a pair of
152-hints for name errors and for type errors. An inductive type's `| name : ...` alternative is replaced
153-with the original constructor's own source. A structure's `name ::` header
154-can carry a name fix but not a field fix, so its type errors keep `outer`,
155-the suggestion that replaces the whole restatement. A constructor without
156-syntax also falls back to `outer`.
157--/
158-def ctorHints (ctorRef : Syntax) (origCtor origShort : Name) (outer : MessageData) :
159-    TermElabM (MessageData × MessageData) := do
160-  try
161-    if ctorRef.isOfKind ``Lean.Parser.Command.ctor then
162-      let origSrc := dedent (← sourceOf origCtor)
163-      -- A restatement without a doc comment gets a suggestion without one;
164-      -- the meaning check does not compare documentation.
165-      let origSrc := if hasDocComment ctorRef then origSrc
166-        else stripLeadingComments origSrc
167-      let restatedSrc ← sourceOfSyntax ctorRef
168-      let h ← replaceWithOriginalHint ctorRef origSrc restatedSrc
169-      return (h, h)
170-    if ctorRef.isOfKind ``Lean.Parser.Command.structCtor then
171-      let restatedSrc ← sourceOfSyntax ctorRef
172-      let h ← replaceWithOriginalHint ctorRef s!"{origShort} ::" restatedSrc
173-      return (h, outer)
174-    return (outer, outer)
175-  catch _ => return (outer, outer)
176-
177-/--
178-Checks a re-elaborated declaration against the original, definitionally.
179-Errors point at `ref`, the restated command, except for constructor
180-mismatches, which point at the offending constructor within it.
181--/
182-def checkMatch (x chk : DeclId) (ref : Syntax) (hint : MessageData := .nil) :
183-    TermElabM Unit := do
184-  checkTypesMatch x chk ref (hint := hint)
185-  let origInfo ← getConstInfo x.actual
186-  let chkInfo ← getConstInfo chk.actual
187-  match origInfo, chkInfo with
188-  | .defnInfo orig, .defnInfo restated =>
189-    let chkVal := (renameBack chk x restated.value).instantiateLevelParams
190-      restated.levelParams (orig.levelParams.map .param)
191-    unless ← isDefEq chkVal orig.value do
192-      throwErrorAt ref
193-        (m!"the value of '{x.display}' does not match.\n\
194-            Original:{indentD orig.value}\nRestated:{indentD chkVal}" ++ hint)
195-  | .inductInfo orig, .inductInfo restated =>
196-    unless orig.numParams == restated.numParams && orig.numIndices == restated.numIndices do
197-      throwErrorAt ref (m!"parameters or indices of '{x.display}' do not match" ++ hint)
198-    unless orig.ctors.length == restated.ctors.length do
199-      throwErrorAt ref
200-        (m!"'{x.display}' has {orig.ctors.length} constructors, \
201-            the restatement has {restated.ctors.length}" ++ hint)
202-    -- A `structure` that writes no `name ::` header has a constructor
203-    -- without syntax; the whole command remains the fallback position.
204-    let ctorRefs := ctorStxs ref
205-    let mut i := 0
206-    for origCtorActual in orig.ctors, chkCtorActual in restated.ctors do
207-      let origCtor := DeclId.ofActual origCtorActual
208-      let chkCtor := DeclId.ofActual chkCtorActual
209-      let ctorRef := ctorRefs[i]?.getD ref
210-      let origShort := origCtor.actual.replacePrefix x.actual .anonymous
211-      let (nameHint, typeHint) ← ctorHints ctorRef origCtor.actual origShort hint
212-      let renamedChkCtor := DeclId.ofActual <|
213-        chkCtor.actual.replacePrefix chk.actual x.actual
214-      unless origCtor.actual == renamedChkCtor.actual do
215-        throwErrorAt ctorRef
216-          (m!"constructor '{renamedChkCtor.display}' does not match \
217-              '{origCtor.display}'" ++ nameHint)
218-      checkTypesMatch origCtor chkCtor ctorRef (renChk := chk) (renOrig := x) (hint := typeHint)
219-      i := i + 1
220-    -- A structure's field names are part of its interface, and the
221-    -- constructor's type does not record them, so they are compared
222-    -- through the environment's structure information.
223-    let env ← getEnv
224-    match getStructureInfo? env x.actual, getStructureInfo? env chk.actual with
225-    | some origSi, some chkSi =>
226-      let origFields := origSi.fieldNames.map DeclId.ofActual
227-      let chkFields := chkSi.fieldNames.map DeclId.ofActual
228-      unless origFields.map (·.actual) == chkFields.map (·.actual) do
229-        throwErrorAt ref
230-          (m!"the fields of '{x.display}' do not match.\n\
231-              Original:{indentD (toMessageData (origFields.map (·.display)).toList)}\n\
232-              Restated:{indentD (toMessageData (chkFields.map (·.display)).toList)}" ++ hint)
233-      unless getOutParamPositions? env x.actual == getOutParamPositions? env chk.actual
234-          && getOutLevelParamPositions? env x.actual == getOutLevelParamPositions? env chk.actual do
235-        throwErrorAt ref (m!"the type-class metadata of '{x.display}' does not match" ++ hint)
236-    | some _, none =>
237-      throwErrorAt ref (m!"'{x.display}' is a structure, but the restatement is not" ++ hint)
238-    | none, some _ =>
239-      throwErrorAt ref (m!"'{x.display}' is not a structure, but the restatement is one" ++ hint)
240-    | none, none => pure ()
241-  -- A theorem's proof is not compared; restating it as a `def` is also
242-  -- accepted, since only the statement matters.
243-  | .thmInfo _, .thmInfo _ => pure ()
244-  | .thmInfo _, .defnInfo _ => pure ()
245-  | .axiomInfo _, .axiomInfo _ => pure ()
246-  | .opaqueInfo _, .opaqueInfo _ => pure ()
247-  | _, _ =>
248-    throwErrorAt ref
249-      (m!"'{x.display}' and its restatement are different kinds of declaration" ++ hint)
250-
251-/--
252-`sf_recall` restates a definition from earlier in the development and checks
253-that the restatement means the same thing. `sf_recall statement x : T` checks
254-that `T` matches the statement of the theorem `x`.
255--/
256-syntax (name := recallChk) "sf_recall " command : command
257-
258-@[inherit_doc recallChk]
259-syntax (name := recallChkStmt) "sf_recall " &"statement " ident " : " term : command
260-
261-elab_rules : command
262-  | `(sf_recall $cmd:command) => do
263-    let decl ← declaredName cmd
264-    let xActual ← liftCoreM <| withoutExporting <|
265-      realizeGlobalConstNoOverloadWithInfo decl.ident
266-    let x := DeclId.ofActual xActual
267-    -- The restatement elaborates unchanged inside a fresh hidden namespace:
268-    -- self-references (an inductive's own name in its constructor types, in
269-    -- resulting-type position included) resolve to the hidden copy, and
270-    -- every other name resolves as it would at the recall site. The
271-    -- namespace comes from the name generator: `_uniq` names cannot be
272-    -- written in source, so it is collision-free, and unlike a macro-scoped
273-    -- name it is an ordinary component, so declarations under it keep the
274-    -- prefix structure that `renameBack` and the constructor comparison
275-    -- rely on.
276-    let ns ← liftCoreM (mkFreshId : CoreM Name)
277-    -- Any mismatch gets a clickable fix: replace the restatement with the
278-    -- original's source text, indented like the restatement. The helpers
279-    -- for recovering and re-indenting source are shared with the
280-    -- byte-for-byte variant.
281-    -- A failed hint must not fail the check: not every constant has a
282-    -- declaration range or sources on the search path.
283-    let hint ←
284-      try
285-        let original := dedent (← sourceOf x.actual)
286-        let original := if hasDocComment cmd then original
287-          else stripLeadingComments original
288-        let restated ← sourceOfSyntax cmd
289-        liftCoreM <| replaceWithOriginalHint cmd original restated
290-      catch _ => pure .nil
291-    let envBefore ← getEnv
292-    try
293-      let chk ← withScope (fun sc => { sc with currNamespace := sc.currNamespace ++ ns }) do
294-        let saved ← getResetInfoTrees
295-        try
296-          elabCommand cmd
297-          -- this could be a private name
298-          let userName := (← getScope).currNamespace ++ decl.written
299-          let chk ← tempDeclId userName
300-          let inner ← getResetInfoTrees
301-          modifyInfoState fun s => { s with trees := saved ++ inner.map (renameBackInfoTree chk x) }
302-          return chk
303-        catch e =>
304-          let inner ← getResetInfoTrees
305-          modifyInfoState fun s => { s with trees := saved ++ inner }
306-          throw e
307-      runTermElabM fun _ => checkMatch x chk cmd (hint := hint)
308-    finally
309-      setEnv envBefore
310-  | `(sf_recall statement $ident:ident : $stmt:term) => do
311-    let xActual ← liftCoreM <| withoutExporting <|
312-      realizeGlobalConstNoOverloadWithInfo ident
313-    let x := DeclId.ofActual xActual
314-    addConstInfo ident x.actual
315-    let region := mkNullNode #[ident.raw, stmt.raw]
316-    let restated ← sourceOfSyntax region
317-    runTermElabM fun _ => do
318-      -- The suggestion restates the original's type as the pretty-printer
319-      -- renders it. The statement cannot be carved out of the original's
320-      -- source, since finding its boundary would require parsing the
321-      -- source in the elaboration context of its declaration site.
322-      let hint ←
323-        try
324-          let origInfo ← getConstInfo x.actual
325-          let printed ← ppExpr origInfo.type
326-          replaceWithOriginalHint region
327-            s!"{ident.getId} : {printed}" restated
328-        catch _ => pure .nil
329-      let t ← Term.elabType stmt
330-      Term.synthesizeSyntheticMVarsNoPostponing
331-      -- Remaining level metavariables become parameters, so the restatement
332-      -- must carry as many universe parameters as the original; comparing
333-      -- against fresh level metavariables instead would let a fixed
334-      -- universe pass for a polymorphic original.
335-      let t ← instantiateMVars (← Term.levelMVarToParam t)
336-      let origInfo ← getConstInfo x.actual
337-      let stParams := (collectLevelParams {} t).params
338-      unless stParams.size == origInfo.levelParams.length do
339-        throwErrorAt stmt
340-          (m!"universe parameters of '{x.display}' do not match" ++ hint)
341-      let t := t.instantiateLevelParams stParams.toList
342-        (origInfo.levelParams.map .param)
343-      unless ← isDefEq t origInfo.type do
344-        throwErrorAt stmt
345-          (m!"the restated statement of '{x.display}' does not match.\n\
346-              Original:{indentD origInfo.type}\nRestated:{indentD t}" ++ hint)
347-
348-end
